PHCC's briefing on the 2024/25 release states that for the first time since the NZHS began, daily smoking remained the same (within 0.1%) for three consecutive years and that 'progress in reducing daily smoking prevalence has stalled'; Smokefree.org.nz says rates 'have plateaued over the past three years'. Checked for the opposite: the long-run decline from 16.4% in 2011/12 is genuine, and 6.9->6.8 is a nominal 0.1pp fall, but it is within the confidence interval and is officially characterised as no change, which is exactly the 'flattens' branch of the criterion.

statement: If those trends continue, New Zealand will hit the deadline smokefree goal of less than 5 percent of the population daily by 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 measurement year: true if below 5 percent of adults, false if 5 percent or above.
reasoning: Criterion: NZHS daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 measurement year, true if below 5% of adults. The NZHS 2024/25 (July 2024-June 2025) reports 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4), about 294,000 daily smokers - well above 5%, and far above it for Maori (15.0%), Pacific peoples (10.3%) and the most deprived quintile (12.9%). PHCC concludes the findings 'strongly suggest that the government's goal to reach a daily smoking prevalence of less than 5% for all population groups will not be achieved'. No reading of the available NZHS data puts the 2025 rate under 5%.

statement: It’s going to be Māori people, Pacific people, low socio-economic people who will be hugely impacted by this.
criterion: Ministry of Health / NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence broken down by ethnicity and deprivation quintile for the years following the repeal: true if Māori, Pacific and high-deprivation prevalence stalls or rises relative to the pre-repeal trend while other groups continue to fall, false if those groups' prevalence continues declining at or above the pre-repeal trend.
reasoning: Criterion requires NZHS prevalence by ethnicity and deprivation 'for the years following the repeal', with Maori/Pacific/high-deprivation stalling or rising WHILE other groups continue to fall. Only one full post-repeal survey year is published (2024/25, released late 2025); the 2025/26 and 2026/27 releases the criterion needs are not out, and the resolve-by date of 2027-06-30 has not passed. What exists does not establish the differential either way: Maori 17.1% (2022/23) -> 14.7% (2023/24) -> 15.0% (2024/25); Pacific 18.1% -> 12.3% -> 10.3%; European/Other 6.1% -> 6.1% -> 5.7%; most deprived quintile 12.9% in 2024/25. The overall rate stalled for all groups, not selectively, and Pacific prevalence is still falling - disconfirming evidence for the claim so far, but with wide confidence intervals and one data point it settles nothing.

statement: But the really simple question for them, which they have not been able to front up to and be honest with the New Zealand public about, is that this legislation will—must, by virtue of the evidence and the advice that they themselves have commissioned—result in a slower decline in rates of smoking in this country.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence series: true if the average annual percentage-point decline in the years following the March 2024 repeal is smaller than the average annual decline over the 2019–2023 period; false if the decline holds steady or accelerates.
reasoning: NZHS adult daily smoking: 2019/20 11.6%, 2021/22 8.0%, 2022/23 6.8%, 2023/24 6.9%, 2024/25 6.8%. The 2019-2023 average annual fall was ~1.6 pp/yr; the one published post-repeal year (2024/25) fell 0.1 pp, and PHCC/MoH describe the rate as plateaued for three consecutive years. So the criterion's comparison (post-repeal decline smaller than 2019-2023) is met. Downgraded from 'correct' for two reasons: only one of the post-repeal years in the resolve-by-2028 window is published (2025/26 is still in the field), and the flattening began in 2023/24 — a survey year running Jul 2023-Jul 2024, mostly before the 27 Feb 2024 repeal, and before any repealed measure (denicotinisation, retailer reduction, smokefree generation, all scheduled for 2025-2027) had taken effect. The slower decline is real; Swarbrick's stated causal mechanism ('must, by virtue of the evidence') is not what the data isolate.

statement: If these trends continue, New Zealand will hit the smoke-free goal of less than 5 percent of the population smoking daily by 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2024/25 or 2025/26 year; true if the published daily smoking rate is below 5.0%, false if it is 5.0% or above.
reasoning: The criterion allows either the 2024/25 or 2025/26 NZHS year. 2024/25, released 19 November 2025, puts adult daily smoking at 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4), ~294,000 people — well above 5.0%. 2025/26 is not yet published (fieldwork Jul 2025-Jul 2026), but daily smoking has been flat within 0.1 pp for three consecutive years (6.8 / 6.9 / 6.8) and reaching under 5% would have needed ~80,000 extra quitters against a historic 20,000-40,000 per year; commentary and the Ministry both treat Smokefree 2025 as missed. The trends Campbell relied on did not continue.

statement: As Dr Campbell said, we are on track to reach Smokefree 2025, where 5 percent or less smoke.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the survey year covering 2025: true if it is 5 percent or less, false if it is above 5 percent.
reasoning: The survey year covering 2025 is NZHS 2024/25 (collected Jul 2024-Jul 2025, published 19 Nov 2025): adult daily smoking 6.8%, above the 5% threshold the criterion sets. New Zealand was not on track — the rate has been static at 6.8-6.9% since 2022/23, and the Smokefree 2025 goal was missed, on the Ministry's own series and on the Smokefree Aotearoa all-population-groups definition (Maori 15.0%, Pacific 10.3%).

statement: They have halved smoking in New Zealand in the last 10 years, and they will get us through the next 10 as well.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence in 2033/34 compared with 2023/24; true if the rate has continued to fall substantially (reaching or approaching the 5% Smokefree goal), false if it plateaus or rises.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against the 2033/34 NZ Health Survey, eight years away. Interim data cut against the prediction rather than supporting it: adult daily smoking was 6.8% (2022/23), 6.9% (2023/24) and 6.8% (2024/25) — the first three-year plateau since the survey began in 2011/12 (16.4%), and the Smokefree 2025 <5% goal was missed (Maori 15.0%, Pacific 10.3%). Nothing yet settles the 2033/34 comparison.

statement: So we are ending up with, instead of being on the track for a reduced number of people as a result of the plan that this Government is now repealing, more people going to be smoking than otherwise would.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence together with published Ministry of Health or peer-reviewed modelling of the repeal; true if observed prevalence exceeds the projected path under the retained measures, false if prevalence matches or beats that projected path.
reasoning: The criterion requires observed NZHS prevalence compared against a published Ministry of Health or peer-reviewed projected path under the retained measures. That comparison does not yet exist — the endgame measures (denicotinisation, retail reduction, smokefree generation) were repealed on 5 March 2024 before taking effect, and I found no published modelling of the post-repeal counterfactual path; existing modelling compares the pre-repeal package to business-as-usual, and one study estimates NZ$12.4b extra industry revenue to 2040 under repeal, which is not the prevalence comparison the criterion names. Observed prevalence has plateaued (6.8/6.9/6.8), directionally consistent with the claim but not a resolution. The 2027-06-30 date has not passed and the 2025/26 survey is not yet out.

statement: Our ability to sell and our reputation at the international markets will be degraded by passing this legislation that will increase the number of people smoking and taking up tobacco and will have unlimited levels of nicotine and products that will drive addiction.
criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the years following the repeal, plus any documented market-access or trade barrier arising from it; true if smoking prevalence rises above its pre-repeal level or a trade/market consequence is documented, false if prevalence continues its downward trend and no trade consequence is recorded.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-12-31 and neither limb of the criterion is met yet. Prevalence has not risen above its pre-repeal level: 6.8% in 2022/23 (pre-repeal) and 6.8% in 2024/25, with 6.9% in between — a plateau, not an increase. And I found no documented trade barrier or market-access consequence to NZ exports arising from the repeal; searches on trade/export effects returned only health-policy commentary. The one documented reputational effect is NZ falling from 2nd to 53rd on the 2025 Global Tobacco Industry Interference Index, which speaks to standing on FCTC implementation rather than to the 'ability to sell' O'Connor predicted. On evidence to date the claim is trending toward wrong, but the criterion's window is still open.

statement: In an earlier response, the Minister said that the goal was to reduce smoking rates, which is why we are repealing this, and I can’t quite understand that, because, actually, the evidence that I’ve seen is that repealing this won’t lead to reducing smoking rates to the extent that we need to in order to achieve the goals.
criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence by population group: true if prevalence fails to reach under 5 percent across all populations (notably Māori and Pacific) by the Smokefree 2025 target date, false if the under-5-percent goal is met across all groups.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether daily smoking prevalence failed to reach under 5% across all population groups by the Smokefree 2025 target date. The 2024/25 NZ Health Survey (the survey year ending June 2025) reports total adult daily smoking at 6.8%, Māori 15.0%, Pacific 10.3%, European/Other 5.7%, Asian 4.5% — every group except Asian is above 5%, and the total is well above. Prevalence has been flat at 6.8-6.9% for three consecutive survey years, so no path to <5% by end-2025 existed. PHCC, ASH and University of Auckland commentary all state the goal will not be / was not achieved, missed 'by a substantial margin for Māori and Pacific peoples'. Boyack's prediction that the repeal would not deliver the reduction needed to hit the goal is borne out on the criterion as written. Caveat noted for completeness: the criterion is about goal attainment, not causation, and separate 2026 analysis finds the plateau predates the repeal — so this verdict does not establish that the repeal caused the miss.

statement: We are, as many members have indicated, left with going backwards in terms of the number of people who will now suffer smoking-related illnesses or will take up smoking.
criterion: Ministry of Health New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the years following the February 2024 repeal, together with Ministry of Health smoking-attributable mortality/hospitalisation reporting; true if daily smoking prevalence rises, or its year-on-year decline halts, in any two consecutive survey years after the repeal, false if prevalence continues to fall year on year through to the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The criterion's 'true' limb is met in part: NZHS daily smoking prevalence was 6.8% (2022/23), 6.9% (2023/24) and 6.8% (2024/25) — the decline has halted, and the only available post-repeal year-on-year comparison (2023/24 to 2024/25) shows no decline, the first such plateau since the survey began. But the substance of Robertson's claim — that things go 'backwards', with more people suffering smoking-related illness or taking up smoking — is not supported. Prevalence has not risen; youth uptake has not risen (ASH Year 10 2025: daily smoking 1.1%, a record low, with 89.4% never-smokers); and no Ministry of Health smoking-attributable mortality or hospitalisation series yet shows a post-repeal increase. Crucially for attribution, a 2026 Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific joinpoint analysis finds no statistically significant change in trend from 2022/23 onward — the plateau predates the February 2024 repeal and is better explained by compositional saturation among remaining smokers. Only one full post-repeal survey year (2024/25) exists; 2025/26 is not published, and the resolve-by date is 2028-06-30, so the two-consecutive-post-repeal-years test cannot yet be run strictly. Stalled progress: yes. Going backwards, and because of the repeal: not shown.

statement: I’m suggesting this because we’ve heard through the policy debates that we’ve had in the House today—and, of course, that we had in the House in 2022—that the point of the legislation that has been repealed was to make us achieve those targets and that the impact of this repeal will be that those targets will not be met.
criterion: Ministry of Health / New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for 2025; the Smokefree 2025 goal is under 5% daily smoking for the total population and for each population group. False if the published figures show the goal met by 2025, true if prevalence (overall or for Māori and Pacific populations) remains at or above 5%.
reasoning: The criterion: false if published figures show the Smokefree 2025 goal (<5% daily smoking for the total population and each population group) met by 2025; true if prevalence overall or for Māori and Pacific remains at or above 5%. The 2024/25 NZ Health Survey reports 6.8% total, Māori 15.0%, Pacific 10.3% — all at or above 5%, and the rate has been flat at 6.8-6.9% across 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25. PHCC's briefing states the findings 'strongly suggest' the goal will not be achieved and will be 'missed by a substantial margin for Māori and Pacific peoples'; September 2026 University of Auckland/Newsroom commentary refers to 'our failure to achieve Smokefree 2025' as settled. One limitation: the survey year covering the second half of calendar 2025 (2025/26) is not published until late 2026, so the last word on calendar-2025 is not yet in print — but with the total three times the target and Māori at three times again, the margin removes any doubt. Brooking's prediction that the targets would not be met holds. As with item 67, the criterion tests attainment, not causation; the 2026 Lancet analysis finds the plateau predates the repeal, so this does not confirm the repeal was the cause.

statement: Like other forecasters, the NZIER is expecting near-term weakness in the economy but recovery over the longer term.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series; true if 2024 shows at least two quarters of contraction or flat growth and 2025 shows sustained positive quarterly growth, false if growth is sustained through 2024 or if no recovery appears by end-2025.
reasoning: Near-term weakness: confirmed. Stats NZ production GDP contracted in both the June 2024 (-1.1%) and September 2024 (-1.0%) quarters, satisfying the criterion's 'at least two quarters of contraction in 2024'. Longer-term recovery: arrived, but 2025 was NOT sustained positive quarterly growth as the criterion's true-branch requires — Mar 2025 +0.9%, Jun 2025 -0.9% (a sharp broad-based contraction, 10 of 16 industries down), Sep 2025 +1.1%, Dec 2025 +0.2% (subsequently revised to +0.5%). Growth continued into 2026 (Mar +0.8/0.9%, Jun +0.2%). Neither false-branch fires: growth was not sustained through 2024, and a recovery clearly had appeared by end-2025. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for evidence that 2024 growth held up (it did not — the June 2024 quarter was revised down from -0.2% to -1.1%) and that no recovery came (it did, from the Sept 2025 quarter on). So the substance holds, but the recovery was interrupted by a further contraction rather than being the sustained 2025 upswing the criterion specifies.

statement: This is a bill that will kill people; it is a bill that will increase smoking in New Zealand.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence in the years after the repeal takes effect; true if prevalence rises above the 2022/23 level of 6.8 percent in a subsequent survey year, false if it continues to fall.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 2027-06-30 and the relevant post-repeal survey years are not all in. Available NZ Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence: 2022/23 6.8%, 2023/24 6.9%, 2024/25 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4, ~294,000 people). The repeal took effect in early 2024, so 2024/25 is the first full post-repeal survey year and it sits exactly at the 6.8% baseline, not above it. The 2023/24 reading of 6.9% is nominally above 6.8% but is within 0.1pp (inside the confidence interval) and covers a period mostly preceding the repeal, so it does not satisfy 'rises above' in any meaningful sense. The criterion's false-branch ('continues to fall') has also not been met: for the first time since the survey began, daily smoking has been flat for three consecutive years, and commentators describe progress as stalled. The 2025/26 survey (due around late 2026) and 2026/27 fall inside the resolution window. Disconfirming check: I searched for reports of smoking rates rising after the repeal and found none — the finding is a plateau, not an increase. The 'will kill people' element is not addressed by this criterion, which restricts resolution to prevalence.

statement: In answer to the Deputy Prime Minister’s supplementary question, he makes a good point, which is that the revenue that the coalition Government is likely to receive from tobacco revenue in the forecast future years will be considerably less than was received by the previous Labour administration in 2020, where they earned $2.2 billion in tobacco excise revenue, which they happily invested in roads, hospitals, schools, and the like.
criterion: Treasury forecast and outturn tobacco excise revenue for the forecast years 2024/25 to 2027/28; true if annual tobacco excise revenue in those years is materially below the 2020 level she cites, false if it holds at or above it.
reasoning: Her baseline checks out: tobacco excise revenue peaked at about $2.17b in 2020, so '$2.2 billion' is accurate to the rounding. Revenue has fallen steadily since: $1.86b (2022), $1.66b (2023), $1.47b (2024), and $1.47b in 2024/25 per Treasury. For 2025/26, actual excise receipts to 31 March 2026 were $210m (17.1%) below the same period a year earlier, implying roughly $1.2b for the year — about 45% below the 2020 level. Treasury's Budget Economic and Fiscal Update 2026 cut the tobacco excise forecast by a further $1.58b across the forecast period, citing a weaker demand profile, so the remaining forecast years (2026/27, 2027/28) are projected lower still, not higher. Disconfirming check: the only upward pressures identified are indexation increases in the excise rate itself, and these have been swamped by falling legal volumes (illicit tobacco is estimated to have cost around $817m in lost excise and GST in the past year). Two of the four forecast years the criterion names are now observed and both are materially below the 2020 level; there is no plausible path back to $2.2b. Resolve-by 2028-06-30 has not passed, but the false-branch ('holds at or above it') is already ruled out for the observed years and contradicted by the current forecasts.

statement: On the way we’re going, we will reach our goal of having the average under 5 percent by 2025.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence covering 2025; true if the published rate is below 5 percent, false if it is 5 percent or higher.
reasoning: The 2024/25 New Zealand Health Survey reports adult daily smoking prevalence of 6.8% (95% CI 6.2-7.4), about 294,000 people — well above the 5% Smokefree goal. The trajectory Uffindell invoked also did not hold: the rate has been statistically flat at 6.8-6.9% across 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25, the first plateau since the survey began, after falling from 16.4% in 2011/12. The PHCC briefing on the same data concludes the <5% goal 'will not be achieved'. The 2025/26 survey (covering Jul 2025-Jun 2026) is not yet published, but a drop from 6.8% to under 5% in a single year is not plausible against a three-year plateau, and the published NZHS figure covering 2025 is 6.8%.

statement: If you read Hāpai te Hauora’s comments on this particular kaupapa, Māori will not reach the 5 percent target for a smoke-free 2025.
criterion: Ministry of Health / New Zealand Health Survey reporting of Māori adult daily smoking prevalence for 2025; the forecast is true if that prevalence is still above 5% when the 2025 figures are published, false if it is at or below 5%.
reasoning: Māori adult daily smoking prevalence in the 2024/25 New Zealand Health Survey is 15.0% (95% CI 13.2-17.0), roughly 99,000 people — three times the 5% target and the highest of any ethnic group alongside Pacific peoples at 10.3%. The PHCC briefing states the goal will be 'missed by a substantial margin for Māori and Pacific peoples'. Checked for the opposite: Māori rates have genuinely roughly halved over five years and ASH NZ reports them still declining while the national rate plateaus, but no published figure puts Māori prevalence anywhere near 5% for 2025.

statement: It will be delivered under the coalition Government in 2026—unlike light rail, or “light fail”, as I call it: $228 million and not one metre of track laid after six years, spinning the wheels on the ghost train in Auckland and not getting anywhere.
criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport opening records; true if CRL is delivered and opens for passenger service during calendar year 2026, false if delivery slips into 2027 or later.
reasoning: The City Rail Link was formally opened on 11 September 2026 by the Prime Minister and Auckland Mayor, and public passenger services began on 13 September 2026, with 528,007 boardings in the first week — a network record. Delivery therefore occurred within calendar year 2026 as the criterion requires, under the coalition Government. Judged only against the criterion as written, which covers CRL delivery timing and not the light-rail figures in the rest of the quote.

statement: Now, I’ve picked this date for a very specific reason, and the reason is that on 31 May 2025, Winston Peters will stop being the Deputy Prime Minister.
criterion: The official record of Deputy Prime Minister appointments (Governor-General's warrants / DPMC ministerial list); true if Winston Peters ceased to hold the office of Deputy Prime Minister on or about 31 May 2025, false if he remained in the role past that date.
reasoning: The official DPMC Ministerial List dated 31 May 2025 shows Hon David Seymour (ACT) holding the Deputy Prime Minister warrant, and Rt Hon Winston Peters listed under New Zealand First Ministers with only Foreign Affairs, Racing and Rail — no Deputy PM. Wikipedia's office list records Peters' term as 27 November 2023 – 31 May 2025 and Seymour's as beginning 31 May 2025, matching the coalition agreement's mid-term handover. Boyack named the date exactly right. Disconfirming check: no source shows Peters holding or resuming the DPM title after 31 May 2025.

statement: This is a reduction in the regulatory framework that protects the wider community from the impacts of tobacco and nicotine, and this will mean smokier environments.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the years following the repeal: true if prevalence rises, or the pre-repeal downward trend halts, relative to the 2023/24 baseline; false if daily smoking prevalence continues to fall.
reasoning: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence: 6.8% (2022/23), 6.9% (2023/24), 6.8% (2024/25). PHCC's analysis of the 2024/25 survey states that 'progress in reducing daily smoking prevalence has stalled' and that 'for the first time since the NZHS started, daily smoking rates remained the same (within 0.1%) for three consecutive years'; Smokefree.org.nz likewise says rates 'have plateaued over the past three years'. The criterion's second limb — the pre-repeal downward trend halting — is therefore satisfied, and the claim is not wrong. But it is materially overstated on two counts: prevalence did not rise (no measured increase in smoking), and the plateau began in 2022/23, before the repeal received Royal assent on 5 March 2024, so the stall cannot be attributed to the regulatory rollback Abel was describing. The 2025/26 survey would be the first read covering a fully post-repeal period.

statement: But, I tell you what, she probably won’t take a call because she has failed to do so since many of these issues have been raised.
criterion: Hansard record for the committee of the whole House stage of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill, 27 February 2024: false if Casey Costello takes a call on the part under debate before the committee stage closes; true if she does not speak again before the closure motion.
reasoning: The Hansard record for 'Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill — In Committee—Part 2' (27/28 February 2024) shows Tangi Utikere taking a call on Part 2 ('This is my first opportunity to take a call on what is Part 2') and questioning the Minister on clause 29, the repeal of the smokefree generation provisions. Hon Casey Costello, Associate Minister of Health, then took a call in reply on that same Part, saying 'We're not changing any other components of the smoking regulations that currently exist—we're only making amendments to things that are not yet in place', and that she could not 'see that there would be any logic to raise alarm about smoking increasing'. Lan Pham (Green) spoke after her. The criterion is explicit: false if Costello takes a call on the part under debate before the committee stage closes. She did. Caveat on method: parliament.nz is behind bot protection and would not serve the page to a direct fetch, so this rests on two independent search-engine reads of that Hansard page, which agreed on both the quotations and the running order.

statement: The answer to that is that this country’s supply of gas is imperilled for the next five years now, and no planning forward has been admitted—worse still, it’s been stopped.
criterion: MBIE gas production and supply statistics plus Gas Industry Company reporting to 2029: true if New Zealand experiences material gas supply shortfalls or curtailment of industrial gas users during the period; false if supply meets demand without curtailment or shortfall notices.
reasoning: The criterion's true-branch (material shortfalls or curtailment of industrial gas users in 2024-2029) has already been met well inside the window. MBIE: gas supply fell 20.9% in 2024 (115.70 PJ), reserves down 27% at 1 Jan 2025 and a further 23% at 1 Jan 2026; MBIE itself says supply is 'reducing faster and sooner than previously forecast'. Curtailment is documented: Methanex idled Motunui Aug-Oct 2024 and again for ~7 weeks mid-May to end-June 2025, on-selling contracted gas to Genesis/Contact; Ballance was outbid for Kapuni's gas and warned it may shut the urea plant; RNZ reports roughly half of surveyed gas consumers (31 of 66) cut operations, raised prices or cut staff. Gas Industry Co. modelled a shortfall of up to ~40 PJ even with LNG imports. The false-branch (supply meets demand without curtailment) is excluded. The quote's second clause about planning being 'stopped' is political characterisation the criterion does not cover.

statement: As a result, the economy will almost certainly be in a weaker position this year than was anticipated before Christmas, and this has a direct flow-on to tax revenue.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP releases and Treasury's Budget 2024 / Pre-election forecasts for calendar 2024, compared against the December 2023 HYEFU track: true if actual GDP growth and tax revenue for 2024 come in below the HYEFU forecast; false if they meet or exceed it.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion resolve against the December 2023 HYEFU track. Stats NZ reports GDP fell 0.5% over the year ended December 2024 versus the year ended December 2023, with deep contractions in the June (-1.1% revised) and September (-1.0%) quarters that far exceeded forecaster expectations; HYEFU 2023 had assumed growth. On tax: Treasury's Budget Policy Statement 2024 stated that September-quarter 2023 GDP released after HYEFU was 'much lower than forecasters had predicted' and that the economy was 'materially weaker in recent years than previously thought', and BEFU 2024 forecast core Crown tax revenue lower than HYEFU 2023 across the forecast period on a softer economic outlook, delaying the OBEGAL surplus by a year. No source indicates 2024 met or exceeded the HYEFU track.

statement: They are unlikely to be made available to the select committee in a four-week process.
criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill and the departmental advice published with it: false if modelling of the policy's effect on fleet emissions was provided to the committee before it reported back, true if no such figures were supplied.
reasoning: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee received the bill on 5 March 2024 and reported back on 14 March 2024 (an eight-day process, submissions closed 7 March, 518 submissions, 19 oral submitters). Advice came from the Ministry of Transport and NZTA and focused on the RUC discount rate for BEVs and PHEVs; the evidence on the appropriate discount rate was described as limited. No modelling of the policy's effect on fleet emissions appears in the report or the published advice: Labour's differing view records that the modelling sought from the Ministry of Transport or the Climate Change Commission on the change's impact on emissions budgets 1 and 2 was not available in the timeframe, and the committee's own commentary only recommends that a fair transition 'should also take into account the impact of the proposed RUC discount rates on emissions' - a forward-looking recommendation, not a report of figures received. Caveat on verification: parliament.nz and legislation.govt.nz both refuse automated fetches, so the 25-2 commentary text was read via search-engine extracts rather than a directly loaded page.

statement: Of course they’ll exist—it is simply who is going to present the reports.
criterion: Ministry of Justice or Department of Corrections data on the number of written cultural reports and section 27 submissions provided to sentencing courts in the twelve months after the Act's commencement, compared with the twelve months before. True if the volume of such reports/submissions is broadly sustained; false if it falls away substantially once funding is withdrawn.
reasoning: The criterion names Ministry of Justice / Department of Corrections counts of written cultural reports and s27 submissions provided to sentencing courts, 12 months after commencement vs 12 months before. The pre-change figure is well documented (~2,500 reports costing $7.5m in 2023, per Goldsmith's own release and the Regulatory Impact Statement), but no post-change counterpart exists publicly. That is structural rather than accidental: the count existed because legal aid was paying the invoices, and the Legal Services Amendment Act 2024 (in force 21-22 March 2024) removed that funding line, taking the collection point with it. Searched MoJ publications, Corrections statistics, the RIS, Law Society / Law Association / Bar Association commentary, Equal Justice Project's one-year review, RNZ's one-year-on coverage and Gledhill's AUT/Conversation work; none reports a volume figure for the post-commencement period, and the Equal Justice Project piece explicitly falls back on practitioner interviews rather than statistics. Disconfirming check: I looked for evidence the volume HAD been sustained as well as that it had collapsed, and found neither quantified. The qualitative record cuts both ways on Foster's substance — s27 material does still reach courts, now gathered by defence counsel or privately funded (Snelgar, Reed, Dyhrberg), which matches his 'it is simply who is going to present the reports'; but legal-aid spend has migrated into psychiatric reports ($200k Apr 2025 to $470k+ Jul 2025) and alcohol/drug reports ($17k to $222k+), and lawyers report strain and access disparity. Resolve-by (2025-12-31) has passed, so not_yet_due does not apply; the named evidence simply is not findable.

statement: Well, time will tell, but it’s pretty clear from the advice that costs will rise, the length of trials will rise, incarceration rates will rise, and—I think it’s important to say this—needlessly rise; rise not because people belong in prison, but because judges don’t have the information to provide a more appropriate sentence which is better and safer for the community and more likely to lead to less offending.
criterion: Ministry of Justice criminal court statistics on average case disposal time and criminal legal aid expenditure, and Department of Corrections prison population figures, for the two years following the Act's commencement in March 2024; true if all three rise relative to the pre-commencement trend, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires all three of (a) criminal legal aid expenditure, (b) average case disposal time, (c) prison population to rise relative to the pre-commencement trend; false if flat or falling. Two rose and one clearly moved the opposite way. (a) Legal aid expenditure rose: MoJ spent $308m in 2024/25, up $23m on the prior year, and Vote Justice estimates put legal aid at ~$321m estimated actual 2024/25 rising to $328m in 2025/26. Caveat: it was already on a steep pre-commencement trend (+42% since 2020/21), so a rise 'relative to the trend' is arguable rather than clear. The one cost movement directly attributable to the s27 change is substitution — legal-aid spending on psychiatric reports went from $200k (April 2025) to over $470k (July 2025), and on alcohol/drug addiction reports from $17k to over $222k, which AUT's Kris Gledhill characterises as displacement from one part of the legal aid pot to another, i.e. Webb's mechanism confirmed in miniature. (c) Prison population rose sharply: from 9,294 in February 2024 to a record 10,881, a level the justice sector projections had not expected until early 2030, and hitting Budget 2025's mid-2026 funded capacity a year early. But attribution runs mostly to three strikes reinstatement, gang legislation and remand growth (remand up to 43% of the muster in 2025), not to the absence of s27 information. (b) Disconfirming evidence, and it is decisive against the full claim: case timeliness improved rather than deteriorated. District Court criminal cases disposed within agreed timeframes went from 81% to 83% by October 2025, against an earlier projected decline to 77% by 2027; the national criminal backlog fell 26.7% from its January 2022 peak of 9,000+ to 6,660 by July 2025; and sentencing adjournments — the measure closest to Webb's specific concern — dropped from 36% to 29% over two years, about 2,900 fewer delayed sentencing hearings. So the substance holds on cost and incarceration but fails on trial length, and the causal attribution Webb asserted ('because judges don't have the information') is not demonstrated for the two that did rise.

statement: Maybe one of those principles will be reviewed when we see the next bill come through the House on that one.
criterion: The Parliamentary bills register. True if a Government or member's bill whose subject is the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi is introduced and read in the House by the resolve-by date; false if no such bill is introduced.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a Government or member's bill whose subject is the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi was introduced and read in the House by 2024-12-31. It was. The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill (the Treaty Principles Bill), arising from the ACT-National coalition agreement and advanced by David Seymour, was introduced to Parliament on 7 November 2024 and passed its first reading on 14 November 2024, after which it was referred to the Justice Committee. Both events fall inside the resolve-by window. Disconfirming check: I verified the bill was genuinely introduced and read rather than merely announced or released as a draft — the Beehive release and 1News coverage both record the first reading vote completing on 14 November (after the sitting was suspended by a haka and Willie Jackson's ejection), and the bill went on to a select committee report on 4 April 2025 and defeat at second reading 112-11 on 10 April 2025, which confirms it existed as a live bill on the register. The bill's later fate is outside the criterion, which asks only about introduction and a reading by 2024-12-31.

statement: The Minister pointed out that there will be a bill, which I predict will be called the “Bayly Bill”, which will actually address a lot of the issues that they raised, in a much more comprehensive way, in a much more cost-effective way, and bring all of the stories of woe that were brought before us under control.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register; true if a Government bill dealing with business payment practices or late payment to small suppliers is introduced by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, false if no such bill is introduced by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: No Government bill dealing with business payment practices or late payment to small suppliers was introduced by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs by 31 December 2025. The government bill disclosure register lists only the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill (2024) and nothing comparable in 2025. The coalition's announced approach after the repeal was explicitly non-regulatory: an industry-led voluntary code, faster government procurement payment rules, and eInvoicing uptake. Disconfirming check: Labour's 2026 policy proposes restoring the repealed Business Payment Practices Act disclosure requirements within 100 days, which would be unnecessary had a replacement statute been enacted. The only payment-related Commerce and Consumer Affairs bill in the window was the Retail Payment System (Ban on Merchant Surcharges) Amendment Bill (Sept 2025), which concerns card surcharges to merchants, not business-to-business payment practices or late payment to suppliers.

statement: And I would suggest that some of the suggestions from the last member, who was obviously trying to be helpful, those are the type of things I would expect to be taken up in the industry code which will be developed and, hopefully, in place by the end of this year, which I would expect, because that will pick up some of those elements.
criterion: Whether a voluntary business payment / prompt payment industry code was published and operative in New Zealand on or before 31 December 2024 (MBIE announcements, the Minister's press releases, or the code's own launch materials); true if the code was in place by that date, false if it was still unlaunched or launched only in 2025 or later.
reasoning: No voluntary business payment / prompt payment industry code was published or operative in New Zealand by 31 December 2024. The February 2024 repeal announcement stated only an intention to work with BusinessNZ on an industry-led voluntary code. The government's actual November 2024 action was new procurement rules requiring agencies to pay 90% of domestic invoices within 10 working days from 1 Jan 2025 — contemporaneous coverage of that announcement makes no mention of an industry code. BusinessNZ material from late 2025 and 2026 still describes the code as design work ('Government asked BusinessNZ to help design a voluntary Business Payments Code'; 'BusinessNZ is instead working with its large business group to develop a voluntary code'), and MBIE's live repeal page still frames the code as an intention rather than an existing instrument. Searches for launch materials, code text, or a signatory list under the obvious names returned nothing for New Zealand — the only prominent 'Fair Payment Code' launched in December 2024 is the UK's. So the code was still unlaunched at the resolve-by date.

statement: That is the biggest nudge you will see, because that will drive CEOs of our large Government agencies, and, in time, the Crown entities—nearly 100 entities spending over $50 billion a year—to promptly pay.
criterion: MBIE's published payment-times data for government agencies: true if, once published, average or median agency payment times improve materially against the first published baseline; false if they are unchanged or worse, or if agency payment times are never published.
reasoning: The publication branch of the criterion is satisfied — MBIE does publish agency payment-times data — but the improvement test is not. The first published round (Quarter 1 2025, released 4 August 2025) reported 96.1% of central government domestic invoices paid within 10 working days across 111 agencies, with 78 of them above the then 90% threshold. The most recent quarter inside the resolve window, Q1 2026, reports 95.9% across 106 agencies, described as up 0.3 percentage points on Q4 2025 (implying ~95.6% then). Every published quarter therefore sits at or slightly below the first published baseline, i.e. unchanged to marginally worse, which the criterion calls false. Two caveats worth recording: MBIE publishes percentage-paid-within-threshold rather than an average or median days series, so that is the closest available measure; and the first published figure was already ~96%, leaving little headroom for the criterion to detect movement. The one newly published measure that is far from target is eInvoices, at 74% paid within 5 working days against a 95% requirement from 1 January 2026.

statement: Does he think it is fair that Kiwis will be hit with a petrol price hike of between 40c and 50c a litre, based on that carbon price of $235 a tonne, because of his Government’s plan of cutting transport projects and programmes that will reduce emissions?
criterion: MBIE retail petrol price data and the NZ ETS carbon price series; true if the ETS-attributable component of the pump price is 40-50c per litre higher than in March 2024 by 2030, false if the increase is materially smaller.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against MBIE retail petrol data and the NZ ETS price series 'by 2030'; today is 2026-09-26, so the window has not closed. Context only, not a verdict: the NZU secondary market closed around NZ$52.35-52.75 in June 2026 and the legislated auction floor rises only to NZ$87 by 2030, so nothing yet indicates a $235/t price or a 40-50c/L ETS-attributable component — but absence of the 2030 data means no score.

statement: Well, the good news for the good people of Nelson and Tasman is that they will be getting the Hope Bypass under this GPS. I encourage the regional land transport plan to put forward its proposals, and the national land transport programme will be developed by the NZTA over the coming six months.
criterion: NZTA publication record: true if the 2024–27 National Land Transport Programme is developed and adopted by NZTA within roughly six months of 5 March 2024; false if the NLTP is not produced within that window.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether NZTA developed and adopted the 2024-27 National Land Transport Programme within roughly six months of 5 March 2024. NZTA published the 2024-27 NLTP on 2 September 2024 (initial allocation of funds to activity classes dated 2 September 2024; Transport Minister's $32.9b announcement; independent coverage published 3 September 2024), about 5.9 months after the statement — inside the window. The adjacent Hope Bypass element also holds as stated: the 2024-27 NLTP allocated roughly $73m for pre-implementation (design and consenting), with stage 1 construction marked implementation-ready beyond 2027, so the project was carried in the programme though not funded to build.

statement: By then, it will be too late; it would have passed in the next hour.
criterion: The Hansard record and division for the third reading of the bill before the House on 5 March 2024; true if the bill completed its third reading that sitting, within about an hour of the statement, false if it did not pass that day.
reasoning: The bill before the House was the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill, taken under urgency. Hansard records its committee stage and third reading within the same continuous sitting that began on 5 March 2024 (sections HansDeb_20240305_20240306_16 and _36); the third reading passed on a party vote of 68 ayes to 54 noes and the Act received royal assent on 7 March 2024. So the bill did complete its third reading in that sitting, as predicted. Two caveats, neither fatal to the criterion as written: the sitting ran past midnight, so the third reading carries a 6 March date rather than 5 March; and parliament.nz returned 404 to every fetch attempt, so I could not time-stamp the gap between the statement and the vote to confirm 'the next hour' to the minute — the passage-in-that-sitting element is confirmed by the Hansard section IDs, the recorded division and the assent date.

statement: This will result in cuts to critical transport projects that will make a huge difference.
criterion: Auckland Council and Auckland Transport programme decisions and the Regional Land Transport Plan following the repeal: true if projects on the RFT-funded list are cancelled, deferred or reduced in scope as a consequence of the lost revenue; false if the RFT-funded programme proceeds substantially unchanged.
reasoning: The RFT was repealed effective 30 June 2024 and the RFT-funded programme did not proceed substantially unchanged. AT's RFT page records that funding support for all RFT projects other than three was revoked effective 8 March 2024, and AT put the loss at ~$1.2b from its capital programme over four years. Work was paused on the Great North Road cycleway and the Glenvar Road and Lake Road improvements; AT's Glenvar/Lake Road page still states there is insufficient funding to commence construction (only $500k for detailed design). Eastern Busway stage 4 (Botany Interchange) lost ~$298.7m, 88% of the project, and appears in NLTP 2024-27 as 'Possible - unlikely to be funded'. Disconfirming check: the repeal legislation directed the ~$350-400m unspent residual to a short list (Eastern Busway next stage, electric trains, road corridor improvements) and NLTP 2024 funded some Auckland work, but that covered only part of the list and did not restore the cancelled/deferred projects. Caveat: the Eastern Busway stage 4 deferral is attributed partly to cost growth and alignment with Airport-to-Botany as well as the funding shortfall, so causation there is mixed; the Glenvar/Lake Road/Great North Road deferrals are directly attributed to the RFT loss.

statement: What we also know, on that side of the House and on this side of the House, is that road-user charges are coming and that is going to be the way of the future in terms of charging, rather than petrol taxes.
criterion: New Zealand transport revenue legislation and Ministry of Transport revenue statistics. True if legislation extending road user charges to light petrol vehicles is enacted and RUC becomes the principal road-charging mechanism in place of fuel excise; false if fuel excise duty remains the primary charging mechanism with no enacted transition.
reasoning: The criterion's window runs to 31 December 2027; today is 26 September 2026, so neither branch is settled. Status: the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill was introduced and passed its first reading on 18 November 2025 (under urgency, with Labour also voting for it), removing barriers to moving all light vehicles from FED to RUC; select committee submissions closed 8 January 2026. It is not enacted - as of 31 August 2026 the bill was still awaiting its committee stage, and Transport Minister Chris Bishop said it was 'unlikely to complete its passage through Parliament before the upcoming election', was 'not an immediate priority', that there is 'no set date in mind' for universal RUC, and that work might begin in a second term around 2028-29. Fuel excise duty therefore remains the primary charge on light petrol vehicles (confirmed by the August 2026 FED-schedule announcement, which still legislates future FED increases). Disconfirming check for the 'true' branch: no enacted transition and no commencement date exist, so the criterion's true branch is not met yet and looks unlikely by end-2027; but the deadline has not passed, so the correct answer is pending.

statement: Not only that, but a few years down the track, they’re going to whack the fuel tax back up again by another 22c a litre, and, on top of this, something that just simply cannot be justified by reference to the cost of living, the other side is increasing vehicle registration fees, so another $50 a year—whack!—out of people’s back pockets.
criterion: Legislated/gazetted fuel excise duty rates and the Government Policy Statement on land transport: true if cumulative fuel excise increases announced or implemented by the end of 2029 total approximately 22c per litre, false if materially less (e.g. the 12c signalled in GPS 2024) or if no increase occurs. Registration fee element checked against NZTA motor vehicle licensing fee schedules.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on cumulative fuel excise to end-2029; today is 26 September 2026 and the schedule has already been revised twice, so the total cannot be fixed yet. What is established: (a) the registration-fee element is confirmed - motor vehicle licensing fees rose $25 in January 2025 and a further $25 in January 2026, $50 total for most vehicles, as announced alongside GPS 2024; (b) the criterion's premise that GPS 2024 signalled only 12c is inaccurate - the 12c was the first step of a signalled path of 12c (Jan 2027) + 6c (Jan 2028) + 4c/yr from 2029, i.e. about 22c cumulative by 2029, which is exactly the figure Russell used; (c) on 31 August 2026 the Government cancelled the 12c 1 January 2027 increase and replaced it with 5c from 1 January 2028 plus three further 5c increases at six-month intervals, with annual 5c increases resuming 1 January 2030, and topped up the NLTF by ~$1.476b. On one reading those four steps land by mid-2029 (~20c by end-2029, i.e. close to 22c); one industry account instead reads the revised path as ~20c cumulative by end-2030. Either way the end-2029 figure is not yet determined, and a general election falls between now and then, so this is pending rather than settled. Note for the record: the $50 rego half of the statement is true.

statement: And the number one issue that came up time and time again—and I suspect she might be the Labour candidate for Northcote at the next election—was the cost of living, and I’m really happy to support this because this bill addresses the cost of living of those in Northcote, it addresses the cost of living of those in Pakuranga, those in Takanini, those in Mount Roskill, those in Upper Harbour, and I really support this bill.
criterion: The New Zealand Labour Party's confirmed electorate candidate for Northcote at the next general election, per the Electoral Commission candidate nominations and Labour's own announcements; true if Camilla Belich is selected as Labour's Northcote candidate, false if any other person is.
reasoning: Labour's confirmed candidate for Northcote at the 2026 general election is Shanan Halbert, the former Northcote MP (2020-2023), who confirmed the bid in March 2026 and is listed as "Candidate for Northcote" on Labour's own 2026 campaign site; Wikipedia's 2026 candidates-by-electorate table also lists Halbert for Labour in Northcote. Camilla Belich, the person the criterion names, is standing for Labour in Epsom, per her own Labour 2026 campaign page. The criterion states it is false if any person other than Belich is selected, so the prediction fails as written. Note for the dataset: the quoted excerpt does not name the "she" Bidois referred to, so the criterion's identification of Belich appears to be the criterion writer's inference rather than something in the speech; under either reading, Labour's Northcote candidate is Halbert.

statement: Gone, and the March madness will persist.
criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA congestion data and reporting for March 2025 on the choke points named in the speech; true if severe March congestion recurs at those points, false if congestion at them measurably eased.
reasoning: March 2025 congestion recurred at full severity. Auckland Transport recorded traffic up 41% on state highways and 17% on arterial roads during March 2025 (reported by NZ Herald in its March 2026 March Madness piece, which cites AT's data for "March last year"). AT's February 2025 peak-speed dataset put Raleigh Rd/Lake Rd - the Devonport choke point Russell named in the same speech - at 9 km/h in the morning peak, among Auckland's 16 most congested roads, alongside Manukau Rd/Broadway and Ponsonby Rd/Newton Rd at 8-9 km/h. The March 2025 cost-of-congestion reporting had the trend worsening, not easing ($2.3bn/yr rising toward an estimated $2.6bn by 2026, 29m hours lost, ~17 hours per Aucklander). Checking for the disconfirming case: the $23m regional-fuel-tax-funded Lake Rd upgrade remained paused after the tax ended in June 2024, and as late as June 2026 AT was still proposing only low-cost interim changes at Belmont shops, explicitly noting the upgrade funds had been de-prioritised - so there is no evidence of measurable easing at the named points.

statement: Well, they’re going to whack up the cost of registration by $50.
criterion: NZTA's published motor vehicle licensing fee schedule; true if the annual licensing fee rises by a cumulative $50 relative to its early-2024 level, false if it rises by materially less or not at all.
reasoning: The Government's May 2024 decision (Regulatory Impact Statement, Increasing annual vehicle licence fees 2024) raised the annual motor vehicle licence fee for most vehicles by $50, phased as $25 on 1 January 2025 and a further $25 on 1 January 2026 - the exact amount Russell named, and fully in effect before the 30 June 2026 resolve-by date. The licence fee component had not risen since 1994. Motorcycles/trailers/ATVs rose $28 and mopeds $16.50, so "$50" is right for the standard case she was describing. Confirming the schedule: the 12-month private petrol fee was $172.97 from 1 January 2026, with a further separate rise of $8.48 from 1 July 2026 (after the window, so it does not affect the verdict). No evidence found that the increase was reduced, deferred or reversed.

statement: But what people are going to notice is that projects they were expecting to be built—like the Lake Road upgrade in Devonport and a whole lot of other ones—are no longer going to happen.
criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA project records for the Lake Road (Devonport–Takapuna) upgrade. False if the upgrade as scoped proceeds to construction under an alternative funding source; true if it is cancelled, indefinitely deferred, or cut back to a materially smaller scheme following the regional fuel tax repeal.
reasoning: The Lake Road (Devonport) upgrade as scoped did not proceed. RFT-funded work where construction contracts were not executed was paused after the repeal announcement, explicitly including 'Glenvar and Lake Road improvements', and in March 2024 funding support was revoked for all but three RFT projects, effective 8 March 2024. AT had planned ~$23m of RFT revenue on Lake Road within a ~$47m scheme. As of June 2026 AT is consulting only on 'low-cost, high-impact changes' at the Belmont Shops intersection (morning clearway, lane markings, crossings), with Cr Richard Hills confirming funds for the Lake Road upgrade 'were de-prioritised through government budgets' and this project 'brings part of the solution forward in the meantime'. The criterion's condition — cancelled, indefinitely deferred, or cut back to a materially smaller scheme — is met. Qualification not required by the criterion: AT's board had already stripped the $47m from its capital programme in June 2023, before the repeal, so the repeal confirmed rather than caused the outcome. Disconfirming check: no evidence the full upgrade proceeded to construction under any alternative funding source.

statement: Cutting the regional fuel tax at this time means either a rates rise or a cut in projects.
criterion: Auckland Council's adopted 2024–34 Long-term Plan and transport programme. True if, relative to the pre-repeal plan, the council adopts a higher rates increase or removes/defers transport projects previously funded by the regional fuel tax; false if the programme and rates path are both maintained without either.
reasoning: The criterion is disjunctive and the project-cut branch is decisively met: of 14 RFT-funded projects, funding support was revoked for all but three effective 8 March 2024, scrapping roughly $600m of planned spend, and the mayor ordered a halt on RFT-funded work. The repeal left a $1.2bn four-year transport funding shortfall. The rates branch is also supported: the LTP 2024-34, adopted 27 June 2024, carried a 6.8% average residential rates rise for 2024/25 (then 5.8% and 7.9%), after the mayor had initially ruled out a rates rise to cover the shortfall. Disconfirming check: there is no evidence the pre-repeal transport programme and rates path were both maintained intact — the opposite is documented.

statement: I also just want to tell them something that’s a bit of bad news, which is that if they expect to see the fuel come down 10c a litre every time they go to the pump, unfortunately that’s very unlikely to happen.
criterion: MBIE weekly fuel price monitoring (and AA/Gaspy retail data) for Auckland versus the rest of the North Island either side of the regional fuel tax's removal on 30 June 2024: the prediction is true if the Auckland average fell materially less than the tax amount (11.5c/L including GST), false if the average fell by approximately the full amount.
reasoning: The Commerce Commission's focus report addresses the criterion's exact question and its headline finding runs against the prediction: 'the removal of the ARFT was passed through to consumers in the form of lower prices by 1 July.' Prices inside the two Auckland border areas dropped an average of 8-11 cpl relative to stations just outside Auckland between 29 June and 1 July, against the 11.5 cpl ARFT (10c plus 1.5c GST); South Auckland diesel fell 10.5 cpl. So motorists broadly did see roughly the 10c she named come off. However the pass-through was neither complete nor uniform nor fully sustained: South Auckland Regular 91 fell 'nearly 8 cpl', about 3.5c short of the tax; the northern border retained a ~4 cpl Auckland premium in the two weeks after removal versus ~11 cpl before; the Commission observed the southern gap 'started to close in the two weeks following' and that cross-border price differences 'have not returned to their pre-tax levels', concluding the difference 'has not always fully reflected the 11.5 cpl ARFT'. White's 'every time they go to the pump' qualifier holds up better than her 'very unlikely to happen' framing, which is materially overstated relative to what the data show.

statement: This is one more of those stupid pieces of legislation being passed through this House in urgency, where people don’t get a chance to scrutinise it, don’t get a chance to put up the counterargument and, indeed, I’d say to you, will be reversed in the future—will be reversed.
criterion: The New Zealand statute book and Hansard: true if an Auckland regional fuel tax, or an equivalent regional fuel tax power for Auckland, is re-enacted and in force at any point before the resolve-by date; false if no such tax has been reinstated by then.
reasoning: The Auckland regional fuel tax was repealed by the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Act 2024 (assented 7 March 2024) and the tax ceased on 30 June 2024. Searching the statute book and 2026 coverage for any re-enactment: as at September 2026 no regional fuel tax, and no equivalent regional fuel tax power for Auckland, is in force or before the House — the live 2026 fuel-tax dispute concerns the national fuel excise rate and road user charges, not restoring the regional power. Checked for disconfirming evidence (a Labour or council-driven bill to reinstate it) and found none. However the criterion's window runs to 31 December 2029, covering the 7 November 2026 election and the following term, so the prediction cannot be graded yet.

statement: I believe that it does require consultation with Aucklanders over and beyond an election, because the greater question in front of us is actually: how do we invest in a modern transport infrastructure for a global city that will have a population of 2 million people come 2030?
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region: true if the estimated resident population of Auckland reaches 2,000,000 or more at any point up to 31 December 2030, false if it remains below that.
reasoning: The criterion is the Stats NZ subnational estimate for the Auckland region reaching 2,000,000 at any point up to 31 December 2030. The latest published estimate is ~1,816,000 at 30 June 2025 (Aotearoa Data Explorer, via Stats NZ subnational population estimates); the 2026 release is due October 2026. Stats NZ's own subnational projections have Auckland reaching 2 million in 2033, i.e. after the criterion's window, which is evidence against the claim. But reaching 2 million by 2030 requires about 33,000 a year from the June 2025 base, a rate Auckland has exceeded in high net-migration years, so the outcome is not yet determined and the resolve-by date has not passed.

statement: So it’s all very sensible stuff, which I’m sure the Opposition is very happy to support.
criterion: The voting record for the remaining stages (committee of the whole House and third reading) of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if the Opposition parties supported the bill, false if any of them voted against it.
reasoning: The criterion is the voting record for the bill's remaining stages: false if any Opposition party voted against. The bill was taken through all stages under urgency on 5 March 2024. Hansard records the party vote on the third reading as Ayes 68 (National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8) to Noes 54 (Labour 34, Green Party 14, Te Pati Maori 6), and WhereTheyStand records the same 68-54 split at every reading. So all three Opposition parties voted against, not 'very happy to support'. Looked for the contrary case (an Opposition party splitting or supporting at the committee stage or third reading) and the tallies are identical across stages with no abstentions or absences recorded.

statement: The cancelation of cycleway and walkway projects will contribute to road congestion, and, by extension, the increase of congestion charges at peak hour traffic.
criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport congestion metrics for the main centres, plus the statute book on time-of-use charging: true if measured peak congestion rises over the period and a peak-hour congestion charge is enacted or raised; false if congestion is flat or falling and no congestion charging scheme is legislated.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2027-06-30; today is 2026-09-26, so the period the criterion measures is not closed. Partial state of the evidence: the criterion's 'false' limb is already ruled out because a congestion-charging scheme HAS been legislated — the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 10-11 November 2025 (Beehive/Scoop). But the 'true' limb is not met either: no peak-hour charge is being levied. Auckland Transport's own project page (checked Sept 2026) lists the project as 'Planning', with Auckland Council's Transport and Infrastructure Delivery Committee approving three candidate charging options in August 2026, public engagement expected from around November 2026, and no start date decided (media reporting points to ~2028). On the congestion limb, AT's Cost of Congestion white paper (Jan 2025) projects congestion costs rising to ~$2.6b/year by 2026 and ~6.7% growth in peak road congestion, but no NZTA/MoT peak-congestion series for the full period is yet available, and nothing attributes any change to cancelled cycleway/walkway projects. Both limbs of the criterion need re-checking after mid-2027.

statement: Whilst you might still set Sunday aside for a day of rest, it is my contention that given the fact that, for example, we’ll more likely than not be sitting to midnight on Wednesday night and sitting extensively on Thursday, the committee will then also quite likely be sitting on Friday, notwithstanding that it is a sitting week, and then quite possibly Saturday.
criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's published meeting record for the nine-day report-back period on this bill (March 2024): true if the committee held a meeting on a Saturday, false if it held no Saturday meeting during that period.
reasoning: Context from the primary record: on 5 March 2024 the House referred the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee with a report-back of 14 March — nine days (Hansard 5 Mar 2024, p.1841). Webb's quoted words are verbatim at p.1846, spoken to his amendment 'but not on Saturdays, despite any Standing Order to the contrary', which was defeated 54-68 (p.1848), so a Saturday meeting remained legally possible. What actually happened: committee chair Andy Foster told the House at the second reading (Hansard 19 Mar 2024, p.2167) that 'We heard from submitters Friday before last' — Friday 8 March — that submitters had 'less than 48 hours to make submissions' and '19 who appeared the following day on that Friday', and that the committee 'dealt with the officials' feedback, drafting, and final decisions by Zoom, because the House wasn't sitting'. No Saturday meeting is recorded anywhere in that account, and the only Saturday in the report-back window was 9 March. Judged strictly against the criterion as written (true only if a Saturday meeting was held), this fails. It is scored partly_correct rather than wrong because the concrete, unhedged part of Webb's prediction — that the committee would be sitting on the Friday, a non-sitting day, in the middle of a sitting week — is exactly what the chair confirms happened; only the hedged 'quite possibly Saturday' did not eventuate.

statement: So that one’s a pretty straightforward question, and I’m pretty confident the Minister will be able to come and stand to his feet and be able to answer that.
criterion: The Hansard record of this committee stage on the Sentencing Amendment / legal aid clause; true if Goldsmith rises and names the consultation he undertook, false if he does not respond or declines to address the consultation question.
reasoning: The bill is the Legal Services Amendment Bill (removing legal aid funding for section 27 cultural reports), taken in committee of the whole House under urgency on 5 March 2024, with Paul Goldsmith as Minister of Justice. Henare's quoted sentence is verbatim in Hansard, 5 Mar 2024, p.1878, attached to his question asking the Minister to share the conversations he had had with his Maori Cabinet colleagues and who was representing Maori views to him. Goldsmith rose immediately: 'Very happy to answer the questions of the member', answered the first question (why legislation was required given the Legal Services Commissioner's statutory independence), then asked 'what was the second question?'; Henare said 'Consultation.'; Goldsmith replied 'Consultation — well, yes, we had wide-ranging consultation with many Maori over this', and when Willie Jackson interjected 'Name one organisation' he answered 'Winston Peters, for one, has a very strong view on these matters, and I've had long conversations with him and many others.' He had also earlier named the previous Minister of Justice Kiri Allan as someone he had talked to (p.1863). So the criterion's failure branch — that he does not respond or declines to address the consultation question — did not occur. Disconfirming detail worth recording: the answer was thin, he named no iwi or organisation despite being pressed, and by p.1880 he conceded 'Given the urgency with which we've moved on this, there has not been formal consultation with different groups — with the legal community or with iwi'; other members that night (Willow-Jean Prime, p.1875) complained he left their questions unanswered. But on Henare's own question he did stand and answer.

statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
criterion: MBIE weekly fuel price monitoring comparing Auckland pump prices with the rest of New Zealand either side of the regional fuel tax's removal on 30 June 2024; true if the Auckland premium falls by approximately 11.5c per litre, false if the reduction is materially smaller.
reasoning: MBIE's weekly series is national (it only adds a weighted-average RFT line to the duties data) and publishes no Auckland-vs-rest split, so I used the two instruments that do measure the Auckland premium directly. The Commerce Commission's focus report (Gaspy end-of-day board prices, 17+16+17+13+15 stations in five in/out-of-region groups) concluded the ARFT removal 'was passed through to consumers in the form of lower prices by 1 July', with border-area prices dropping 8-11 cpl between 29 June and 1 July 'in the context of the 11.5 cpl ARFT'. Its Table 2 for Regular 91 shows the cross-border gap moving from +10.73 to -6.77 cpl at the southern border and from +10.82 to +4.07 cpl at the northern border. McNamara's later difference-in-differences study on daily station-level data (Auckland vs Northland/Waikato) puts the repeal effect at -11.6 cpl, 'near-complete and symmetric pass-through'. The AA and BP/Z/Mobil reported a full 11.5 cpl cut, and Auckland 91 fell $2.92 to $2.809 on 1 July, level with Whangarei. Disconfirming checks: pass-through was only about three-quarters for stations facing oppositely-taxed competitors (notably the northern border), and national importer margins rose from late September 2024 - but that is a nationwide move that does not reopen the Auckland premium the criterion tests. The claim is not materially overstated.

statement: But in the short term, there’s going to be a gap in revenue and then, in order for projects that were on the books in Auckland to continue being funded with a share from the council, it would have to come from some other source—probably rates or those projects simply won’t go ahead.
criterion: Auckland Council's 2024–2034 Long-term Plan and subsequent annual transport programme decisions: true if the Council either raises rates or defers/cancels previously programmed transport projects, with the regional fuel tax repeal cited as a cause of the shortfall; false if the affected projects proceed on schedule without a rates increase or an equivalent substitute revenue source.
reasoning: Both branches of the criterion were satisfied, and the repeal is explicitly cited as the cause. Auckland Council put the revenue gap at about $600m of RFT receipts and up to $1.2b once lost NZTA matching funding is counted. The Long-term Plan 2024-2034, adopted 27 June 2024, both raised rates (6.8% in 2024/25, 5.8% in 2025/26, 7.9% in 2026/27) and cancelled or cut previously programmed transport projects: Mayor Wayne Brown recorded that 'Stage 4 of the Eastern Busway (the Botany Interchange) is no longer funded - a reduction of $298.7m or 88 percent', alongside cuts to Glenvar Road (-30%), cycleways, network resilience, Henderson rail-bus station and Matiatia park-and-ride, with the ending of the regional fuel tax named as the reason. Testing the false branch: the affected projects did not proceed on schedule without a substitute. Eastern Busway Stage 4 stayed unfunded through the criterion's 30 June 2025 resolve date and was only re-funded in late 2025 ($101m, 51% National Land Transport Fund / 49% council), with early works starting March 2026 - a later substitute source, not continuity.

statement: This will have a cost of living impact by reducing the cost of petrol for Aucklanders, and that is something which is, of course, good news to people in Auckland and I know has significant support from the people of Auckland.
criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price data comparing Auckland with the rest of New Zealand either side of the repeal date: true if Auckland's average 91-octane price falls relative to the national average by an amount approaching the regional fuel tax rate (11.5c/L plus GST) within three months of 30 June 2024; false if the Auckland–national gap is materially unchanged.
reasoning: The criterion tests whether Auckland's 91 price fell relative to the rest of the country by an amount approaching 11.5c/L within three months of 30 June 2024. MBIE publishes no Auckland-vs-national retail split, so the evidence comes from the equivalent station-level work. The Commerce Commission found the removal was passed through to lower Auckland prices by 1 July, with 8-11 cpl falls relative to stations just outside the region; Auckland 91 dropped from $2.92 to $2.809 overnight, matching Whangarei. Over the longer horizon the criterion asks about, McNamara's difference-in-differences estimate on daily station-level data for Auckland against untaxed Northland and Waikato is a 11.6 cpl fall on repeal - near-complete pass-through, not a materially unchanged gap. Disconfirming checks: the ComCom noted the southern-border gap starting to close in the two weeks after repeal and the northern border retaining a 4 cpl premium, and national petrol importer margins pushed above 15% from late September 2024 - but the margin rise applied countrywide and so does not restore an Auckland-specific premium. Note the criterion covers only the price limb; the quote's second limb ('significant support from the people of Auckland') is untested by it, and a November 2023 poll had 44% of Aucklanders wanting to keep the tax against 22% preferring a rates rise.

statement: There are a number of reasons why we are removing the regional fuel tax: firstly, because it will save Aucklanders money as they fill up their cars from 1 July this year: $5 to $10 per tank.
criterion: MBIE weekly petrol price monitoring comparing Auckland pump prices against the rest of New Zealand before and after 1 July 2024: true if the Auckland-specific price falls by approximately 11.5c per litre, yielding $5–$10 on a typical 45–90 litre tank; false if retailers absorb the cut and the Auckland differential does not close.
reasoning: The RFT (10c + GST = 11.5c/L) ended 30 June 2024 and the Commerce Commission's August 2024 focus report found the cut was passed through to consumers: Auckland pump prices fell by an average of 8-11 c/L relative to stations just outside the region between 29 June and 1 July 2024 (Gaspy data, 15-17 stations in each of three Auckland zones); Z Energy said it passed the reduction on in full. The criterion's failure branch - retailers absorbing the cut so the Auckland differential does not close - did not occur. Caveat noted by ComCom: the inside/outside differential 'has not always fully reflected the 11.5 cents per litre' and cross-border gaps had not returned to pre-tax levels, so at 8-11c the saving is about $3.60-$5 on a 45 L tank and $7.20-$9.90 on a 90 L tank - the '$5 to $10 per tank' figure is right at the nominal 11.5c and slightly optimistic at the small-tank end, but not materially overstated.

statement: This will result in cuts to critical transportation projects in Auckland, projects that will make a huge difference.
criterion: Auckland Transport's Regional Land Transport Plan 2024-34 and Auckland Council's 2024 Long-term Plan: true if projects previously funded from regional fuel tax revenue are cancelled or deferred and the councils attribute this to the repeal, false if the affected programme is funded from other sources with no project cancellations.
reasoning: The repeal revoked RFT funding support for all projects except three (projects 4, 6 and 12) effective 8 March 2024, and the resulting 2024 ten-year budget / RLTP 2024-34 cut projects that Auckland Council explicitly attributed to the repeal. Eastern Busway Stage 4 (Botany interchange) lost $298.7m, 88% of the project; the Glenvar Rd and Lake Rd improvements were removed; Rosedale Bus Station, city-centre bus infrastructure and cycleway projects were also listed at risk. Mayor Wayne Brown put the shortfall at $1.2b over four years and said the axing of the regional fuel tax 'required the council to reconsider several projects that have been cut from the budget or descoped' - satisfying the criterion's requirement that the councils attribute the cuts to the repeal. Disconfirming evidence checked: Stage 4's deferral also had a non-funding cause (uncertain alignment with the Airport-to-Botany busway), and NZTA/Council later confirmed $101m for the Botany link route in 2026 - but that restoration is after the 30 June 2025 resolve date and does not undo the cuts made in the 2024 plan.

statement: However, capital expenditure for charging infrastructure for electric ferries, among other things, will not happen as a result of this bill.
criterion: Auckland Transport / Auckland Council capital programme and annual reports on electric ferry charging infrastructure at the downtown ferry terminal; true if that charging capital expenditure is cancelled or left unfunded following the repeal, false if the charging infrastructure is funded and delivered from another source.
reasoning: The premise was correct at the time: AT chief executive Dean Kimpton confirmed in March 2024 that 'the charging infrastructure for the electric ferries was previously funded by the RFT. It's not provided for in the change legislation' - the repeal restricted the remaining ~$360m to three directives that excluded ferry charging. But the criterion's false branch is what happened: the capex was funded from other sources and is being delivered. AT proposed reallocating ~$20m from other capital projects, and pier electrification (~$30m) sits inside a Council/Government ferry programme now above $150m. The $27.6m ABB megawatt charging system is under construction at Queens Wharf: under-wharf cabling from October 2025, above-wharf electrical equipment from January 2026, charger installation on piers 4 and 5 from April 2026, project completion expected mid-2027 (AT page updated 24 August 2026). It is badly delayed - the chargers were originally due in 2024 and the first hybrid ferry charges overnight at Half Moon Bay in the meantime - but the charging capital expenditure was neither cancelled nor left unfunded, so the prediction that it 'will not happen as a result of this bill' did not hold. The cost was that other AT projects were raided to pay for it.
