statement: So we’re going to save a tiny amount of money for people in the short term, but in the medium term and long term, we’re going to keep having this same problem of households having to own more cars.
criterion: Ministry of Transport annual fleet statistics and Stats NZ census/household data on vehicles per household; true if vehicles per household in New Zealand is the same or higher five years after the statement, false if it has fallen.
reasoning: The criterion measures vehicles per household five years after the statement, i.e. 5 March 2029; today is 26 September 2026, so the measurement point has not arrived and Stats NZ has no post-2023 census household-vehicle point. Interim MoT fleet statistics do not point the other way either: light vehicles per capita was ~815 per 1,000 people in 2024 (4.7m vehicles), flat-to-rising rather than falling.

statement: The Government’s creation of the priority one category will prioritise getting families with children out of emergency housing, under stable social housing, sooner.
criterion: HUD/MSD emergency housing reporting on households with children in emergency housing and median length of stay; true if the number of families with children in emergency housing and their median stay fall after the priority one category takes effect (April 2024), false if they are unchanged or higher.
reasoning: The criterion required BOTH the number of families with children in emergency housing AND their median stay to fall. The numbers fell steeply: DPMC Target 8 reports households in EH down from 3,141 (Dec 2023 baseline) to 501 (June 2025), an 84% reduction, with children in EH down from 3,339 (April 2024) to 519 (April 2025); and the Priority One Fast Track itself housed 1,041 households with 2,220 children into social housing tenancies as at 30 June 2025 (972 households / 2,055 children to March 2025 per HUD). But length of stay did not fall: HUD's June 2025 Homelessness Insights report states the average length of time spent in emergency housing is about six months, the same as a year earlier — which the criterion treats as failing. Attribution caveats: the population drop is substantially driven by the tightened gateway (EH application decline rate rose from 4% in March 2024 to 32% in March 2025), HUD says it cannot determine how much is attributable to policy changes, 14% of exits go to unknown destinations, and unsheltered homelessness rose over the same period (Auckland outreach providers: 426 in Sept 2024 to 809 by May 2025).

statement: The simple reality is that this will be one of the most well consulted on bills and regimes in recent history.
criterion: The Environment Committee's record for the Fast-track Approvals Bill — number of written submissions received and hours of oral hearings — compared with other Government bills of the 53rd and 54th Parliaments; true if it ranks among the highest on submission volume and hearing time, false if it is middling or low.
reasoning: The Environment Committee received 26,855 submission files (25,017 verified unique, plus 28,746 petition signatures) between 14 March and 19 April 2024, and heard 66 hours of oral evidence from roughly 1,100 submitters across 22 meetings over six weeks. Against other bills of the 53rd/54th Parliaments this ranks among the highest on both measures the criterion names: written volume sits behind only the Treaty Principles Bill (307,000), Conversion Practices (~107,000) and Three Waters (88,000) and far above essentially every other bill, while on hearing time it is at or near the top (Treaty Principles heard 529 oral submitters over 79 hours; Three Waters heard only 227 oral submissions). Disconfirming check: the bill was materially rewritten after the committee reported (the late-2024 SOP), and the 2025 Fast-track Approvals AMENDMENT Bill got an 11-day submission window the Law Society called rushed — but both fall outside the original bill's select committee process the criterion measures.

statement: There are veins of wealth throughout the South Island, and with this legislation, mining will be turbocharged.
criterion: NZ Petroleum and Minerals / MBIE mining permit statistics and the list of mining projects approved under the fast-track regime; true if mining permits granted and mining projects consented rise materially above the 2023 baseline, false if approvals and activity remain flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion's named source already settles this well inside the resolve-by window. NZP&M's 2025 permitting release gives minerals permit applications received of 296 (2023) → 450 (2024) → 551 (2025) and outcome decisions of 287 → 498 → 521, against a post-2017 annual average of 363 decisions — a material rise above the 2023 baseline on both measures. 178 new permits were granted in 2025 (28 prospecting, 73 exploration, 62 mining), 163 of them gold, and the gold permits are concentrated exactly where Jones said the veins were: West Coast 68, Otago 36, Tasman 25. NZP&M's Jan–Mar 2026 quarterly update reports a further 'sharp rise in the number and complexity' of applications pressuring its timeframes, so the trend has not reversed. On the fast-track leg specifically the record is thinner: OceanaGold's Waihi North was approved in December 2025 (112 working days), Bendigo-Ophir, Auld Creek and Taharoa ironsands are in process, but the largest application — Trans-Tasman Resources' South Taranaki Bight seabed mine — was draft-declined in February 2026 and withdrawn. Disconfirming check: the permit surge is Crown Minerals Act permitting, plausibly driven more by record gold prices and the Crown Minerals Amendment Act than by the Fast-track Act Jones was speaking to, and few fast-track mines are yet in production rather than consented. The criterion as written asks only whether permits granted and projects consented rose materially above 2023, not whether the bill caused it, and they did. Marked correct rather than not_yet_due because the metric has moved decisively with two full calendar years of data; the window runs to 2027-12-31 and a collapse in approvals could still soften this.

statement: Gas will be around for at least another 30 years.
criterion: MBIE energy statistics for 2054; true if natural gas is still commercially produced or imported and consumed in New Zealand at that date, false if gas supply has ceased.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against MBIE energy statistics for 2054 — 28 years away. Nothing observable now can settle whether gas is still produced or imported and consumed in New Zealand at that date, and the criterion explicitly permits imports, so field depletion alone would not falsify it. Context, for the record rather than as a verdict: MBIE reported that 2P gas reserves fell 23% over 2025 to 731 PJ at 1 January 2026, the lowest since records began 20 years ago, with 108 PJ of the 217 PJ fall being production and 109 PJ downward revisions to existing estimates. Māui is now expected to stop producing at the end of 2026 and Pohokura in 2033, ten years earlier than previously indicated, and annual production is forecast to drop below 100 PJ. At that production rate the remaining 2P reserves represent well under a decade, so continued domestic supply to 2054 would require new discoveries or LNG imports. That is a headwind, not a falsification — the claim's date has not passed.

statement: Our country is going to grow at long last, because this bill will not only build dams, open mines, develop infrastructure, it has the Ruataniwha clause.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts; true if New Zealand records materially positive real GDP and real GDP per capita growth over the two years following, false if growth is flat or negative over that period.
reasoning: The criterion requires materially positive growth in BOTH real GDP and real GDP per capita over the two years following 2024-03-07, and is failed if growth is flat or negative. Data now runs to the June 2026 quarter, so the window is closed. Aggregate real GDP: mildly positive. On the OECD/FRED year-on-year series the March 2025 quarter was −0.36% on a year earlier and the March 2026 quarter +2.13%, which chains to roughly +1.8% over the two years from March 2024, plus +0.2% in the June 2026 quarter — about +2% over the full span, or under 1% a year. Per capita: not positive. Stats NZ has GDP per capita up just 0.1% in the June 2026 quarter, and population grew about 1.7% over the same period (0.7% in the year to June 2025 and 0.7% in the year to June 2026, down from 1.7% in the year to June 2024), which leaves real GDP per person flat at best. On the annual-average measure quoted in the House against the June 2026 release, real GDP per person is $53,375 versus $54,635 in late 2023 — lower than when Jones spoke. Disconfirming check: the government's own framing is that the June 2026 quarter 'defied expectations' and GDP rose 1.7% over the year to June 2026, so there is real recovery in 2026, and I looked specifically for a per-capita series that had turned materially positive; it has not. What actually happened after the speech is the opposite of 'grow at long last' in the near term: GDP contracted through most of 2024 and again in the June 2025 quarter, in what was described as the worst non-Covid recession since 1991, before recovering from the September 2025 quarter. So the aggregate-GDP leg of the criterion is weakly satisfied and the per-capita leg fails.

statement: Accordingly, you will find that the other side of politics will react the other way and you will create investment uncertainty. In some of those consents, there is a risk that they will not last.
criterion: The public record of the fast-track approvals regime after the next change of government: true if a subsequent government repeals or materially rewrites the fast-track regime, or if any approval granted under it is revoked, overturned or re-litigated; false if the regime and its approvals stand unaltered through the next parliamentary term.
reasoning: The criterion is disjunctive and its second limb is satisfied: granted fast-track approvals are being re-litigated. Auckland Council appealed the Delmore approval (approved Aug 2026, appeal confirmed Sept 2026) and separately Sunfield; Jones v Environmental Protection Authority [2026] NZHC 1872 (30 June 2026) is a High Court challenge concerning the Kings Quarry Expansion approvals; and the High Court earlier overturned the EPA's acceptance of the Port of Tauranga Stella Passage application, ordering no further FTAA work. But the distinctive content of Parker's prediction is untested: the next election is November 2026, so no subsequent government has acted. Labour has explicitly ruled out repeal while promising to 'fix the many things that are wrong with fast-track'; the Greens and campaign groups want repeal. The material rewrite that has occurred (Fast-track Approvals Amendment, effective 31 March 2026, partly to patch the Stella Passage judicial review) came from the same government, so it does not count for this claim. No approval has actually been revoked or quashed. Hence partly_correct: the litigation risk he named is real and live, the change-of-government consequence remains open until the new term (resolve-by 2029).

statement: I expect this will lead to tougher sentences for gang members and send a strong message that gangs’ unlawful activities will not be tolerated.
criterion: Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics for offenders with recorded gang affiliation, comparing the two years before commencement of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Act with the two years after; true if average custodial sentence length or imprisonment rate for that cohort rises, false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion requires Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics for offenders with recorded gang affiliation comparing the two years before commencement of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Act with the two years after. Commencement was 21 November 2024, so the post window does not close until 21 November 2026 (today is 26 September 2026), and MoJ sentencing statistics publish with a further lag. MoJ does publish Gangs Act 2024 offence tables (finalised charges and convictions for offences such as displaying gang insignia, by outcome and most serious sentence), but that is not the measure the criterion names — average custodial sentence length or imprisonment rate for the gang-affiliated cohort. Corrections data give context (3,124 gang members and associates among 10,623 prisoners in Sept 2025, ~29% of the muster; Mongrel Mob prisoner numbers down 24% over five years) but do not answer the sentencing question either way. Not findable yet; this is a timing verdict, not a failing grade.

statement: Bills like this create more gang members, they fill our prisons, they increase tensions with police, and ultimately they make our communities less safe.
criterion: New Zealand Police National Gang List membership and Department of Corrections prison muster in the two years after the Gangs Act 2024 came into force (21 November 2024). True if both rise materially over that period; false if gang list numbers and the prison muster fall or hold flat.
reasoning: Both quantities the criterion names have risen materially since the Gangs Act came into force on 21 November 2024. National Gang List: 9,270 at the 2023 general election, 10,478 in February 2026 — up 13% (1,208 people) over the term and about 6.5% in the year to Feb 2026 alone, enough that gang members narrowly outnumbered the 10,475 sworn police officers. Prison muster: crossed 10,000 in late 2024, hit a record 10,881 in September 2025 (beating the 2018 peak of 10,820, which earlier projections had not expected until 2029), 11,240 in February 2026 and 11,256 at 30 June 2026; June 2026 Justice Sector Projections forecast 15,200 by 2036. So neither figure fell or held flat — both rose. Two caveats that do not change the verdict as written: the criterion tests only two of Paul's four claims (police tensions and community safety are not measured), and it measures direction, not causation — researchers including Jarrod Gilbert caution the National Gang List partly tracks police recording effort rather than membership. Final in-window data (to 21 Nov 2026) is not yet published, but a reversal of this magnitude in two months is implausible.

statement: So I know this bill is going to be about enabling more work to be done remotely, but I just say: be very careful, because it will work fine for about one or two years, but, all of a sudden, in five years, like we did with the tag and release, we will actually start to regret this.
criterion: The status of the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill's provisions as at March 2029: an official review, Ministry of Justice evaluation, Law Commission report or select committee inquiry finding adverse effects from expanded remote participation, or legislative amendment/rollback narrowing those provisions. True if such a review or rollback exists by the resolve-by date; false if the provisions remain in force with no official finding of adverse effect.
reasoning: The bill was enacted as the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Act 2024 on 2 September 2024 and its expanded audio-link and remote-observation provisions remain in force. Searching for the named evidence — a Ministry of Justice evaluation, Law Commission report, select committee inquiry finding adverse effects, or an amendment narrowing the provisions — turns up nothing as at September 2026; the only adverse material is pre-enactment submissions to the Justice Committee (NZLS and others raised exactly O'Connor's worry about off-camera pressure and diminished participation on audio-only links), which is not a post-implementation finding. I also checked for the disconfirming case (an official review affirming the provisions) and found no review either way. O'Connor's own horizon was five years and the criterion's resolve-by date is 2029-03-07, so the window is roughly two and a half years from closing.

statement: Does he care at all about the evidence that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness, poverty, and inequality, or is he intent on running this Government on vibes?
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship measure) and the Stats NZ/HUD severe housing deprivation and emergency-housing series for the years following March 2024: true if material hardship and measured homelessness both rise beyond sampling error over the period; false if either holds steady or falls.
reasoning: The criterion requires material hardship AND measured homelessness to both rise beyond sampling error after March 2024; it fails that conjunction, but not because the underlying pressures eased. Material hardship for children ran 12.5% (YE June 2023) to 13.4%/156,600 (2024) to 14.3%/169,300 (2025), and Stats NZ explicitly headlined the latest release 'No annual change in child poverty rates' — each annual step is inside sampling error, and the 2024 step was flagged not significant too. Only the longer 2022-to-2025 move (10.6% to 14.3%, about 47,500 more children) is statistically significant, and most of that predates March 2024. The measure also switched from HES to HILS for 2024/25, which weakens the comparison. On homelessness the named series disagree: Census severe housing deprivation (99,462 in 2018 to 112,496 in 2023) has no post-2024 update, so it cannot move within the window; the emergency-housing series fell sharply — 3,342 households in Nov 2023 to 516 in Apr 2025, down 84.5% — but by policy design (Priority One plus a rising decline rate on applications), not by need falling. Against that, unsheltered homelessness rose: Auckland counted 653 rough sleepers in Jan 2025 against 706 in Jan 2026, having peaked at 940 in Sept 2025, and Community Housing Aotearoa described homelessness at its highest level ever. So the substance of the prediction holds on the rough-sleeping measures and on the elevated level of hardship, but the specific test as written does not pass: hardship held steady within error and the emergency-housing series fell.

statement: So just to make that abundantly clear to all who may be following along at home—I apologise for not being able to make all this too exciting, but I guarantee you the fireworks will be coming, because we will not be letting this Government get away with increasing inequality, which, they know full well and their advice bears out, will occur as a result of them progressing this policy agenda.
criterion: Stats NZ household income and wealth inequality measures (Gini coefficient and top-decile income share, Household Economic Survey) for the years following commencement of the brightline, interest deductibility and depreciation changes, together with any Treasury distributional analysis of those measures: true if inequality on those measures rises outside sampling error after the changes take effect; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Stats NZ household income and wealth inequality measures for the years following commencement of the three tax changes. Those commencements are recent: the brightline period reverted to two years on 1 July 2024, interest deductibility was restored to 80% from 1 April 2024 and 100% from 1 April 2025, and the building-depreciation removal applies from the 2024/25 tax year. Only one partly-post-change income year is published — Household income and housing-cost statistics for YE June 2025 (released 2026) — and it reports incomes and housing costs (average equivalised disposable income up 5.9% to $63,009, renters' weekly rent up 9.0%, 40.6% of households calling their income 'not enough' or 'only just enough', up 2.1 points) without a Gini coefficient or top-decile income share. The HES-to-HILS survey replacement from July 2024 also breaks the series at exactly the point the criterion wants measured. On the Treasury side I found the pre-change regulatory impact assessments, which argued the distributional benefit ran to prospective owner-occupiers and that denying interest deductions would partly pass through to renters, but no post-commencement Treasury distributional analysis of the enacted changes. The resolve-by date is 2027-06-30 and the wealth/income inequality readings covering the first full post-change year are not out yet.

statement: Now, if the current form of this particular bill holds on to that, we would support it all the way through to third reading, but it will not—it will not—and we will head into the committee having to challenge and continue to challenge this Government’s agenda for tax breaks for the rich and for the wealthy.
criterion: The bill as enacted (Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Act) compared with the version reported back at second reading: true if the lodged Amendment Paper's changes (interest deductibility, bright-line reduction, depreciation) are incorporated before enactment; false if the bill passes third reading without them.
reasoning: Amendment Paper No. 20 was lodged 14 March 2024 (commentary dated 12 March), before Waititi spoke at the second reading on 19 March. It was moved at the Committee of the whole House on 26 March 2024, the bill was read a third time the same day, and it received royal assent on 28 March 2024 as the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Act 2024. All three measures named in the criterion were incorporated: interest deductibility for residential rental property phased back (80% for 2024-25, 100% from 2025-26), the bright-line period reduced to two years for disposals on or after 1 July 2024, and commercial building depreciation removed from 2024-25. The criterion's true-condition -- the lodged Amendment Paper's changes incorporated before enactment -- is met exactly, so the bill did not reach third reading in the form reported back, which is what Waititi predicted. Disconfirming check: no source indicates the Amendment Paper was withdrawn or the provisions split into a separate bill.

statement: That will encourage more landlords to purchase large numbers of houses, which is what we have seen previously, which makes the market tighter.
criterion: CoreLogic NZ buyer classification data (and REINZ equivalents) on the investor/multiple-property-owner share of residential purchases, comparing the period after the brightline test was shortened against the early-2024 baseline. True if the investor share rises materially above that baseline; false if it stays flat or falls.
reasoning: CoreLogic/Cotality buyer classification data: mortgaged multiple property owners sat at roughly 20-21% of purchases in Q1 2024 (the early-2024 baseline; 21% trough in Q2 2024, 21.7% for full-year 2024), then rose to 22.6% in Q4 2024 and 23% in Q1 2025 (with cash MPOs at 14%, ~37% combined). So the investor share did rise, meaning the criterion's false-condition ('stays flat or falls') is not met. But the rise is about 2 percentage points and never reached the series' long-run average of ~24-24.5% since 2005; it has since receded to 22.5% in Q2 2026 (~23.2% July-August 2026). The 'large numbers of houses' element is directly disconfirmed: landlords with mortgages on 10 or more properties cut their share to 2.3% of purchases in Q2 2026, a seven-year low, down from a 4.1% peak in Q4 2023, and total investor purchases were ~5,000 homes in Q2 2026 against ~7,000 in Q2 2021. The market also loosened rather than tightened -- national values are 18.2% below peak and fell for three consecutive months to August 2026, total stock on market is historically high at 27,306, and first-home buyers hit a record 29.1% share. Verdict: a real but modest rise that falls short of 'materially above' the baseline, with the specific mechanism claimed (bulk landlord buying, a tighter market) contradicted.

statement: So restoring interest deductibility is really going to look at downward pressure, it’s going to look at lowering rents, opening more houses up, so that we’re not inflicting more cost on landlords.
criterion: MBIE tenancy bond median weekly rent series following the restoration of interest deductibility from 1 April 2024. True if national median weekly rents fall, or rent growth stalls against its prior trend; false if rents continue rising at a comparable or faster rate.
reasoning: MBIE tenancy bond data (the source the criterion names): the national median weekly rent for new tenancies first reached $600 in December 2023 and stayed at $600 for 19 of the 30 months to May 2026, finishing at $600 -- up $5 a week, or 0.8%, year-on-year. The prior trend was materially faster: the national median had been rising by roughly $15-25 a week per year (about 3-5%) through 2022-23, with most districts above 5% in the year to Q1 2023. So the criterion's stall arm is satisfied -- rent growth clearly stalled against its prior trend. The fall arm is not satisfied nationally: Auckland ($650) and Canterbury ($550) were unchanged year-on-year to May 2026, Hawke's Bay fell 3.7%, but Southland rose 5.3%. Other series show intermittent year-on-year declines (realestate.co.nz average rent $631 in April 2026, down 1.4%, about $30 below the May 2024 peak of $660). Two things cut against the claim as Wedd framed it: the flattening began in December 2023, before interest deductibility was restored on 1 April 2024, so the timing does not support attribution to that policy; and market commentary attributes the softening to increased listings supply and migration shifts. 'Lowering rents' materially overstates what the series shows, which is that rent growth stopped.

statement: When you combine the outcome of this policy with the outcome of removing the Clean Car Discount—which was having a transformational impact on the vehicles coming into the country—then the reality is we’re going to import fewer electric vehicles in the next few years.
criterion: NZTA / Ministry of Transport vehicle registration and import statistics for battery electric and plug-in hybrid light vehicles. True if annual EV imports/registrations in 2024 and 2025 are lower than in 2023; false if they hold steady or rise.
reasoning: New light EV registrations fell from 31,400 in 2023 to 10,632 in 2024 (7.7% of new sales, down from 19.8%), and 2025 remained far below 2023 (~6,800 BEV; ~11% of new car registrations including PHEVs). EV fleet growth corroborates: +~41,700 in 2023 vs +~11,700 in 2024 and +~16,300 in 2025. The Motor Industry Association attributes the steeper part of the decline to exactly the two policies Genter named — the end of the Clean Car Discount (31 Dec 2023) and RUC on light EVs/PHEVs from 1 April 2024 — on top of weak overall auto sales. Disconfirming check: 2025 was the first year of growth off the 2024 floor, but it is still well under 2023, which is the comparison the criterion specifies. Both 2024 and 2025 are lower than 2023, so the criterion's true condition is met.

statement: Because I think that the Minister of Transport will come back to this House, in this Government, and propose that road-user charges go up.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / ministerial announcements and the Road User Charges (Rates) Orders made during the 2023–2026 parliamentary term. True if the Minister of Transport announces or brings forward an increase in RUC rates before the term ends; false if RUC rates are left unchanged or reduced across the whole term.
reasoning: The final Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024, issued by Transport Minister Simeon Brown and in force from 1 July 2024, set out a revenue package of 12c, 6c then ongoing annual 4c per litre fuel excise duty increases in January 2027, 2028 and 2029 with equivalent increases in road user charges. Transport Minister Chris Bishop reaffirmed and rescheduled the package on 31 August 2026 (5c steps from January 2028 through 2030). So the Minister of Transport did, in this Government, propose that RUC go up — the criterion's 'announces or brings forward an increase in RUC rates before the term ends' condition is satisfied. Two qualifications worth recording: RUC rates were never actually raised within the term (FED and RUC have not increased since 2020) and the announced increases were deferred to 2028, past the term's end; and the draft GPS carrying the proposal was released around 6 March 2024, roughly two weeks before O'Connor spoke, so the claim was close to restating already-announced policy rather than forecasting it. Neither changes the verdict under the criterion as written.

statement: The Government’s killed off light rail for Tāmaki-makau-rau, stopped Wellington moving, and supported road speed increases which will increase fatalities on our roads, so, no, they haven’t started.
criterion: Ministry of Transport road toll and NZTA crash data for roads whose speed limits were raised under the government's speed limit rule changes: true if fatalities on those roads rise relative to the pre-change baseline beyond normal year-to-year variation, false if they are flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion requires fatalities on the specific roads whose limits were raised to rise beyond normal year-to-year variation, and sets a resolve-by date of 2027-12-31, which has not passed. Most reversals took effect on 1 July 2025 (NZTA automatically reversed 38 state highway sections and consulted on a further 49), leaving barely 15 months of post-change data. The best available analysis — Dr Tim Welch, University of Auckland — finds crashes on SH6 Nelson-Blenheim rose from an average 12.5 to 17.2 per year after the June 2025 reversal and an upward crash trend on reversed Auckland roads, but he states explicitly that the post-reversal dataset is still too small to draw firm conclusions, and NZTA cautions against attributing short-term crash changes to speed limits alone. Disconfirming evidence exists too: the national road toll fell to 273 in 2025 from 292 in 2024. No fatality-level, per-road comparison against a pre-change baseline has been published, so the criterion cannot yet be settled either way.

statement: This will not be a transitional process that will be resolved quickly.
criterion: Whether the interim RUC settings introduced by this bill have been replaced by the full universal light-vehicle road-user charges regime — legislated and in force — within two years of the statement. True (prediction correct) if the transition is still incomplete at that date; false if universal light-vehicle RUC is enacted and operative by then.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether universal light-vehicle RUC was legislated and operative by 2026-03-19; it was not, so the transition was still incomplete and the prediction holds. The enabling Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill was only introduced in November 2025, passed first reading 18 November 2025, was before select committee until 8 January 2026 and was still in the parliamentary process through mid-2026; it is expected to pass during 2026. Even that bill only removes barriers to a future transition — it does not itself move petrol light vehicles onto RUC. Officials target ~2027 and no start date for petrol light vehicles has been set; the Transport Minister has said universal RUC could be years away. Checked the disconfirming side (any earlier enactment or in-force universal light RUC) and found none.

statement: The reason that this is only a transition is because we’re going to be moving to a fairer system, as more and more people buy EVs—and they will, because the price of EVs, surprise, surprise, is coming down.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA light vehicle fleet statistics for new and used light EV registrations; true if annual light-EV registrations in the calendar years after the statement exceed the 2023 level, false if annual registrations fall below it.
reasoning: The criterion's test is whether annual light-EV registrations in the calendar years after the statement exceed the 2023 level. They did not. New EV registrations fell from about 31,400 in 2023 to 10,632 in 2024 (about -70%), with EV share of new sales down from 19.8% to 7.7%, after the Clean Car Discount ended on 31 December 2023 and EVs came onto RUC from 1 April 2024. 2025 recovered only partly — plug-ins were about 11% of new car registrations, BEVs up 13% and PHEVs roughly doubling off the 2024 floor — leaving the year still far below 2023 in both absolute volume and share. Both complete calendar years after the statement therefore fall below 2023, the criterion's stated false condition. Disconfirming evidence checked and noted: 2026 has surged sharply (plug-ins 28.5% of passenger registrations in H1 2026 vs 12.8% a year earlier; BEV registrations +172% YoY in August 2026), so full-year 2026 may reach or pass 2023 — but 2026 is incomplete, falls after the 2026-06-30 resolve date, and industry reporting attributes the surge to a fuel-price crisis rather than to EV affordability. The subsidiary part of the claim, that EV prices are coming down, is supported: median EV prices have fallen and used Tesla Model 3s now sell under NZ$35,000. The criterion, however, is scored on registrations alone.

statement: Now, that piece of work means that there’s a whole lot of vehicles out there that are electric and that will now move into the second-hand market and will mean that a whole lot of families that would never be able to buy a car that was new electric will be getting one.
criterion: NZTA used light-EV registration and change-of-ownership data for 2024–2026; true if second-hand EV transfers rise materially over the period and median used EV prices fall, false if used EV volumes are flat or declining.
reasoning: The resolve-by date is 2027-03-19, still in the future as of 2026-09-26, and the criterion explicitly requires NZTA used light-EV registration and change-of-ownership data across 2024-2026 — a window that will not be complete until early 2027. Partial evidence so far cuts both ways. Volume side (supports the claim): used-import BEV registrations rose from 129 in March 2025 to 613 in March 2026, a 375% increase, with the Nissan Leaf going from 103 to 448 units and climbing to fourth most popular used import overall; July 2026 Leaf imports nearly doubled year-on-year to 264. Price/affordability side (unresolved, possibly against): the surge has left yards short of stock — reporting describes dealers running out of second-hand EVs — which pressures used prices upward rather than down, and analysis notes most New Zealand households shop below $15,000 where even used EVs remain out of reach. Median used EV prices have drifted down for some models (2019-2022 Model 3 under NZ$35,000), but the criterion requires both rising transfers and falling median used prices, and the price limb cannot be settled on the data available for the full window. Not finding a settled answer here reflects the prediction's own horizon, not an absence of searching.

statement: By us being able to look at having enforcement on 1 May, which is what we’re working towards now with the prompt consideration that the committee is providing on this bill, that will actually provide a direct financial benefit to a number of those exporters in terms of the percentage of product they would otherwise be exporting through that month of May, in particular.
criterion: MFAT / EU Official Journal record of the entry-into-force date of the NZ–EU FTA; true if it entered into force on or about 1 May 2024 so that May exports received preferential tariff treatment, false if entry into force fell materially later.
reasoning: The NZ-EU FTA entered into force on 1 May 2024, the date van de Molen said they were working towards. The EU's Access2Markets notice is titled 'Application of EU-NZ FTA Agreement on 1 May 2024' and MFAT records that 91% of NZ's current trade into the EU became duty free from that date, so product exported during May 2024 received preferential tariff treatment. The predicted direct financial benefit is documented: the 8.8% EU tariff on NZ kiwifruit was removed immediately (~NZ$47m/yr), with onion exporters also named as beneficiaries of the May rather than mid-year start. Entry into force did not fall materially later, so the criterion's falsifying condition did not occur.

statement: In the case of kiwifruit, if we can get this work done this week, then the agreement will enter into force on 1 May, not 1 June or July or even 1 August, which was what some people thought it may take the time for the House to get through.
criterion: The NZ–EU FTA entry-into-force date as recorded by MFAT and the EU Official Journal; true if the agreement entered into force on 1 May 2024, false if it entered into force on any later date (the condition having been met by the bill passing that week).
reasoning: The stated condition was met (the European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Act 2024 passed that week, Royal Assent 25 March 2024) and the predicted consequence followed exactly: the agreement entered into force on 1 May 2024, not 1 June, July or August. Confirmed by MFAT (which lists the FTA as in force from 1 May 2024) and by the European Commission's Access2Markets entry-into-force notice for that date. Contemporary reporting explicitly attributes the May date to NZ Parliament expediting the legislation to help kiwifruit and onion exporters, which is the causal chain McClay asserted. No source records any later entry-into-force date.

statement: That is something that we are going to have to phase out after a transition period: we won’t be able to use that term.
criterion: NZ law and the NZ–EU FTA GI annex as implemented; true if, after the stated transition period, New Zealand cheese may no longer lawfully be sold domestically under the name 'feta', false if the term remains available to NZ producers.
reasoning: The criterion asks what is lawful AFTER the stated transition period, and that period has not ended: IPONZ records 'Feta' as a protected EU GI in New Zealand with a nine-year phase-out beginning 1 May 2024, i.e. running to about May 2033 (the criterion's own resolve-by date is 2033-05-01, still in the future as of September 2026). The enabling law is already in force (European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Act 2024, Royal Assent 25 March 2024, in force 1 May 2024), and legal commentary notes Feta has no grandfathering clause for existing NZ users, so on current law NZ-made cheese will not be able to be sold as 'feta' after the transition, and during it must carry a visible indication of NZ origin. I checked for a disconfirming carve-out or permanent prior-use right for NZ producers and found none. So the prediction is on track, but the state of affairs the criterion tests cannot be observed yet.

statement: But that is not going to change with pseudoephedrine being available as a suitable, practical, medical solution for colds and flus.
criterion: NZ Police clandestine laboratory detection statistics and pseudoephedrine-diversion reporting for the two years following the bill's commencement; true if pseudoephedrine-based clandestine lab detections stay at or near the pre-2024 baseline, false if they rise materially above it.
reasoning: Criterion: pseudoephedrine-based clan-lab detections stay at or near the pre-2024 baseline. NZ Police OIA data (IR-01-25-22265) gives 44 clandestine meth labs in the 12 months before pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacies (Jun 2023-May 2024) and 51 in the 12 months after (Jun 2024-May 2025) - a ~16% move on small, noisy counts, and nowhere near the pre-2011 era (211 labs in 2006). On diversion, the Pharmacy Guild and NZ Police report 'only a small number of isolated pseudoephedrine-related thefts from pharmacies' since the products returned, against 285,802 packs sold in the year to March 2026. The meth market's actual growth is attributed by Police and drug researchers to bulk importation and a ~41% real price fall, not domestic pharmacy-sourced manufacture; no expert commentary on the 2024-2026 consumption records names pseudoephedrine as a driver. Two limits worth stating: Police do not publish lab detections broken out by precursor type, so the criterion's exact measure does not exist as a published series, and no data covers the second year of the window (Jun 2025-May 2026). On everything published, the prediction holds; I looked for a post-2024 surge in labs or pharmacy diversion and did not find one.

statement: What was done back then hasn’t really fitted with what we wanted to see, so bringing this back in, as the Minister is doing at the moment—we don’t believe it’s going to lead to an explosion in methamphetamine consumption.
criterion: NZ Police/ESR wastewater methamphetamine consumption estimates and NZ Police clandestine-laboratory and precursor-diversion detections for the two years after pseudoephedrine returns to pharmacy sale. True if there is no marked rise in domestic manufacture from pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine and consumption does not step-change following the reclassification; false if lab detections or pharmacy precursor diversion rise sharply after the change.
reasoning: The criterion has two conjuncts and they split. (a) No marked rise in domestic manufacture from pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine: holds. Clan-lab detections went 44 (Jun 2023-May 2024) to 51 (Jun 2024-May 2025) per the NZ Police OIA - not a sharp rise - and the Pharmacy Guild and Police report only isolated pseudoephedrine thefts from pharmacies since May 2024. (b) Consumption does not step-change following the reclassification: fails on the face of it. Wastewater meth consumption went from 732 kg (2023) to 1,434 kg (2024), a 96% rise, with the jump landing between Q2 2024 (18.1 kg/week) and Q3 2024 (32.4 kg/week) - i.e. immediately after pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacies on 20 May 2024 - then 1,751 kg in 2025 and a record ~36.6 kg/week in Q1 2026, up 15% on the prior four quarters. Researchers called a doubling that fast 'almost unheard of'. So an explosion in consumption did occur in the period, but the causal link Uffindell was denying is not supported: Police, the Science Media Centre commentators and the UNODC attribute it to bulk importation (Asian and now North/Central American supply), offshore-run labs using imported precursors, and a 41% real price decline, and no analysis I found names pharmacy pseudoephedrine. The scale also rules it out arithmetically - total national pharmacy sales of ~285,802 packs a year could not yield the ~700 kg/year increase. Substance of the causal claim holds; the flat 'no explosion' framing does not. Second-year lab data (Jun 2025-May 2026) is not published, so (a) rests on year one.

statement: The good news for them is that in the not too distant future, there will be pseudoephedrine available from pharmacies, so they can take that and then recover their health and wellbeing and get back to work and continue living their lives in a lot more peaceful and enjoyable manner.
criterion: Whether pseudoephedrine-containing cold and flu products are actually on sale at New Zealand pharmacies (Medsafe product approvals plus pharmacy availability reporting). True if such products are purchasable from pharmacies within roughly a year of the bill's passage; false if supply does not materialise in that period. Note the speaker himself said importation had previously dried up for want of a market, so passage of the bill does not guarantee stock.
reasoning: Criterion: pseudoephedrine cold and flu products actually purchasable from NZ pharmacies within roughly a year of the bill's passage. The Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Act 2024 passed its third reading in March 2024 and products went on sale on 20 May 2024 - about two months later, and roughly ten weeks after this 19 March 2024 speech. Medsafe approved 11 pseudoephedrine cold and flu products (Nurofen, Codral, Sudafed, Demazin, Chemists' Own among them), sold as restricted/pharmacist-only medicines after a counter consultation. The speaker's own caveat about supply not materialising for want of a market did not come to pass: in the 12 months to 15 March 2026 pharmacies sold 285,802 packs, about 6.36 million doses, equivalent to roughly 5.4% of the population making a purchase. I checked for the disconfirming case - stock-outs, no approvals, products withdrawn - and found the opposite: Reckitt is now applying to move the products from behind the counter to open shelves. The prediction's other half (people 'recover their health and wellbeing') is rhetorical and not part of the criterion.

statement: As a result of this slowing in demand, the IMF expects inflation to come back into the Reserve Bank’s 1 percent to 3 percent target range in the third quarter of 2024.
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, annual inflation for the September 2024 quarter; true if the annual rate is between 1.0% and 3.0%, false if it is above 3.0% (or below 1.0%) in that quarter.
reasoning: Stats NZ recorded annual CPI inflation of 2.2% for the September 2024 quarter (quarterly rise 0.6%), inside the RBNZ's 1-3% target band and the first quarter back in band since 2021. The criterion's test — annual rate between 1.0% and 3.0% in the September 2024 quarter — is met.

statement: Conditions on the ground across Marlborough, Tasman, and Nelson districts are extremely dry and likely to get worse in the coming months.
criterion: NIWA soil moisture deficit / New Zealand Drought Index readings for Marlborough, Tasman and Nelson: true if deficits deepen relative to their March 2024 levels during the following months, false if conditions ease.
reasoning: The dry conditions were real and deepened for about three weeks, then reversed. Baseline (NIWA Hotspot Watch 22 March 2024): 'very dry to extremely dry' in Nelson and parts of Marlborough, a precipitation drought after Blenheim's driest Oct-Feb since 1941, hotspots in eastern Tasman, Nelson, parts of Marlborough; McClay had classified a medium-scale adverse event on 14 March. On 4 April soil moisture had decreased further and hotspots had expanded (northern and eastern Tasman, Nelson, parts of Marlborough), with northern Tasman the driest soils relative to normal — so 'likely to get worse' held short-term. But rain on 11-12 April (20-120 mm, Nelson 30-110 mm) ended 'one of the driest eight-month periods for Marlborough in 84 years'; by 23 April Marlborough had the South Island's wettest soils for the time of year; by the season's final Hotspot Watch (16 May) no hotspots remained in Tasman, Nelson or Marlborough and NZDI dryness was confined to Canterbury. Tasman/Nelson stayed drier than normal through autumn (50-79% of normal rainfall, pockets <50%; soils drier than normal at end of May), so dryness persisted — but deficits did not deepen relative to March levels over the following months, which is what the criterion required. Substance (extremely dry) holds; the 'get worse in the coming months' part failed after mid-April.

statement: And now, the changes—which I believe are probably just the start, because this Government, we know, has asked Whaikaha to find another 7.5 percent of cuts in funding.
criterion: Vote Social Development / Whaikaha disability support appropriations and purchasing rules in Budget 2024 and Budget 2025; true if further reductions to disability support funding or further narrowing of eligibility followed the March 2024 changes, false if the March changes stood alone with no subsequent reductions.
reasoning: Further reductions and narrowing followed the March 2024 purchasing-rule changes, as the criterion requires. The NZMJ editorial (14 Feb 2025) records that in August 2024 the government restructured Whaikaha, transferred DSS delivery to MSD (from October 2024), applied 'no financial uplift for the care and support of individuals with disabilities', froze new residential placements and kept flexible-funding restrictions in place; IHC confirms the freeze on residential facility-based care rates for the remainder of 2024/25, with NASCs and EGL sites directed to prioritise those most in need. Budget 2025 lifted the residential freeze (+$60m/yr, $240m over four years) but gave Disability Allowance only a 2.4% uplift and no new targeted funding for community-based support, and the April 2025 reset of individual budgets to 2023-25 actual spend reduced many allocations; the March 2024 rules were only reversed in 2026. So the March 2024 changes were not standalone. Caveat on the reason she gave rather than the prediction: Budget 2024 did add ~$1.1b over five years for cost pressures, and I found no source confirming Whaikaha specifically carried a 7.5% savings target — agencies were asked for either 6.5% or 7.5% of departmental baselines, not of disability support funding.

statement: We expect to receive an update on how they’re progressing with the implementation of a monitoring system by the end of this year.
criterion: Health Committee records and published correspondence: true if an update from the Ministry of Health or Te Whatu Ora on the pseudoephedrine monitoring/electronic dispensing system was provided to the committee on or before 31 December 2024; false if no such update was received in that period.
reasoning: The criterion points at Health Committee records and published correspondence, which are not publicly retrievable for 2024: parliament.nz publishes the committee's report on the bill but not incoming briefings or correspondence, the compendium of 2023/24 annual review reports is not text-searchable, and no news or parliamentary source records whether an update on the pseudoephedrine monitoring/electronic dispensing system reached the committee before 31 December 2024. Adjacent evidence exists but does not settle the criterion as written: the real-time monitoring system the Pharmaceutical Society of NZ asked for was never implemented (PSNZ: 'That hasn't happened so our focus now is on looking at how we can offer education resources'), and as of September 2026 New Zealand still does not require buyers to show ID or have purchases logged on a tracking system. That speaks to whether a system was built, not to whether a progress update was provided to the committee — an update reporting little or no progress would still satisfy the criterion. Absence of a public record is not evidence the update did not occur, so no score.

statement: So, actually, during the select committee process, we have been informed that there is little value to people interested in commercially supplying meth, and there are now cheaper and easier ways to manufacture it. This means that making pseudoephedrine products more available will have little effect on the New Zealand drug market.
criterion: New Zealand Police national wastewater methamphetamine consumption data and Police/Customs/National Drug Intelligence Bureau assessments in the 12–24 months after reclassification took effect: true if no documented rise in domestic pseudoephedrine-based meth manufacture or in market supply is attributed to the change; false if enforcement agencies report a material increase in pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine diversion into meth production.
reasoning: The criterion is satisfied: over the 12-24 months after pseudoephedrine products returned to pharmacies (June 2024), no Police, Customs or NDIB assessment attributes any rise in domestic pseudoephedrine-based manufacture or in market supply to the reclassification. Reporting as at September 2026 records that the Pharmacy Guild and New Zealand Police have seen 'only a small number of isolated pseudoephedrine-related thefts from pharmacies since the products returned'. Methamphetamine supply did rise sharply across the window — Police wastewater data show at least 1,751 kg consumed in 2025, continuing the elevated levels first seen in 2024, with 36.6 kg/week in Q1 2026 (up 15% on the prior four quarters) and prices lower than previous years — but that increase is attributed to bulk importation, not pharmacy diversion: Customs seized an estimated 976 kg of meth from January to May 2025, including 175 kg in a Mexican-origin scrap metal container at the Port of Tauranga, and the DEA's March 2025 assessment documents Mexican cartel supply into Australia and New Zealand. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for enforcement reports of pharmacy-sourced pseudoephedrine turning up at clan labs and found none; the one significant 2026 lab case (Operation Haste, June 2026) involved charges of importing precursors by an offshore cell. Note that officials' own pre-decision advice (the January 2024 RIS, reported by the Herald) did expect some increase in small-scale production, which has not been documented as materialising. Caveat on the market-supply limb of the criterion: supply rose materially in absolute terms; the prediction holds because the rise is not attributed to the change.

statement: But, of course, that level of supply coming into the country has meant the price of meth has dropped a lot, so any supply from pseudoephedrine would be at a fairly low level.
criterion: NZ Police clandestine laboratory detection statistics and wastewater methamphetamine data following the Act's commencement; true if pseudoephedrine-based domestic manufacture stays near post-2011 levels, false if clan lab detections or pseudoephedrine-linked seizures rise materially toward pre-2011 levels.
reasoning: Both limbs hold. The price premise: Police wastewater reporting confirms consumption at markedly elevated levels through 2025-Q1 2026 with prices 'lower than previous years', and 2025's average per-gram price was about a third of the 2010 price. The prediction — that any supply from pseudoephedrine would be at a fairly low level: pseudoephedrine-based domestic manufacture shows no move back toward pre-2011 levels. Clan lab detections had already fallen from roughly 130 in 2010 to 68 in 2015 (Bogun et al., 2009-2021 trend study), and no Police, Customs or NDIB source reports a resurgence after the Act commenced; the Pharmacy Guild and Police report only isolated pseudoephedrine thefts from pharmacies. Detected manufacture runs on imported precursor chemicals rather than pharmacy stock — the June 2026 Operation Haste arrests in Auckland charged an offshore cell with importing precursors, seizing an operational lab, ~10 kg of meth and pseudoephedrine. Disconfirming check: I searched for clan labs or seizures linked to pharmacy-sourced cold and flu tablets since 2024 and found no such case reported. Evidence limit: Police no longer publish an annual clandestine laboratory report and the 2023-25 OIA response holding monthly detection counts was not retrievable, so the specific detection series named in the criterion is inferred from the absence of any contrary enforcement reporting rather than read directly.

statement: The scheme will be fully operational next year, funded via industry levies. It will protect the first $100,000 of a deposit.
criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand announcements and the Deposit Takers Act commencement orders; true if the Depositor Compensation Scheme is in force during 2025 with a $100,000 per-depositor cap funded by levies on deposit takers, false if it has not commenced by the end of 2025 or commences on materially different terms.
reasoning: The Depositor Compensation Scheme came into force on 1 July 2025 under the Deposit Takers Act 2023 — within 'next year' of the March 2024 statement. It protects $100,000 per eligible depositor per licensed deposit taker and is funded by levies on deposit takers, administered by the Reserve Bank. All three elements of the criterion (in force during 2025, $100,000 per-depositor cap, levy-funded) are satisfied; no evidence of delay past 2025 or materially different terms.

statement: In the animal kingdom, a mayfly is an insect that lasts for one day; it is born, and then it perishes, and that will be the outcome for this bill—it will be addressed, it will be voted upon, and it will go the way of the mayfly.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of Rawiri Waititi's Goods and Services Tax (Removing GST from Food) Amendment Bill; true if the bill is defeated at that reading, false if it passes and is referred to select committee.
reasoning: Rawiri Waititi's Goods and Services Tax (Removing GST from Food) Amendment Bill was defeated at its first reading on 20 March 2024 by 117 votes to 6 — only Te Pāti Māori supported it, with National, ACT, NZ First, Labour and the Greens opposed. It was not referred to select committee, so the criterion's 'defeated at that reading' condition is met.

statement: I’d like to begin this final speech by saying, well, I’m pretty sad that this bill looks like it won’t make it through the first reading.
criterion: The division record for the question that the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill be now read a first time: the forecast is true if the noes exceed the ayes and the bill is defeated, false if the ayes prevail and the bill proceeds to select committee.
reasoning: The division on the first reading of the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Bill (20 March 2024) was 66 ayes to 57 noes — the ayes prevailed (Labour, Greens, Te Pāti Māori and ACT in support; National and NZ First opposed) and the bill was referred to select committee. It went on to receive royal assent on 18 November 2025 as the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Act 2025, confirming it survived the first reading. The criterion's 'true' branch (noes exceed ayes, bill defeated) did not occur.

statement: Now ratepayers are getting hit in the pocket, and it’s not going to end this year.
criterion: Council rates-setting decisions for the 2025/26 year and the LGNZ/Stats NZ local authority rates series; true if average rates increases in 2025 are again well above general inflation, false if they fall back to around the CPI.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether 2025 rates rises were again well above general inflation. Stats NZ's June 2025 quarter CPI release names local authority rates and payments as the largest upward contributor to annual inflation, up 12.2% against headline CPI of 2.7%; the Taxpayers' Union 2025 Rates Dashboard puts the average 2025/26 council rates increase at 8.39% vs ~2.5% annual inflation, and the three-year cumulative rise at 34.5% vs 13.7% inflation. Rates did not fall back toward CPI — central government's 2-4% cap was only announced in December 2025 and does not bite until 2027-29, so it cannot explain away the 2025 outturn.

statement: Well, congratulations to the member for getting this bill drawn, and, as is apparent from the speeches that have gone before, it looks pretty certain to make its way through, I imagine, the Justice Committee, and we look forward to having a good, old look at it there.
criterion: The House's first reading vote record for the Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passed first reading and was referred to the Justice Committee, false if it was defeated at first reading or referred to a different committee.
reasoning: The Corrections (Victim Protection) Amendment Bill (Rima Nakhle's member's bill) passed its first reading on 20 March 2024 without opposition and was referred to the Justice Committee, which opened submissions closing 6 May 2024. The criterion's true branch (passed first reading AND referred to the Justice Committee) is satisfied on both limbs; the bill later had its second reading on 6 November 2024 and committee of the whole House on 20 November 2024, confirming it survived the committee stage Webb predicted.

statement: Others will sympathise with this bill, but will not go as far as supporting this bill to eliminate poverty from this country.
criterion: The division record for the first reading of the Goods and Services Tax (Removing GST from Food) Amendment Bill; true if members or parties expressing sympathy in the first reading debate voted against it and the bill failed, false if the bill passed its first reading with the support of those members.
reasoning: The Goods and Services Tax (Removing GST from Food) Amendment Bill was defeated at first reading on 20 March 2024 by 6 votes to 117 — only Te Pati Maori's six MPs supported it. Parties that voiced sympathy in the debate voted against: Labour's Barbara Edmonds acknowledged the cost-of-living crisis but said there were 'better ways to support whanau without the removal of GST'; the Greens' Marama Davidson said there were 'better ways to combat poverty' while appreciating the intent; National cited the $2.6b fiscal cost. That is exactly the criterion's true condition (sympathisers voted against, bill failed). Disconfirming check: one search summary asserted the Greens voted 15 in favour, but three independent reports of the division (Waatea, Te Ao Maori News, Newsroom) record 6 for / 117 against with Te Pati Maori the sole supporter, so that summary is wrong.

statement: And thank you to the Minister of Local Government for declaring that we will be having an election in July.
criterion: Electoral Commission and Tauranga City Council records: true if polling for the Tauranga City Council election closed during July 2024; false if the election was held outside July 2024 or deferred again.
reasoning: The 2024 Tauranga City Council election ran 29 June to 20 July 2024; voting closed at 12 noon on Saturday 20 July 2024, with progress results that afternoon and final results 23-25 July. Polling therefore closed during July 2024, satisfying the criterion. No evidence of any further deferral.

statement: GDP is expected to pick up this year, although strong population growth will limit per capita growth.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and GDP per capita series covering calendar 2024; true if real GDP growth turns positive over 2024 (headline growth exceeding per capita growth), false if quarterly real GDP contracts over that period rather than picking up.
reasoning: Stats NZ reports real GDP FELL 0.5% over the year ended December 2024 versus the year ended December 2023. Quarterly real GDP went +0.2% (Mar), -1.1% (Jun), -1.0% (Sep), +0.7% (Dec) - two consecutive contractions, a technical recession and the worst non-COVID six months since 1991. The criterion's explicit false condition (quarterly real GDP contracting over the period rather than picking up) is met. Disconfirming check: the December 2024 quarter did grow 0.7% and per-capita GDP rose 0.4% that quarter, so the very end of the year turned up; but headline annual growth did not turn positive, and the 'headline exceeding per capita' test cannot be satisfied when headline is negative. Population growth also slowed sharply through 2024 rather than remaining strong.

statement: Today, the House will complete the final legislative process required to bring the New Zealand - European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) into force on 1 May, many months earlier than expected.
criterion: The official entry-into-force date of the New Zealand–European Union Free Trade Agreement, per MFAT and the EU's Official Journal. True if the agreement entered into force on 1 May 2024; false if it entered into force on any later date or not at all.
reasoning: MFAT's page on the agreement states plainly that the NZ-EU FTA 'entered into force on 1 May 2024', and the EU's own summary lists the same entry-into-force date. The criterion asked only for the official entry-into-force date, and it matches the predicted 1 May 2024 exactly.

statement: It’s a world of increasing geopolitical tension and growing protectionism, and that’s not going to change in the near future.
criterion: Global Trade Alert counts of new harmful trade-distorting interventions and the WTO Trade Monitoring Reports for 2024-2026; true if new trade-restrictive measures in 2025 are at or above the 2023 level, false if they fall materially and major trade tensions ease.
reasoning: Criterion: true if new trade-restrictive measures in 2025 are at or above the 2023 level; false if they fall materially and tensions ease. Global Trade Alert records >3,000 harmful interventions per year in 2022, 2023 and 2024, with 2025 G20 intervention volume on track to exceed 2023-24. WTO's Dec 2025 monitoring report: imports covered by new import-restrictive measures mid-Oct 2024 to mid-Oct 2025 were USD 2,640bn (11.1% of world imports) vs USD 611bn in the prior 12 months - more than fourfold and the highest coverage since the monitoring exercise began in 2009; cumulative coverage since 2009 rose from 12.6% to 19.7% of world imports in one year. Disconfirming check for easing found the opposite: the WTO-IMF Trade Policy Activity index for Jan-May 2026 is an all-time high, ~25% above the 2025 average and near double 2024, driven by restrictive measures and subsidies. Neither leg of the false condition holds.

statement: And so the end result is, by being able to complete the third reading today, we will see this agreement come into force on 1 May.
criterion: MFAT and European Commission announcements of the NZ–EU FTA's entry into force: true if the agreement entered into force on 1 May 2024, false if it entered into force on any other date or had not entered into force by then.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the NZ-EU FTA entered into force on 1 May 2024. It did. The European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Act 2024 received Royal assent on 25 March 2024 (four days after the third reading van de Molen was speaking in), and both MFAT and the European Commission's Access2Markets notice confirm the agreement applied from 1 May 2024. No delay or alternative date found.

statement: There will be more exports as a consequence of this, and the benefits to the New Zealand economy will be greater than that.
criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade statistics for New Zealand goods exports to the EU; true if the value/volume of exports to the EU rises above the pre-entry-into-force baseline within two years of the agreement taking effect, false if it is flat or falls over that period.
reasoning: Criterion: true if NZ goods exports to the EU rise above the pre-entry-into-force baseline within two years of 1 May 2024; false if flat or falling. Exports to the EU were $8.8bn in the year to December 2025, up 29% (~$1.9bn) on $5.7bn two years earlier, and the government's second-anniversary tally (May 2026, drawing on Stats NZ merchandise trade data) puts cumulative extra sales at about $3bn. Year to June 2025 alone was up 28% to $7.88bn, with dairy +64%, horticulture +38%, seafood +28% and industrial products +44%. Checked for the opposite - a flat or declining EU line - and found none; the EU is reported as NZ's fastest-growing goods export market since entry into force. The criterion tests only the export leg, so Parker's wider 'benefits to the economy will be greater than that' is not separately graded here.

statement: But remember, Hamas, you are not safe; you will face justice—that is clear. The Israelis will come after you.
criterion: Credible reporting on whether senior Hamas figures responsible for the 7 October 2023 attack were killed, captured or prosecuted; true if Israel demonstrably targeted and reached the Hamas leadership, false if the leadership remained intact and unpursued.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether Israel demonstrably targeted and reached the Hamas leadership responsible for 7 October. It did, repeatedly and within the window: Ismail Haniyeh assassinated in Tehran (July 2024), Mohammed Deif — head of the Qassam Brigades and an Oct 7 architect — confirmed killed (July 2024), Yahya Sinwar, the attack's principal architect, killed in Rafah on 17 October 2024, and Gaza chief Izz al-Din al-Haddad, also named by the IDF as an Oct 7 architect, killed in May 2026. On the prosecution limb, Israel's Knesset established a special military tribunal and roughly 2,300 detained participants in the attack await prosecution. Disconfirming check: the criterion's false condition was 'leadership remained intact and unpursued' — Hamas did survive as an organisation and elected Khalil al-Hayya political bureau chair in July 2026, but that is continuity of the movement, not an intact or unpursued leadership, so the criterion's true condition is the one that is met.

statement: A famine is imminent in Gaza.
criterion: A formal famine determination for any area of Gaza by the IPC Famine Review Committee: true if famine (IPC Phase 5, famine classification) is declared for a Gaza area within the period; false if the FRC reviews the evidence and declines to classify famine.
reasoning: The criterion required a formal IPC famine classification for some Gaza area by 2024-12-31, and named its own falsifier: the FRC reviewing the evidence and declining to classify famine. That falsifier fired. The IPC's 18 March 2024 analysis projected famine as imminent in North Gaza and Gaza governorates, but the FRC's June 2024 review concluded 'the available evidence does not indicate that Famine is currently occurring', attributing the change to increased food and non-food commodity flows into the northern governorates; it kept a high risk warning. The FRC's 8 November 2024 output was an alert about an imminent and substantial likelihood of famine, again not a classification, with the Strip in IPC Phase 4. So no famine classification landed inside the period. The substance was vindicated later: on 22 August 2025 the FRC confirmed Famine (IPC Phase 5) occurring in Gaza Governorate, projected to expand to Deir al-Balah and Khan Younis. Genuine catastrophic food insecurity throughout, and famine did eventually arrive — but 'imminent' overstated the timing by roughly 17 months against the window the criterion set, hence partly correct rather than correct.

statement: If we think, or that Government thinks, that what is going on in Gaza is going to secure the rights of the Jewish State, or peace in the Middle East, they are dreaming.
criterion: The state of the Israel–Palestine conflict two years on. False (i.e. the forecast failed) if a durable settlement or lasting cessation of hostilities is in force and holding by the resolve-by date; true (forecast correct) if hostilities, occupation or recurrent conflict continue without a settled peace.
reasoning: The criterion fails the forecast only if a durable settlement or lasting cessation of hostilities was in force and holding by 2026-03-26. Checking the disconfirming side first, since a ceasefire does exist: the 10 October 2025 ceasefire was in force at the resolve-by date and had largely held, and the US declared transition to Phase Two on 14 January 2026. But it was not a settled peace. Reporting dated 27 March 2026 describes a shaky ceasefire with continuing Israeli operations against Hamas from air, sea and land; Gaza's health ministry counted 702 killed and 1,913 injured between 10 October 2025 and 29 March 2026, and Gaza's media office documented over 2,073 violations in that period. Phase Two negotiations on disarmament and Israeli withdrawal were stalled, the Board of Peace and the NCAG had been named in January 2026 but neither was operational on the ground, and Israeli forces still held territory inside Gaza. Hostilities, occupation and recurrent conflict continued without a settled peace, which is the criterion's true condition.

statement: We know that the economic modelling suggests that by 2035 this agreement will generate up to $1.4 billion to New Zealand.
criterion: MFAT/NZIER modelling published with the National Interest Analysis, checked against realised NZ export gains to the EU attributable to the agreement by 2035; true if the annual uplift approaches the $1.4 billion figure, false if realised gains are materially below it.
reasoning: The cited modelling is real and accurately stated: MFAT's National Interest Analysis / economic modelling for the NZ-EU FTA projects up to NZD$1.4 billion per year added to NZ's real GDP (and up to $1.8b/yr in extra exports to the EU) by 2035. The criterion asks for realised export gains attributable to the agreement by 2035; the FTA only entered into force 1 May 2024 and the target year is 2035, so no realised-outcome evidence can exist yet. Found no source claiming the target has been met or missed.

statement: An estimated 21,000 low to middle income families will qualify for the maximum reimbursement of $975 every three months, and, in total, FamilyBoost will help support more than 140,000 children and their families.
criterion: Inland Revenue's published FamilyBoost uptake statistics after the scheme's first year; true if roughly 21,000 families received the maximum $975 quarterly payment and more than 140,000 children/families were supported, false if the actual numbers fall materially short of either figure.
reasoning: Both figures fell materially short. IR data to 9 April 2025 show 249 families receiving the maximum $975 per quarter, versus the 21,000 forecast (~84x short); Willis publicly conceded the modelling was wrong. To 2 July 2025 IR had paid ~$50.6m across 138,800 claims for 60,500 households, against 'more than 140,000 children and their families'; registrations were only ~60,000-78,000 households and IR revised its estimate of families entitled to any payment down from ~130,000/100,000 to 106,000. The shortfall drove the July 2025 amendments (rebate 25%->40%, cap $75->$120/week, income limit to ~$230k/yr). The later figure of 97,500 families having received a payment (July 2026) is under those changed settings, not the ones described.

statement: Other countries are progressing trade negotiations with the UAE—including Australia, who are expected to conclude a deal by the end of this year—so the Government is committed to ensuring New Zealand exporters remain competitive in that market.
criterion: Australian DFAT announcements on the Australia-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement: true if negotiations were declared concluded on or before 31 December 2024, false if they remained open past that date.
reasoning: DFAT records Australia-UAE CEPA negotiations as commencing 13 December 2023 and concluding on 17 September 2024, with the agreement signed 6 November 2024 and entering into force 1 October 2025. Conclusion occurred well before the 31 December 2024 deadline in the criterion, so the expectation McClay reported held. No evidence of negotiations remaining open past 2024.

statement: With that context, as laid out, I have a few questions which I’d love to get the Minister of Revenue’s response on, particularly because what we’re seeing with the Amendment Papers in the Minister’s name are amendments primarily to Part 2 of this legislation with regard to the commitments that were made throughout the election process and that we’ll obviously see reflected in the upcoming Budget in May.
criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Budget Economic and Fiscal Update and the tax package announced on Budget day): true if the Budget delivered in May 2024 implements the governing parties' election tax commitments, in particular the personal income tax threshold changes; false if the Budget contains no such measures or they are deferred beyond it.
reasoning: Budget 2024, delivered 30 May 2024, implemented the governing parties' election tax commitments as the criterion specifies. The Taxation (Budget Measures) Bill introduced on Budget day raised the bottom three personal income tax thresholds — to $15,600 (from $14,000), $53,500 (from $48,000) and $78,100 (from $70,000) — effective 31 July 2024, alongside an expanded Independent Earner Tax Credit, increased In-Work and Minimum Family Tax Credits, and FamilyBoost. IRD and commentators describe these as the last of the tax commitments National and its coalition partners campaigned on. Disconfirming check: the measures were not deferred past the Budget (they were legislated on Budget day under urgency and took effect 31 July 2024), so the false branch of the criterion does not apply. Minor slippage from the campaign package — the start date moved from 1 July to 31 July 2024 and the foreign buyer levy that was to fund part of it was dropped — does not touch the criterion, which turns on whether the threshold changes appeared in the May Budget. They did.

statement: I’m personally confident, based on, you know, the history of these things, in terms of how long it takes to thrash out these arguments as fully as I think we’re doing now, that we will be done in time.
criterion: The Hansard and Order Paper record for the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill. True if the bill completed its committee of the whole House and remaining stages before 1 April 2024; false if the House was still on the bill on or after that date.
reasoning: The bill completed its remaining stages well before 1 April 2024. On 26 March the House agreed to a motion by the Minister of Revenue 'that the sitting of the House today be extended into tomorrow morning to complete the remaining stages of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill' (Hansard p. 2378, agreed 102–21). The committee of the whole House was still on Part 3 when the sitting was suspended at 9.58 p.m. and resumed at 9 a.m. on 27 March; IRD's bill page records the committee stage and third reading under 26 March 2024 (the sitting day that ran into Wednesday morning), and the Act received Royal assent on 28 March 2024 as the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Act 2024. Disconfirming check: no stage of this bill appears on the separate 27 March sitting's order of business (that day opened with prayers, oral questions, the general debate, and other bills), and no post-1 April stage exists — the deadline that mattered, enacting the annual rates before the end of the 2023–24 tax year on 31 March, was met.

statement: I think we’re going to have to settle in for quite a long night, because that’s just in the bill, and that’s leaving aside the Amendment Paper.
criterion: Hansard sitting record for 26–27 March 2024; true if the committee of the whole House stage on this bill continued for several further hours or the House sat past midnight, false if the debate concluded during ordinary evening sitting hours.
reasoning: The substance held but the 'long night' did not happen. Hansard for 26 March records the committee stage running from p. 2379 through Part 1, Part 2 and into Part 3 (p. 2435–2438), with Russell speaking in the pre-dinner block (her contributions begin at p. 2380; the maiden statement immediately before the dinner break is at p. 2403) and the debate continuing for several further hours after that — it was still unfinished at the end of the evening, which satisfies the criterion's first true-branch. But the House did not sit past midnight: earlier that evening it had agreed, 102–21, to Simon Watts' motion 'that the sitting of the House today be extended into tomorrow morning to complete the remaining stages' (p. 2378), and Hansard records the Chairperson saying 'The time has come for me to leave the Chair. The House is suspended until 9 a.m. tomorrow' with 'Sitting suspended from 9.58 p.m. (Tuesday) to 9 a.m. (Wednesday)' (p. 2438). Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for a post-midnight sitting — the Hansard section id HansDeb_20240326_20240327_72 does show part of the 26 March sitting occurring on 27 March, but the printed timestamp shows that continuation was the 9 a.m. Wednesday resumption, not an overnight sitting; members rose two minutes before the ordinary 10 p.m. adjournment. The overrun was moved to the morning rather than the night.
