statement: But, specifically, we’re talking here about affordability of homes, and in doing what the Government is proposing, it will do the reverse of what the justification was and the rationale behind bringing it in in the first place—even albeit for two years—right when the housing crisis was really getting going, to try and discourage speculation within the market.
criterion: CoreLogic / REINZ buyer-classification data on the investor share of residential purchases, and Inland Revenue or CoreLogic data on properties resold within two years, comparing the two years after the 1 July 2024 change with the two years before; true if investor share and short-hold resale activity rise materially, false if they are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion's two tests split. Short-hold resale activity did rise materially: Cotality's Nick Goodall reported contemporaneous settlements (a property bought and on-sold the same day — the standard flip) lifted to nearly double 2024's level in 2025, the busiest year since 2007, and higher than the Covid boom, prompting a Real Estate Authority complaint in March 2026. Investor share rose more modestly: mortgaged multiple property owners went from ~21% of purchases in Q1 2024 (near all-time lows) to ~24% across 2025 and ~25% in Q1 2026, then eased to 22.5% in Q2 2026 — a recovery to roughly the long-run average of 24%, not a speculative surge, and Cotality attributes it jointly to the shorter brightline test, the mid-2024 LVR easing, full reinstatement of interest deductibility from 1 April 2025 and falling mortgage rates, so the brightline change cannot be isolated. Crucially, McAnulty framed the claim around 'affordability of homes' doing 'the reverse' of the policy's rationale, and affordability improved over the window: national values fell 1% over 2025 to a median $808,430, 17.6% below the early-2022 peak, with mortgage rates well down. Speculative churn returned as he predicted; the affordability harm he predicted did not.

statement: The broader points that are raised by the member are part of the broader gambling system, and I think what I can say is that the introduction of this gambling duty component to those offshore gambling operators will potentially look to increase the amount of gambling activity from offshore back through to those domestic providers, whether they’re gambling operators in pubs or clubs, Lotto, the TAB in New Zealand, or other aspects such as that.
criterion: Department of Internal Affairs gambling expenditure statistics and TAB NZ / Lotto NZ annual turnover for the first full year after the offshore gambling duty commenced (1 July 2024), compared with the preceding year. True if domestic operator turnover in these categories rises after commencement; false if it is flat or falls.
reasoning: DIA gambling expenditure for 2024/25 — the first full year after the 12% offshore gambling duty commenced on 1 July 2024 — moved in only one of the categories Watts named. TAB racing and sports betting rose about 6%, from $371m in 2023/24 to $393.4m; but NZ Lotteries fell about 5% ($792m to $754.3m), non-casino gaming machines (the 'pubs or clubs' category) fell about 2% ($1,037m to $1,015.4m), and casinos fell about 8% ($592m to $545.1m). Total domestic expenditure fell roughly 3%, from $2.79bn to $2.71bn. Lotto NZ's own result corroborates its decline: sales down 5% to NZ$1.63bn for the year to 30 June 2025. Nor did offshore activity shrink: DIA's May 2026 bank-card analysis put offshore online gambling at NZ$1.36bn a year (Oct 2023–Sep 2025), with monthly spend above NZ$100m continuously since March 2024 and ~360,000 customers by September 2025. So the substance holds narrowly and only where an offshore substitute actually exists — sports and race betting, where TAB grew ~6% in 2024/25 and NZ thoroughbred domestic turnover then rose a further 7.5% to $510.8m in 2025/26 — while the categories with no offshore competitor, which Watts explicitly named, all fell. Watts's prediction was hedged ('potentially look to increase'), but on the criterion as written most named categories fell rather than rose.

statement: We will return to a home-buying market where first-home buyers are systematically—because of the way this is regulated—locked out of the market.
criterion: CoreLogic (or REINZ) buyer-classification data on first-home buyers' share of residential property purchases: true if the first-home buyer share falls materially below its early-2024 level (~26%) and the investor share correspondingly rises over the two years following the change; false if the first-home buyer share holds at or above that level.
reasoning: The criterion's falsifying condition was met directly: the first-home buyer share held at or above its early-2024 level of ~26%, and in fact set repeated records. CoreLogic/Cotality buyer classification put first-home buyers at 26% of purchases in the March 2024 quarter (26.1% for calendar 2024, itself then a record). After the 1 July 2024 change the share rose: 28.2-28.4% in Q4 2025 (a series record), 27.5% in Q1 2026, and 28.3% in Q2 2026, against a long-term average of about 22%. First-home buyers bought roughly 24,800 properties in the year to Q1 2026, the highest annual volume since Q3 2021, and 77% of their purchases were standalone houses, up from 75% a year earlier — they were not pushed into lesser stock. The investor side also fails the 'correspondingly rises' test: mortgaged multiple property owners recovered from ~21% to ~24-25% but were back to 22.5% by Q2 2026, below their 24% long-run average, and the largest landlords (10+ mortgaged properties) cut to 2.3% of purchases, a seven-year low. Commentators in 2026 were describing a 'Goldilocks year' for first-home buyers, the opposite of systematic lock-out. I looked for the disconfirming case — a post-2024 slump in first-home buyer share, or investors outbidding them — and found neither; investors' median price paid actually fell from $770,000 to $759,000 while first-home buyers' rose from $695,000 to $700,000.

statement: Depriving landlords of the ability to be able to claim mortgage interest deductions has made residential property less attractive as an investment, and this is simply a matter of supply and demand, as with more landlords offering properties, upward pressure on rents will resolve.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (annual growth, stock measure) and MBIE tenancy bond mean weekly rents: true if annual rent inflation by mid-2026 is materially below the rate recorded at March 2024, false if it is unchanged or higher.
reasoning: Criterion: rent inflation by mid-2026 materially below the March 2024 rate. Stats NZ CPI 'actual rentals for housing' annual change was 4.66% in Q1 2024 and 0.53% in Q2 2026 — the smallest annual increase since the December 2001 quarter. Stats NZ Selected Price Indexes (via MCERT's June quarter 2026 Housing Market Update) put the year to June 2026 at +1.0% for new tenancies (flow) and +0.2% for existing tenancies (stock), after a period of outright decline through 2024-25 (Wellington -9.0% in the year to May 2025). MBIE bond data agrees in direction: Auckland's median rent for the year to April 2026 was $635/week, down from $650 a year earlier (MBIE bond data is provisional pending a system migration). Disconfirming check: no series shows rent inflation at or above the March 2024 rate; the June 2026 reading is a rebound off a lower trough, but still far below 4.66%. Caveat for the scorecard, not the verdict: the criterion tests only the outcome. MCERT attributes the moderation to elevated housing supply, weak demand, low net migration and a soft labour market, and describes investor activity as weak/subdued — so the specific mechanism Watts named (more landlords offering properties) is not established by this evidence.

statement: Let’s not forget who is paying for this cash handout to landlords: it’s the kids at school who won’t be getting school lunches anymore, it’s disabled people and their carers, and it’s people on benefits, whose lives will get much worse so that landlords can get even richer.
criterion: Budget 2024 and subsequent Ka Ora, Ka Ako | Healthy School Lunches Programme decisions: true if the programme is discontinued or its coverage reduced so that students who were receiving lunches no longer do; false if the programme continues to serve the same or a larger cohort.
reasoning: Criterion: true if Ka Ora, Ka Ako is discontinued or coverage reduced so students who were receiving lunches no longer do; false if it continues to serve the same or a larger cohort. The programme continued and the cohort grew. Before the Budget 2024 changes it served over 220,000 students at 989 schools (May 2023); by late January 2025, under the revamped model, 244,144 students across 1,014 schools. As of 2026 it delivers around a million lunches a week to roughly 240,000 students in over 1,000 schools, and from Term 1 2026 it expanded to 52,000 primary students across 188 schools. On 15 May 2026 the government committed $212m to continue it through the 2027 school year. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for schools or cohorts losing eligibility. What I found was restructuring, not withdrawal of coverage — per-meal funding was cut sharply (from $6.99/$8.90 to about $3-$4), Compass Group was dropped from the 2026 contract, and one iwi provider (Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rārua, 1,200 meals/day across eight schools) withdrew saying funding no longer covered costs. Those are provider and funding changes; no eligible student cohort stopped receiving lunches. The 'cash handout to landlords was paid for by kids losing school lunches' prediction fails against the criterion as written.

statement: Catherine Wedd in her contribution said this bill will improve the economy. No, it won’t. It will have the opposite effect. It will once again encourage over-investment by landlords in the residential property sector, sucking out investment from the productive economy and driving up house prices so that it will no longer be affordable by people who just want one home to live in.
criterion: REINZ House Price Index and RBNZ C31 new-lending-by-borrower-type series for the two years following the bill's commencement (1 April 2024); true if the investor share of new mortgage lending rises materially and the house price index rises in real terms, false if the investor share is flat or falls and real house prices do not rise.
reasoning: Criterion: true if the investor share of new mortgage lending rises materially AND the house price index rises in real terms over the two years from 1 April 2024; false if the investor share is flat or falls and real house prices do not rise. Both legs go against the prediction. Prices: REINZ HPI was -0.6%/-0.7% annually at June 2026, and MCERT describes national house prices as 'broadly flat over the past two years', with average prices back at their March 2021 levels by the March 2026 quarter. With annual CPI inflation at 4.1% in the June 2026 quarter, real house prices clearly fell rather than rose. Affordability moved the opposite way to Parker's claim: rental affordability improved 4.2% annually to March 2026 and mortgage serviceability improved 13.1%. Investor share: Cotality has mortgaged multiple-property-owners at 21% of purchases in Q2 2023, 21% in Q2 2024 and 22.5% in Q2 2026 — still below the ~24% long-run average since 2005. RBNZ C31 for June 2026 has investors at 19.5% of new lending (first-home buyers 19%, other owner-occupiers 60.4%) with investor lending down 8.6% year-on-year. Disconfirming check: one series does support Parker in part — C31 value share rose from about 17% in 2023 to 21.1% in the eleven months to November 2025, and investor loan counts rose from roughly 2,000/month in early 2024 to about 2,900 by May 2026. But that peak has since unwound to 19.5% and MCERT expects investor activity 'to remain subdued'. A modest, partly-reversed rise in investor share plus falling real house prices is the criterion's false condition, not its true one.

statement: They won’t be going up at that rate.
criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services bond-lodgement national median weekly rent for the two years from April 2024; true if the average annual increase is materially below ~$28 per week per year, false if it matches or exceeds that pace.
reasoning: MBIE/Tenancy Services bond-lodgement national median weekly rent first reached $600/week in December 2023 and was still $600/week in May 2026, sitting at that level for 19 of the 30 intervening months; it was $595 in November 2025 (down $5, -0.8% y/y) and $600 in May 2026 (up $5, +0.8% y/y). Over the two years from April 2024 the average annual increase is therefore ~$0-$5 per week per year, far below the criterion's ~$28/week/year threshold. Checked for disconfirming evidence: a $625 national median circulating for April 2026 is the Trade Me Property listings index, not bond data, and was itself $5 lower than a year earlier; regional exceptions exist (Southland +$25/wk, Otago ~$700) but the national bond series is flat.

statement: We will see the bad old days of mum and dad speculators getting into the burbs, competing with their kids on existing houses rather than doing what we as a country need them to do, and that is building new stock.
criterion: CoreLogic NZ buyer classification data on the investor share of purchases of existing dwellings versus new builds; true if the investor share of existing-dwelling purchases rises materially through 2025 relative to 2023-24 while the new-build share falls, false if the pattern does not shift or moves the other way.
reasoning: Both legs of the predicted pattern moved in the direction Woods named, but only marginally, and they reversed. Cotality (CoreLogic NZ) buyer classification: the mortgaged multiple-property-owner share of purchases lifted from cyclical lows of ~22% in 2022-24 to nearly 24% in 2025, and Cotality attributes the lift to smaller/newer investors buying lower price bands and existing properties. Over the same period new builds fell from 31% to ~30% of mortgaged-MPO activity - a 1pp slip Cotality itself calls 'only marginally lower' and still well above the 25% share in 2020. Disconfirming evidence is substantial: by Q2 2026 mortgaged MPOs were back down to 22.5%, below their ~24% long-run average, while first-home buyers took 28.3% of purchases, a record for the series, and landlords with 10+ mortgaged properties cut to 2.3%, a seven-year low (down from 4.1% at end-2023). New stock also kept growing rather than stalling: 37,813 new homes consented in the year to March 2026, up 11% on the prior year. So the substance holds weakly for 2025 but is materially overstated relative to 'the bad old days of mum and dad speculators... competing with their kids'.

statement: What is his response to the fact that this effective cut to the minimum wage will increase child poverty rates, given that 64 percent of families in poverty are in work?
criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics (material hardship and the below-50%-of-median after-housing-costs measures); true if child poverty rises for the year to June 2025 relative to the year to June 2024 beyond sampling error, false if it falls or is statistically unchanged.
reasoning: Stats NZ's Child Poverty Statistics for the year ended June 2025 (released 26 February 2026) is headlined 'No annual change in child poverty rates for year ended June 2025'. On the three primary measures against the year ended June 2024: material hardship 13.5% -> 14.3% (~169,300 children), BHC50 12.7% -> 12.6%, AHC50 18.2% -> 17.8%. Stats NZ states none of the annual changes were statistically significant. The criterion required a rise beyond sampling error and explicitly scores 'falls or is statistically unchanged' as false. Looked for disconfirming evidence: the material hardship point estimate did move up, and it is a statistically significant increase measured against 2022 (10.6%) and 2021, with much higher rates for Pacific children (31%), tamariki Maori (25.1%) and disabled children (26.9%) - but none of that satisfies the year-on-year test as written.

statement: Already, 113,000 cubic metres of dirt has been moved of the 145,000 cubic metres which need to be moved, and there is more work to be done. It will be open over Easter and completed in May.
criterion: NZTA/Waka Kotahi announcements on SH1 Brynderwyn Hills; true if the road opened to traffic over the 2024 Easter period and the recovery works were completed with the highway reopened during May 2024, false if completion slipped past 31 May 2024.
reasoning: The Easter limb of the prediction held: NZTA opened SH1 over the Brynderwyn Hills for six days over Easter 2024 before closing it again. The May limb failed: fresh slips on 26 and 30 April 2024 (including at Kauri Tree Corner, needing up to 55,000 m3 of extra excavation) pushed the planned 13 May reopening out, and the highway reopened to two-way traffic only at 11.59pm on 26 June 2024, with final surfacing in November and cost rising to ~$84m. The criterion's explicit false trigger (completion slipping past 31 May 2024) was met, so the timing claim is wrong; the Easter claim was right, hence partly_correct rather than wrong.

statement: Well, we know what that’s going to mean: more taxes for New Zealanders by that party on the other side.
criterion: Labour's published tax policy for the next general election campaign; true if it proposes any new tax or an increase to an existing tax rate or base, false if it proposes no new or increased taxes.
reasoning: Labour's published tax policy for the 7 November 2026 election, announced 28 October 2025, is a 28% capital gains tax on gains from residential investment property and commercial property made on or after 1 July 2027, with revenue ring-fenced for health (three free GP visits). That is a new tax, which is exactly what the criterion asks. Disconfirming check: Hipkins states CGT is the only new tax Labour will introduce, the family home, farms, shares and KiwiSaver are exempt, and no income-tax-rate rise is proposed — so the burden falls on property investors rather than New Zealanders generally, and the plural framing 'more taxes for New Zealanders' is looser than the policy. Under the criterion as written ('any new tax or an increase to an existing tax rate or base'), the prediction resolves correct.

statement: When it comes into force, it will increase our exports via the EU by $1.8 billion annually—a substantial amount from a Government that is focused on trade and trading with the world.
criterion: Stats NZ / MFAT data on New Zealand goods and services exports to the EU; true if annual exports to the EU are at least NZ$1.8 billion higher than the pre-agreement baseline, false if the increase is materially smaller by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The $1.8 billion figure comes from government-commissioned economic modelling in MFAT's National Interest Analysis, which projects exports to the EU up to NZ$1.8b per annum higher 'by 2035' (plus ~$1.4b GDP) — not on entry into force as the speaker framed it. The FTA entered into force 1 May 2024, so only about two years of data exist. Interim MFAT figures show exports to the EU up 28% to $7.88b in the year to June 2025, directionally consistent but well short of a settled counterfactual test and not attributable to the FTA alone. The criterion's resolve-by date is 31 December 2035, which has not passed, so this cannot be graded yet.

statement: But just another area where we are going to improve things is with interest deductibility, which will put downward pressures on rents and not keep adding costs to landlords, which are then passed on to renters. We need to put downward pressure on rents.
criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price index for new tenancies: true if national median weekly rent growth decelerates materially or turns negative over the two years following the phased restoration of interest deductibility from 1 April 2024; false if rent growth continues at or above its pre-April-2024 pace.
reasoning: The criterion's true-condition is met on both named sources. HUD's new-tenancy (flow) rental price index dates the peak of rental inflation to December 2023 (pre-April-2024; Barfoot's Auckland series was +5.3% YoY then), and by July 2025 national new-tenancy rents were down 0.1% YoY, down 0.4% by September 2025, with Wellington -6%. MBIE bond data shows the national median rent for new tenancies at $600/week in May 2026, up only $5 (+0.8%) in a year, and at $600 for 19 of the preceding 30 months; Hawke's Bay -3.7%, Auckland and Canterbury unchanged. So over the two years after the 1 April 2024 phased restoration, rent growth decelerated materially and in several regions turned negative — the opposite of 'continues at or above its pre-April-2024 pace'. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no national new-tenancy measure shows growth sustained at the 2023 pace. Caveat the criterion does not test: this is an outcome, not attribution — commentators credit falling net migration and record rental listings, and the government's own deductibility change is not established as the cause.

statement: The prospect of the shorter-term gains will stimulate economic activity in New Zealand and increase property transactions, which will lead to higher demand for related goods and services: construction, renovation, real estate agency services, repairs and maintenance, and everything that goes with maintaining a rental property.
criterion: REINZ monthly residential sales volumes: true if national sales counts in the twelve months following the 1 July 2024 brightline reduction exceed the preceding twelve months by a clear margin, false if volumes are flat or lower.
reasoning: REINZ monthly national sales counts in the twelve months after the 1 July 2024 brightline reduction exceeded the preceding twelve months by a clear margin. Month-on-year: Jul 2024 +14.5% (5,070 to 5,806), Aug 2024 -0.7% (5,725 to 5,685), Sep 2024 about -1%, Oct 2024 +20.0%, Dec 2024 +1.8% (5,420 to 5,518), Mar 2025 +12.8% (6,774 to 7,640), May 2025 +8.9% (7,166), Jun 2025 +20.3% (4,877 to 5,865). Only two small negative months, against several double-digit gains. For confirmation on a calendar basis, REINZ's year in review puts 2025 at 80,655 sales, +10.3% on 2024. Disconfirming check: the one headline suggesting June 2025 sales 'declined' refers to month-on-month/seasonally adjusted movement, not the year-on-year raw count. Two caveats the criterion does not test: REINZ and bank commentary attribute the recovery mainly to OCR cuts and easier credit rather than the brightline change, and the quote's other leg (construction, renovation and maintenance demand) was not part of the stated test and was not verified here.

statement: We expect that around 4,500 extra New Zealanders will benefit from this boost.
criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand reporting on national travel assistance uptake after the March 2024 changes; true if the number of people receiving NTA rises by approximately 4,500 (within an order of the stated figure) relative to the pre-change baseline, false if the increase is materially smaller.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Ministry of Health / Health NZ reporting on the number of PEOPLE receiving NTA after the March 2024 changes, and that number is not reported anywhere findable. The pre-change baseline is documented: Health NZ's 26 March 2024 NTA FAQ says the scheme cost $33-35M a year supporting 28,000-33,000 people, and that the changes 'will result in an additional spend of up to $18 million per year and are estimated to benefit an additional 4,500 patients.' The only post-change national figures released are counts of CLAIMS, not patients: Health NZ's OIA response HNZ00095569 (9 September 2025) gives FY2024-25 as 41,122 claims and $50,033,767.82 paid nationally, and expressly refuses the patient-linked questions under s18(g), stating the number of claims 'may not correlate with the number of patients making the claims' and that producing person counts would require creating new information. Searched Health NZ publications, its 2024/25 annual report listing, and FYI OIA releases for any unique-patient series; none exists. Two indirect signals, neither sufficient to settle the criterion: spend did rise roughly in line with the promised $18M boost (about $34M to $50M), which is consistent with wider benefit; but the same OIA states the scheme's current eligibility requirements were put in place in August 2009, and the March 2024 FAQ said eligibility changes were 'yet to be confirmed' - so the main mechanism for adding new claimants appears not to have been implemented, which points toward a smaller increase. Inference either way is not the reported number the criterion names, and absence of the figure is not evidence the boost failed.

statement: At one minute past midnight tonight, State Highway 1 over the Brynderwyns reopens for Easter.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi road status notices and contemporaneous news reports: true if SH1 over the Brynderwyn Hills reopened to traffic in the early hours of 28 March 2024 as stated, false if the reopening was delayed beyond that time.
reasoning: NZTA's media release set the reopening at 12:01am Thursday 28 March 2024 (until 11:59pm Tuesday 2 April), matching McCallum's "one minute past midnight tonight" said on 27 March. RNZ's follow-up report, headlined that the highway "closes after temporarily reopening for Easter", confirms the opening actually occurred rather than being deferred; the road then closed again at 12:01am Wednesday 3 April. Checked specifically for a delay to the 28 March opening and found none — the only Brynderwyns delay reported in 2024 was to the later, post-Easter reopening (pushed from 12 May to end of June after fresh slips), which is a different event.

statement: The rate they proposed for electric vehicles was 60 instead of 78 per 1,000 kilometres, and the reason for this reduced rate is because we are very much in a period where if we don’t have some sort of support or financial incentive to electrify the fleet, it will slow down, and that has very serious consequences for meeting our greenhouse gas reduction targets later in the period.
criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport light EV (BEV) registration statistics: true if new and used light BEV registrations in the 12 months after 1 April 2024 fall materially below the equivalent 12 months to March 2024; false if EV registrations hold steady or rise.
reasoning: The criterion's test is met: light EV registrations in the 12 months from April 2024 fell materially below the 12 months to March 2024. EV share of new registrations fell from 20.6% in December 2023 to 3.8% in March 2024 and was still only 7.1% in December 2024; monthly new EV registrations were 638 in August 2024 against 1,404 in August 2023; and the EV fleet grew 9.7% in 2024 (103,665 to 113,715) versus more than 50% in each of the three Clean Car Discount years. Two qualifications that fall outside the criterion but bear on how much credit the prediction earns: the dominant cause was the Clean Car Discount ending 31 December 2023 plus demand pulled forward into that deadline, not the RUC rate Genter was arguing about, and the slowdown later reversed (BEV registrations up 286% in March 2026 on March 2025). Her incidental figure is also slightly wrong — the gazetted light-BEV rate was $76 per 1,000km, not 78.

statement: But one of the observations is that as pseudoephedrine becomes more readily available, the group of frequent drug users in New Zealand will use this drug and, potentially, use it to manufacture methamphetamine.
criterion: NZ Police clandestine-laboratory detection statistics and ESR/wastewater and Customs precursor reporting for the two years after pseudoephedrine returns to pharmacy sale; true if domestic pseudoephedrine-based methamphetamine manufacture (clan lab detections or pharmacy-diversion prosecutions) rises materially above the pre-2024 baseline, false if detections stay flat or continue falling.
reasoning: The criterion names NZ Police clandestine-laboratory detection statistics, ESR/wastewater and Customs precursor reporting for the two years after pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacy sale (it returned around May-June 2024, earlier than the originally announced 2025). None of those series is publicly available for that window: the most recent published clan-lab detection series ends at 2021 (Bogun et al.), the only newer figures sit in a 2025 Police OIA response whose PDF could not be retrieved, and Customs' drug-interception tables are not broken out by precursor in accessible form. Evidence found in both directions is anecdotal rather than statistical — a Motueka pharmacy burgled for pseudoephedrine within a week of its return in May 2024, and pseudoephedrine seized alongside 10kg of methamphetamine in Operation Haste (June 2026), against the pre-change Regulatory Impact Statement's assessment that NZ manufacture had already shifted to bulk imported precursor. The 96% rise in wastewater methamphetamine consumption in 2024 does not speak to the criterion, since it reflects imported supply, not domestic pseudoephedrine-based manufacture. Nothing establishes either a material rise or a flat/falling trend against the pre-2024 baseline, so no verdict on the criterion as written is supportable.

statement: I think, sadly, it is unlikely that anything we’re doing right now is going to stop that supply.
criterion: NZ Police/ESR national wastewater drug testing programme and Police seizure data: true if methamphetamine consumption/supply remains at or above March 2024 levels through 2025; false if the supply is substantially halted (sustained collapse in wastewater meth consumption) over that period.
reasoning: Criterion: correct if meth consumption/supply stayed at or above March 2024 levels through 2025; wrong only on a sustained collapse. NZ Police/ESR wastewater data shows the opposite of a collapse: Q1 2024 averaged 17.5 kg/week, Q1 2025 33 kg/week, Q4 2025 34.7 kg/week (8% above the prior four-quarter average). The 2025 Annual Overview records at least 1,751 kg consumed across 62 sites and states consumption 'continued at the markedly elevated levels first observed in 2024', maintained throughout the year, with prices lower than previous years — a sign of ample supply, not interdiction. Checked for disconfirming evidence (any sustained quarterly decline or price spike indicating supply disruption): the only decline noted was a slight dip in Q1 2025 that still sat above the trailing average. Seymour's prediction that current measures would not stop the supply holds.

statement: This bill will end up before the Primary Production Committee, which is the best select committee in the Parliament, and will be able to be looked over by myself and my friend Mark Cameron in ACT, Suze Redmayne from National, Catherine Wedd from National, the Hon Jo Luxton and Cushla from Labour, and Steve Abel from across the way there.
criterion: The House's first-reading referral record for the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill on the Parliament website; true if referred to the Primary Production Committee, false if referred to any other committee or not referred.
reasoning: Criterion: correct if the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill was referred to the Primary Production Committee at first reading. The referral record shows the bill (introduced 21 June 2023) was read a first time on 27 March 2024 and referred to the Primary Production Committee that day; the committee called for submissions from 28 March 2024, considered 32 submissions, and reported the bill back, with second reading on 1 April 2025. No evidence of referral to any other committee. The committee-membership roll-call in the quote is outside the criterion, but Cameron, Redmayne, Luxton, Abel and Wedd are all corroborated as Primary Production Committee members of that term.

statement: So, with that, I’m very pleased that this bill is going to the select committee.
criterion: The Hansard division/first reading record for the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee, false if the first reading was defeated or the bill not referred.
reasoning: Criterion: correct if the bill was read a first time and referred to a select committee; wrong if the first reading was defeated or no referral happened. The first reading of the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill passed on 27 March 2024 and the bill was referred to the Primary Production Committee the same day. The committee ran three rounds of submissions (from 28 March 2024, 23 May 2024, and 3 October 2024), heard oral evidence, and recommended the bill be passed; second reading followed on 1 April 2025. Nothing indicates a defeated first reading or a skipped committee stage.

statement: They will import and purchase more brand-new fossil-fuel vehicles instead of electric vehicles, and that will emit more emissions on our roads for at least 20 years.
criterion: NZTA motor vehicle registration statistics for new light vehicles: true if the EV share of new light-vehicle registrations falls (and internal-combustion registrations rise correspondingly) over the five years from April 2024; false if EV share of new registrations continues to grow across that period.
reasoning: The criterion measures EV share of new light-vehicle registrations over the five years from April 2024, i.e. to April 2029; only ~2.5 years have elapsed, so the window has not closed. Interim evidence runs against the prediction rather than for it: plug-in share of new registrations was about 11% across 2024 (the trough after the Clean Car Discount ended 31 Dec 2023 and EV RUC exemption ended 1 April 2024), and by June 2026 electrified passenger registrations reached a record 38.2% (26.2% BEV, 12% PHEV) versus 18.4% in June 2025, with 27.3% electrified share for the six months to June 2026 and no purchase subsidy in place. So from the April 2024 baseline the criterion names, EV share has grown and ICE share correspondingly fallen. A reversal is conceivable within the remaining window (the RUC transition and rising EV running costs are the plausible mechanism), so the verdict is deferred rather than resolved as wrong.

statement: Well, I will take a bet with any member of this House that we will not see that system brought in before the end of this term, and over the next three to five years, that is the critical moment which would have made a consequential difference to the vehicles coming in.
criterion: Legislation and NZTA implementation records: false if a full road pricing / all-vehicle road user charge system is in force and operating before Parliament is dissolved for the 2026 general election; true if it is not (still at bill, consultation or announced-intent stage).
reasoning: The criterion is false only if a full road pricing / all-vehicle RUC system is in force and operating before Parliament is dissolved for the 2026 election; true if it is still at bill, consultation or announced-intent stage. Parliament rose on 24 September 2026 and is dissolved on 1 October 2026 (election 7 November). The enabling legislation, the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill, passed first reading on 18 November 2025 under urgency, took submissions to 8 January 2026, and as of 31 August 2026 was still awaiting its committee stage; no land transport revenue/RUC/tolling Act appears among the Acts of the 54th Parliament. Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the bill would not complete passage before the election ('That's something we can deal with after the election') and described universal RUC as 'medium term', hoping to 'start to look at that around 28, 29'. Government material confirms no start date has been set for light vehicles paying RUC and that fuel excise duty still applies to petrol vehicles. Disconfirming check: the only transport revenue measure actually enacted in the term was the Time of Use Charging Bill (congestion charging enabling legislation) and the 2024 light-electric RUC Act, neither of which is the all-vehicle system Genter was betting about. So the system was not brought in before the end of the term.

statement: It needs money to be able to build, to maintain, to operate roads and public transport systems and so on, and so we are going to need a new way of funding our roading system. That will be RUC, and that is where we need to move as quickly as possible.
criterion: New Zealand legislation and Government policy announcements on extending road user charges to petrol light vehicles: true if RUC is legislated to apply across the light vehicle fleet (replacing fuel excise duty) by the resolve-by date, false if fuel excise duty remains the primary charge for petrol vehicles with no enacted transition.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on whether RUC is legislated to apply across the light vehicle fleet, replacing fuel excise duty, by 31 December 2030 — four years away. As of September 2026 the policy direction Foster predicted has been adopted but not enacted: in 2026 the Government announced that all light vehicles (petrol, hybrid, diesel, electric) will move from fuel excise duty to distance- and weight-based RUC, consultation on supporting regulations closed 12 June 2026, and a market RFI closed 13 February 2026. But the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill — which only removes barriers to the transition rather than effecting it — is still awaiting committee stage and will lapse at the 1 October 2026 dissolution; no RUC/revenue Act was passed in the 54th Parliament; no start date has been set for petrol light vehicles; and Bishop's own target for beginning the transition is '28, 29' contingent on a second term. Fuel excise duty therefore remains the primary charge for petrol vehicles with no enacted transition — which is the criterion's 'false' condition — but the deadline has not passed, and the minister's target sits inside the remaining window, so this is pending rather than wrong. The 'as quickly as possible' element of the quote is a normative statement, not a testable prediction.

statement: I look forward to seeing that detail of work, and I have no doubt that that will come through the hard-working and very diligent Transport and Infrastructure Committee as well.
criterion: Parliament's select committee records; true if legislation extending road user charges beyond light EVs is referred to and reported on by the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, false if no such referral occurs.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether legislation extending road user charges beyond light EVs was referred to and reported on by the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. The Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill — which modernises RUC and removes barriers to transitioning all 3.5 million light vehicles from fuel excise duty to RUC — passed its first reading on 18 November 2025 and was referred to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, with submissions closing 8 January 2026. The committee reported back recommending changes: the Government's May 2026 consultation on RUC regulations is described as following 'the Transport and Infrastructure Select Committee's report on the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill, which recommended changes to strengthen the system for service providers and road users.' Both the referral and the report-back occurred, within the 2026-12-31 resolve-by date.

statement: We’ve just heard from the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries that this is going to go to select committee, and it will go through the normal—because I didn’t hear anything else—Standing Orders process of six months at that select committee.
criterion: The Parliament bill page for the Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if the Primary Production Committee's report-back date was set roughly six months after referral (about late September 2024) and it reported around then, false if a shorter reporting deadline was set or the bill was progressed under urgency.
reasoning: The Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill had its first reading and was referred to the Primary Production Committee on 28 March 2024 — the day Brooking spoke. The select committee report-back date was set at 27 September 2024, i.e. the standard six months after referral, and the committee reported the bill back on 26 September 2024 (bill version 263-2), recommending it be passed with all amendments agreed unanimously. Submissions closed 15 May 2024 and the committee heard oral evidence. No shortened reporting deadline was set and the bill was not progressed under urgency at the committee stage; second reading, committee of the whole House and third reading followed on 25 March 2025, with Royal assent on 29 March 2025. Both limbs of the criterion (roughly six-month deadline set, and reported around then) are satisfied.

statement: The seafood export revenue is forecast to increase 8 percent this year.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries seafood export revenue series for the year ending June 2024; true if the year-on-year increase is approximately 8 percent, false if the increase is materially lower or revenue falls.
reasoning: Wedd was accurately relaying the then-current forecast: MPI's SOPI December 2023 forecast seafood export revenue to increase 8 percent to $2.3 billion in the year to 30 June 2024. But the criterion is about the outturn in the MPI SOPI seafood series for the year ending June 2024, and the outturn was far below that. MPI's published seafood export series (wild capture + aquaculture, as at 20 May 2026) shows $2,097m for the year ended June 2023 and $2,141m for the year ended June 2024 — an increase of about 2 percent, not 8. This is corroborated by the intermediate reports: the June 2024 SOPI had already cut the estimate to a 5 percent rise to $2.2b, and the December 2024 SOPI forecast YE June 2025 at $2.2b as a 3 percent increase on 2023-24 (implying ~$2.13-2.14b for 2023-24). I checked for disconfirming evidence that the final figure might have been revised up toward 8 percent and found none; every post-hoc MPI source clusters around $2.1-2.2b. Revenue did rise, so the direction was right, but at roughly a quarter of the predicted increase the criterion's explicit false condition ('materially lower') is met.

statement: What we know—what we know—is that there will be many, many billion dollars that will have to be spent because of this Government’s inaction on climate.
criterion: Treasury / Ministry for the Environment reporting on the cost of meeting NZ's first Nationally Determined Contribution, including offshore mitigation purchases: true if officially estimated or actual cumulative cost attributable to the shortfall exceeds NZ$2 billion, false if it is materially below that or no such liability is incurred.
reasoning: The criterion's first branch is satisfied: Treasury's June 2026 paper TP 26/01 (and its technical annex) officially estimates the fiscal cost of offshore mitigation to meet NDC1 (2021-2030) at NZ$4.4-5.0bn, and the earlier 2023 Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment gave an illustrative range of NZ$3.3-23.7bn (central $7.7-9.9bn) - all far above the NZ$2bn threshold, and consistent with 'many, many billion dollars'. The criterion's false branch ('no such liability is incurred') is, however, currently the status quo: no purchase has been made, the Crown accounts do not recognise a liability, Treasury expressly says the figures do not represent government decisions or intentions, and PM Luxon has said the government will not send billions offshore. Treasury's own modelling assumes purchases only from 2027-2030, so actual incurrence cannot be settled until then (resolve-by 2031-12-31). Hence: the officially-estimated cost branch is met now; whether the money is actually spent remains open. Separately, the shortfall the estimate prices is largely structural (emissions-budget vs NDC gap) rather than solely attributable to this government's inaction, though the criterion only requires attribution to the shortfall.

statement: What that means is that the cost will be offset to people that use public transport in Auckland, and their fees—as advised by Auckland Council’s submission yesterday—are likely to increase by 126 percent.
criterion: Auckland Transport published fare schedules; true if average Auckland public transport fares rise by roughly 126 percent from their March 2024 level, false if the cumulative increase is materially smaller.
reasoning: Measured against Auckland Transport's published fare schedules from the March 2024 baseline (fares had already risen a weighted 6.2% on 4 February 2024, before the statement), AT raised fares an average of 5.2% on 2 February 2025 (alongside a zone restructure from 14 to 9 zones) and an average of 5.1% on 1 February 2026 - roughly 11% cumulative, not 126%. AT's current adult HOP fares are $3.00 for one zone (up from $2.80) and $7.90 for 4+ zones (up from $7.65). The resolve-by date is 2027-07-01 and one annual review remains, but a 126% cumulative rise would require fares to more than double in a single review, against a recent run rate of ~5% per year; the criterion's false condition ('cumulative increase is materially smaller') is already met and cannot plausibly reverse. Context checked for disconfirmation: NZTA's farebox-recovery push did prompt warnings in late 2024 that fares nationally 'may surge by up to 70%' if targets were fully passed to passengers, but that ceiling was not implemented in Auckland and is itself well below 126%.

statement: And I do question the comments that have been made—particularly from the other side of the House—that this here is going to absolutely sway people away from buying such vehicles. I actually don’t believe in that; I actually believe that people have all sorts of other reasons that they take into account, and I don’t think we’re going to have the demise that the so-called speakers on the other side actually talked to.
criterion: NZTA new light-vehicle registrations by fuel type: true if combined BEV and PHEV registrations in the 12 months from 1 April 2024 are at or near the preceding 12 months' level (no collapse); false if they fall sharply (say by a third or more) over that period.
reasoning: Registrations did collapse, well past the criterion's one-third threshold. New EV registrations fell from ~31,400 in 2023 (19.8% of new vehicle sales) to 10,632 in 2024 (7.7% share) - a drop of about two thirds - and stayed at that depressed level through the criterion's window: BEVs held ~5.4% market share in March 2025 and ~5.6% across 2025, versus the 2023 peak of 27-39% in the final CCD months. The Apr 2024-Mar 2025 window is if anything worse than the calendar-year comparison, because the preceding 12 months (Apr 2023-Mar 2024) contain the November-December 2023 pre-deadline surge. Disconfirming check: EV sales did later recover (BEV +13% in 2025, +286% in March 2026), but that is after the criterion's window closed on 2025-04-30. Note the criterion measures the fall, not its cause - most of it traces to the Clean Car Discount ending 31 December 2023, with RUC from 1 April 2024 compounding it.

statement: It could be resolved now, but instead, unfortunately, we’ve heard in the speech today that there will probably be an amendment moved at the committee of the whole House stage, which the select committee has not seen and cannot be a part of forming the right kind of legislation, going forward.
criterion: The Amendment Paper / Supplementary Order Paper record and Hansard for the committee of the whole House stage of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill; true if a Government amendment not recommended by the select committee was moved at that stage, false if the bill proceeded without such an amendment.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a Government amendment not recommended by the select committee was moved at the committee of the whole House stage of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill. Parliament published a third print of the bill — 'Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill 222-3 (2022)', as reported from the committee of the whole House — which in NZ practice is produced only when a bill is amended at that stage. Te Ohu Kaimoana records that the bill 'shifted form since... the Māori Affairs Select Committee Report, proposing new amendments', and Cabinet's Legislation Committee considered 'Progressing the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill' (LEG-24-MIN-0042, April 2024), the standard vehicle for approving a Government Amendment Paper. Reported committee-stage changes include extending the annual catch entitlement lease term from five to 10 years and amendments to clauses 25, 37, 42, 48 and 49. Disconfirming check: if the bill had gone straight from the select committee version to third reading there would be no 222-3 print and no LEG approval to progress — neither is the case. Caveat: parliament.nz blocks automated fetching, so I could not read the committee-stage Hansard itself and cannot cite the Amendment Paper number; the third print is nonetheless decisive for the criterion as written.

statement: The number of people on the jobseeker benefit is, unfortunately, expected to increase in the coming months due to the challenging economic circumstances: jobseeker benefit recipients are expected to peak at 198,500 in January 2025.
criterion: MSD Jobseeker Support recipient series for 2024 and 2025; true if the series peaks at approximately 198,500 in or around January 2025, false if the peak count is materially higher or lower, or occurs at a materially different time.
reasoning: The criterion is the MSD Jobseeker Support recipient series for 2024-25: true if it peaks at approximately 198,500 in or around January 2025. It does not. MSD's Benefit Fact Sheets record 213,321 people on Jobseeker Support at the December 2024 quarter — roughly 15,000 (about 7.5%) above the forecast peak, and reached before January 2025 arrived. Nor did the series peak then: it fell back to 209,838 at the March 2025 quarter but then rose again, hitting 223,512 at the December 2025 quarter, and MSD's HYEFU 2025 forecasts put the peak at about 221,900 in January 2026. So the prediction is materially wrong on magnitude (the count never came down to 198,500) and on timing (January 2025 was not the peak). Disconfirming check: I looked for any MSD series on which 198,500 could be the January 2025 value — the published quarterly national counts are all well above it from mid-2024 onward.

statement: As has also been said, this is the beginning of a process that will go through this House over the coming weeks and months.
criterion: The parliamentary progress record for the Taranaki Maunga collective redress bill: true if it completes its remaining stages (select committee, second reading, committee of the whole, third reading) within roughly a year of 9 April 2024; false if it is still before the House or has lapsed by then.
reasoning: The criterion is the parliamentary progress record for the Taranaki Maunga collective redress bill: true if it completes its remaining stages within roughly a year of 9 April 2024. It did. The bill passed its first reading and was referred to the Māori Affairs Committee on 9 April 2024 (submissions closed 22 May 2024; 43 written submissions, 14 submitters heard in New Plymouth); the committee recommended it pass; and it took its second and third readings on 30 January 2025, receiving Royal assent as Te Ture Whakatupua mō Te Kāhui Tupua 2025 / Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act 2025 on 1 February 2025 — under ten months. Disconfirming check: the bill did not lapse or stall, and is not still before the House; the enacted Act and the 30 January 2025 third-reading Hansard both confirm completion.

statement: There will be desperate people who will now have a new opportunity for how to procure meth via cooking it from P, and we have introduced a new risk for addiction into our community.
criterion: NZ Police clandestine laboratory detection figures and Customs/Police reporting on pseudoephedrine diversion for the two years after the Act comes into force, compared with the two years before: true if detections of pseudoephedrine-based domestic manufacture or documented pharmacy diversion rise materially, false if they remain flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion's named source is now available: NZ Police OIA response IR-01-25-22265 (18 Aug 2025) gives clandestine meth lab detections by month and district, May 2023 - May 2025. Detections in the 12 months before pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacy shelves (Jun 2023 - May 2024) total 44; the 12 months after (Jun 2024 - May 2025) total 51 - a small rise in a low-count series that stays in the same 0-9 per month band, with no precursor attribution, and with the 2024 uptick beginning in months before products were actually on shelves (regulation change 21 March 2024, sales from ~May 2024). On the pharmacy-diversion limb, Reckitt's September 2026 Medsafe reclassification application states that the Pharmacy Guild and NZ Police have reported only a small number of isolated pseudoephedrine-related thefts from pharmacies since the return, against 285,802 packs (6.36m doses) sold in the year to 15 March 2026; the one prominent case is the Motueka pharmacy burglary days after return in May 2024. Checking the opposite: NZ meth consumption did hit records (36.6 kg/week, Q1 2026 wastewater), but police and market analysis attribute this to bulk importation and large precursor-imported labs, not pharmacy-sourced domestic cooking - one Fijian lab out-produced all NZ domestic labs detected in a year. Caveat: detection figures for the second post-Act year (Jun 2025 - Apr 2026) are not published, so the full two-on-two comparison the criterion specifies is only half covered; on the evidence that exists, detections are essentially flat and documented diversion is isolated, which is the criterion's false branch.

statement: So, dang, it’s a good idea and it’s going to be chucked out, but, again, that’s not surprising, given the current climate that we’re having to deal with.
criterion: Outcome of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act polls held with the October 2025 local elections; true if a majority of councils with Māori wards, including Far North District Council, lose them, false if Māori wards are retained across most affected councils.
reasoning: The Maori ward polls were held with the October 2025 local elections across 42 councils (37 territorial, 5 regional). Outcome: 24 councils voted to remove Maori wards and 18 voted to keep them, so a majority of councils did lose them - the first half of the criterion's true branch. But the criterion explicitly named Far North District Council, and Far North retained its Maori ward: keep 13,346 (54.35%) to remove 10,619 (43.24%), turnout 24,556, binding for the 2028 and 2031 elections. Checking the disconfirming side: nationwide the keep vote also led, 542,134 (50.25%) to 467,923 (43.37%), and the larger centres (Hamilton, Wellington, Porirua, Hutt City, Palmerston North, Nelson) mostly retained theirs, while Whangarei and New Plymouth removed. So the conjunction the criterion requires fails on its named council and on the aggregate vote, while holding on the council count - the substance of the prediction holds but is materially overstated for the speaker's own district.

statement: In my view, the church will hold it on trust for the people of Christchurch, and when it is rebuilt, because it will be rebuilt, it needs to be an open and community space.
criterion: Status of the Christ Church Cathedral reinstatement project; true if the cathedral is reinstated and reopened, false if the project is abandoned, the building demolished, or the reinstatement remains permanently mothballed with no funded path to completion.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 2032-12-31, more than six years away, and the outcome is genuinely open. Current status: construction has been halted since 2024 after the government ruled out further taxpayer funding beyond its $25m. On 11 September 2025 Christ Church Cathedral Reinstatement Ltd announced a staged plan ('Re:Opening') - stage one reinstating the tower, nave and western wall with the Rose Window, ~700 seats - which halved the shortfall to $40-45m, with a further $20m committed by the Anglican Church, construction intended to resume in 2026 and reopening targeted for end of 2030. As of May 2026 the project is still stalled: about $90m spent, ~$45m still to find, and the Christchurch City Council's extra $15m grant is conditional on a government match the Finance Minister has declined. So neither branch of the criterion is met - the cathedral is not reinstated and reopened, but it has not been abandoned or demolished, and there is an active costed plan rather than permanent mothballing.

statement: Well, thanks to the good work of Tama Potaka, the new Minister of Conservation, I was delighted, on behalf of local businesses, tourist operators, and also the hundreds of thousands of visitors who want to come and see Cathedral Cove, that he has now committed to ensuring that his Department of Conservation officials have on his desk, in June, their plan for getting the track reopened for the coming summer season.
criterion: DOC/ministerial records or media reporting on the Cathedral Cove track: true if DOC officials delivered a reopening plan to the Minister in June 2024 and the track was open for the 2024/25 summer season; false if no June plan was delivered or the track remained closed through that summer.
reasoning: Both prongs of the criterion are met. DOC's 1 March 2024 media release records Minister Potaka saying "I expect to receive advice from officials by the end of June on the reinstatement options" — matching Simpson's description of a June plan on the Minister's desk — and on 10 July 2024 DOC announced the chosen temporary reinstatement option plus $5m of International Visitor Levy funding, consistent with advice having arrived on that schedule. The outcome prong is confirmed outright: Mautohe Cathedral Cove reopened to walkers on 1 December 2024, opened by Potaka himself, in time for the 2024/25 summer season. Checked for disconfirmation: no reporting of a missed June deadline or a summer closure. The only gap is that no public record fixes the exact date the officials' plan was delivered, so the June element is inferred from the announced deadline and the 10 July decision rather than directly documented.

statement: Reactive ones include restoring consequences for crime, making sure there are, in fact, tougher sentences—we’ve got the Minister of Justice here who will be introducing laws to limit the amount judges can deduct from offenders when they’re sentenced.
criterion: Parliament's bills register; true if a Government bill limiting sentencing discounts was introduced by the Minister of Justice after 9 April 2024, false if no such bill was introduced by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: A Government bill limiting the discounts judges can deduct at sentencing was introduced by the Minister of Justice after 9 April 2024. Cabinet agreed to the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill on 16 September 2024; it is Government Bill 2024 No 77, in the name of Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, and was referred to select committee on 24 September 2024. Its disclosure statement confirms it "limits the use of sentence reductions to 40% of the sentence when considering mitigating factors personal to the offender" (departure only where the result would be manifestly unjust), bars repeat discounts for youth and remorse, and imposes a sliding scale on guilty-plea discounts (25% down to 5%). It was enacted as the Sentencing Amendment Act 2025 and came into force 30 June 2025. Note the separate, earlier Sentencing Amendment Act 2024 (introduced 7 March 2024) is a different bill about gang-membership as an aggravating factor and does not satisfy the criterion — the discount cap is the September bill, which is inside the window.

statement: A Government that has given tax breaks to landlords, that’s mislaid their cast-iron promise to fund our hospital, and that’s repealed three waters, leading to looming massive rises to rates.
criterion: Dunedin City Council adopted annual plan rates increases for 2024/25 and 2025/26; true if average residential rates rises materially exceed the pre-2024 historical norm (say above 10% per year) with water infrastructure costs cited as a driver following the Three Waters repeal, false if rates rises stay near historical levels.
reasoning: Against the criterion as written, both conditions hold. Dunedin City Council adopted a 17.5% average rates increase for 2024/25 on 25 June 2024, and a 10.7% increase for 2025/26 (year 1 of the 9-year plan 2025-34, settled at deliberations in late May 2025, up from a signalled 10.1-10.5%). Both materially exceed the pre-2024 norm, which ODT reporting puts at about 6.5% for 2022/23 and 6.5% proposed for 2023/24. Water/ageing infrastructure is explicitly cited as a driver: 5.4% of the 17.5% was for maintaining or replacing ageing infrastructure (alongside 4.4% for kerbside), and the 2025/26 rise is attributed to a programme to bring water services up to standard after two decades of underinvestment. Disconfirming check: the one weakness is causal, not factual — DCC's own stated drivers are its historic water underinvestment, kerbside collection, insurance, inflation and debt, not the Three Waters repeal as such, so the repeal's specific contribution to these numbers is not established by the sources. The criterion asks only for large rises with water costs cited as a driver after the repeal, and that is satisfied.

statement: This is just going to allow more things to come—increased crime. It’s another avenue for the ram raids to happen.
criterion: NZ Police recorded crime statistics for burglary/ram-raid offences against pharmacies in the 12 months after pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacy sale, compared with the preceding 12 months: true if pharmacy ram raids/burglaries rose materially over that period; false if they were flat or fell.
reasoning: Pseudoephedrine returned to OTC pharmacy sale on 20 May 2024. The exact series the criterion names (NZ Police recorded burglary/ram-raid offences against pharmacies, 12 months before vs after) is not published with a victim-industry breakdown, so the literal comparison could not be run. All obtainable evidence points the same way, however: Reckitt's September 2026 application to Medsafe's Medicines Classification Committee records that the Pharmacy Guild and New Zealand Police have reported only 'a small number of isolated pseudoephedrine-related thefts from pharmacies since the products returned'; national ram raids continued their decline from the 2022 peak (433 in 2022 to 288 in 2023, a low of 15 in April 2024, and police reporting them down over 60%); and no NZ outlet reported a pharmacy crime wave in the 28 months since, despite having extensively pre-reported pharmacists' fears of exactly that. I checked for the disconfirming case and found only one publicised incident — a Motueka pharmacy burgled for pseudoephedrine days after the return. So there is a documented instance, but nothing approaching the material rise in pharmacy ram raids the criterion requires. Stated limitation: this rests on Police/Guild characterisation and national ram-raid trend rather than the pharmacy-level police counts the criterion specifies.

statement: We fully expect that we’ll have many representatives from Ngāti Hei in the third reading, but I’m sure there will be many tuning in on their computer screens and maybe listening in on the radio to this speech.
criterion: Hansard for the third reading of the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if members of Ngāti Hei are acknowledged as present in the gallery, false if the third reading proceeds without any Ngāti Hei representatives present.
reasoning: The Ngati Hei Claims Settlement Bill had its third reading on 13 May 2026 (royal assent 18 May 2026), alongside the Ngati Rahiri Tumutumu and Ngati Tara Tokanui bills. Ngati Hei were present in person, not merely watching remotely: Goldsmith's own statement on the day acknowledged 'the people of Ngati Rahiri Tumutumu, Ngati Tara Tokanui, Ngati Hei, and others from the wider Pare Hauraki Collective who travelled to Parliament today to witness this auspicious occasion', and local coverage confirms representatives of all three iwi attended the reading in Wellington. The criterion's 'false' branch — a third reading proceeding with no Ngati Hei representatives present — is contradicted. Caveat: the acknowledgement I could retrieve is from the ministerial release and contemporaneous reporting; I could not open the Hansard transcript itself (parliament.nz pages returned 404/blank), so the specific wording of any gallery acknowledgement from the Chair is unverified.

statement: So, to Ngāti Hei at home watching, I want to reiterate this bill continues with the support of the Minister, and soon, will be read a third time.
criterion: Parliamentary records for the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if the bill is read a third time within roughly a year of this speech, false if it is still awaiting third reading or is not passed by then.
reasoning: The bill was read a third time on 13 May 2026 and received royal assent on 18 May 2026 — about 25 months after Henare's 9 April 2024 speech, not 'soon'. The criterion sets the bar at roughly a year and marks it false if the bill was still awaiting third reading at that point; on 9 April 2025 it was, having passed its second reading on 9 April 2024 and then sat awaiting the committee of the whole House stage. The substance of the prediction did eventually hold — the bill passed, with the Minister's support — so this is a timing failure rather than an outcome failure, but the criterion as written assigns that to the false branch.

statement: This bill, effectually, will pass into law in a third reading—I think we’re all of that determination—and final reading which is due in the coming weeks and months, and create a comprehensive settlement agreement of significance to both Ngāti Hei and the Crown.
criterion: The Parliament bills register and the NZ Legislation site for the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if it passed its third reading and received Royal assent by the end of 2024, false if it was still before the House or defeated at that date.
reasoning: The Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill passed its second reading on 9 April 2024 (the day before the speech) and then stalled. Its third reading did not happen until 13 May 2026, with Royal assent 18 May 2026 — over two years after Cameron predicted it in "the coming weeks and months". At the criterion's cut-off of 31 December 2024 the bill was still before the House awaiting the committee stage, which is the criterion's explicit false condition. The substance was eventually vindicated (the settlement was enacted, with $8.5m financial and commercial redress plus 17 cultural redress properties), but the timing was materially wrong and the date test fails.

statement: Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Furthermore, that allowance will be lower than the allowance set by the previous Government. This means that tax relief is affordable, we will not be borrowing extra to pay for it, and tax relief will not add to inflationary pressures.
criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 Economic and Fiscal Update and subsequent RBNZ Monetary Policy Statements; true if the Budget 2024 tax package was assessed as fiscally neutral with no material addition to inflation and annual CPI continued to decline through 2024–25, false if Treasury or RBNZ attributed additional inflationary pressure to the package or if it was funded by additional borrowing.
reasoning: Most of the claim holds. The Budget 2024 operating allowance was held at $3.2b, below the $3.5b the previous government had set, so "lower than the allowance set by the previous Government" is confirmed. The $14.725b five-year tax package was matched by savings and revenue measures (commercial building depreciation, waste disposal levy, immigration/visitor levies, cancelled programmes), and Treasury's BEFU 2024 concluded that Budget 2024 decisions would "on balance reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure" — tax changes boosting demand but more than offset by lower spending and allowances — with the fiscal impulse contractionary across the forecast period. Neither Treasury nor the RBNZ attributed additional inflationary pressure to the package: the August 2024 MPS treated declining government expenditure as contractionary, was uncertain whether the tax cuts would even lift consumption, and the RBNZ began cutting the OCR that month. Two legs of the criterion fall short. The no-extra-borrowing claim is contested rather than clean: the bond programme rose roughly $12b over four years (Westpac and ANZ estimated $10–15b extra), which Willis attributed to weaker revenue and a slowing economy rather than the tax package — "different pools of money" — a separation commentators did not accept. And annual CPI did not "continue to decline through 2024–25" as the criterion requires: it fell 4.0% (Mar 2024) to 3.3% (Jun) to 2.2% (Sep and Dec 2024), then rose to 2.5% (Mar 2025), 2.7% (Jun 2025) and 3.1% by Mar 2026 — within the 1–3% band for most of that stretch, but rising, not falling.

statement: In this increasingly polarised, fractured world, it is fantastic to see our Parliament cooperating around a process step like this so that an important issue like this can be heard, even though the bill’s going to go down, it appears.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of James Shaw's New Zealand Bill of Rights (Right to Sustainable Environment) Amendment Bill; true if the bill was voted down at first reading, false if it proceeded to select committee.
reasoning: James Shaw's New Zealand Bill of Rights (Right to Sustainable Environment) Amendment Bill was voted down at its first reading on 10 April 2024 — the same day Parker spoke — on a party vote of 55 ayes to 68 noes, with no abstentions. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori supported it; it needed NZ First to reach select committee and did not get it, so it never proceeded to committee. Parker's hedged prediction that "the bill's going to go down, it appears" was borne out exactly as the criterion specifies.

statement: And isn’t it appropriate that we can have this discussion and, as it no doubt moves through to select committee and wherever it may go from there, that we can bring different perspectives, that we can have these conversations, but we don’t have to be firing shots at each other.
criterion: The Hansard record for the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Repeal Bill; true if the bill passed first reading and was referred to a select committee, false if it was defeated at first reading.
reasoning: Hansard for 10 April 2024 (p.2765) records a party vote on the first reading of the Restoring Citizenship Removed By Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 Bill: Ayes 74 (Labour 34, Green 15, ACT 11, NZ First 8, Te Pati Maori 6), Noes 49 (National). Motion agreed to, bill read a first time, and immediately 'referred to the Governance and Administration Committee'. The criterion's condition — passed first reading and referred to a select committee — is met exactly. The committee subsequently received ~24,500 submissions, held hearings in June/July 2024 and reported back on 9 October 2024, confirming the select committee stage actually ran. No disconfirming evidence: the only 'no' bloc was National, which was not enough to defeat it.

statement: So, in summary, New Zealand First believes that public safety concerns and the safety of children, who are our most vulnerable and defenceless, far outweighs the privacy or equal protection claims of the sex offender, and it is why we believe that this bill will be well received.
criterion: The division records for the remaining readings of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading with support from a large cross-party majority, false if it is defeated, lapses, or passes only narrowly with substantial opposition.
reasoning: The Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 29 May 2024. Hansard p.3674 records 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' with no division called — i.e. it passed on the voices, unopposed. The debate confirms this was genuinely unanimous rather than merely unchallenged: Grant McCallum (National) said 'it's just great to see that the Greens have reconsidered their position and have rejoined and made it unanimous', and Helen White (Labour) thanked 'the Greens for coming around on this bill and supporting it'. The bill received Royal assent on 4 June 2024 as 2024 No 18. Checked for the opposite — a narrow or contested passage would have produced a party vote in Hansard, and none exists at second or third reading. The criterion's 'large cross-party majority' is satisfied at its strongest form.

statement: So the National Party stands with Mr O’Connor, stands with other parties—minus the Green Party—who look set to support this.
criterion: The Hansard division record for the second reading of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if all parties other than the Greens voted in support, false if any other party opposed or if the Greens supported it.
reasoning: Caveat on the evidence: the criterion names the second-reading division record, but no division was taken. Hansard 10 April 2024 p.2784 records only 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a second time.' — a voice vote, so there is no party-breakdown table to read. The same Hansard nonetheless settles the substance of Brewer's claim. Rima Nakhle (National): 'I'm saddened to hear that the Green Party is not supporting this bill, because children are children no matter where they are around the world. The former speaker from the Green Party Kahurangi Carter said that it only captures convicted, known offenders.' Tom Rutherford (National): 'to think there's a political party here who doesn't want to support this legislation... the Green Party actually sits on that select committee and gave it support at select committee, yet coming back to the second reading they've changed their mind.' Singular 'a political party' — the Greens were the sole dissenting party and every other party supported it, which is exactly what Brewer predicted. Looked for disconfirmation: had any other party opposed, a division would almost certainly have been called, and none was. Note the Greens later reversed again and the third reading on 29 May 2024 was unanimous, but that is after the prediction's horizon and does not bear on the second reading.

statement: How does she intend to reduce the amount of people on jobseeker support - work ready by nearly 50 percent at a time when unemployment is expected to rise?
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate: true if the rate rises materially above the March 2024 quarter level (4.3%) over the following four quarters, false if it holds flat or falls.
reasoning: Criterion baseline confirmed: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment was 4.3% in the March 2024 quarter (up from 4.0% in Dec 2023). Over the four following quarters the seasonally adjusted rate rose materially: 4.6% (Jun 2024), 4.8% (Sep 2024), 5.1% (Dec 2024), 5.1% (Mar 2025) — the highest since Sep 2020. The criterion's false condition (flat or falling) does not occur anywhere in the window; the rise is +0.8pp, not a rounding artefact.

statement: This reading today is another important step in the settlement process before the third reading that will result in the full and final settlement of Ngāti Paoa’s historical Treaty of Waitangi claims.
criterion: The Parliament bill-progress record and the New Zealand statute book: true if the Ngāti Paoa Claims Settlement Bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent as an Act settling the historical claims in full and final form; false if it lapses, is defeated, or remains before the House.
reasoning: The Ngāti Pāoa Claims Settlement Bill passed its third reading on 5 November 2025 and received Royal assent that month as the Ngāti Pāoa Claims Settlement Act 2025 (Public Act 2025 No 61), in force 13 November 2025 — within the 2025-12-31 resolve-by date. The Act gives effect to the 2021 deed as the final settlement of all Ngāti Pāoa historical Treaty claims arising before 21 September 1992, with the usual finality and jurisdiction provisions, $23.5m redress, 12 sites and a Crown apology. Disconfirming check: iwi chair Herearoha Skipper told 1News the Crown has not 'fully delivered the Ngāti Pāoa settlement package' pending the Pare Hauraki Collective Redress Bill and the Marutūāhu Iwi Collective Redress Deed — but that is outstanding collective redress shared with other Hauraki iwi, not unsettled Ngāti Pāoa historical claims, which is what the criterion asks about.

statement: So just being in the second reading, I want to acknowledge this, tautoko this kaupapa, and we look forward to the final reading when Ngāti Paoa people will receive their final dose of justice.
criterion: The Hansard record and the New Zealand statute book; true if the Ngāti Paoa Claims Settlement Bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it lapses, is voted down or remains unpassed by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The final (third) reading Jackson looked forward to took place on 5 November 2025 — Jackson himself spoke, naming the negotiators and wāhine trustees for Hansard — and the bill received Royal assent in November 2025 as the Ngāti Pāoa Claims Settlement Act 2025 (2025 No 61), in force 13 November 2025, inside the 2025-12-31 resolve-by date. Neither of the criterion's false conditions (lapse, defeat, still unpassed) applies.

statement: It is likely that an entity like the New Zealand Superannuation Fund would in future choose to invest in a controlling entity in these sorts of assets and many other sorts of assets where it believes it can get a good return, consistent with the investment principles.
criterion: NZ Super Fund annual reports and investment announcements after the Act comes into force; true if the Fund discloses at least one controlling interest in an operating or infrastructure entity, false if no controlling stake has been taken by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: The Act in question is the NZ Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Act 2024 (second reading 11 Apr 2024, third reading 9 May 2024), which repealed the s59 ban on the Fund holding a controlling interest. As at September 2026 the Fund's disclosed direct investments remain minority holdings: Kaingaroa Timberlands ~42% (its largest single investment), Fidelity Life ~41.1% cornerstone stake, Datacom ~45%; RetireAustralia was a 50/50 joint holding with Infratil and has been sold.
