(b) Emergency housing: households in EH motels fell from 3,141 (Dec 2023) to 471 (Dec 2025) and the government's 75% reduction target was hit five years early — but this fall is driven by tightened eligibility/gatekeeping from Aug 2024, so it is not a measured fall in homelessness. (c) Stats NZ severe housing deprivation has NO post-commencement reading: the only estimates are 2018 (99,462) and 2023 (112,496), and the 2028 census has been cancelled, so this instrument cannot settle the claim at all. (d) The government's own Homelessness Insights Reports do show street homelessness rising materially after commencement: Auckland rough sleepers 426 (Sep 2024) -> 809 (May 2025) -> 940 (Sep 2025) peak, then 706 in Jan 2026 against 653 in Jan 2025; Auckland Council reported ~90% growth over eight months of 2024-25. So the substance the speaker predicted — more people on the street — is measurable and material, but the two administrative measures the criterion names both fell, no source attributes the rise specifically to the 90-day provisions (the emergency-housing eligibility change is the driver more commonly cited), and the latest count is well down from the Sep 2025 peak. Provisional: resolve-by is 2027-06-30.

statement: So, actually, unwinding interest deductibility, lowering the brightline test, making sure that we get the balance right are good things—it will put downward pressure on rents.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond median weekly rents: true if national rent growth falls materially below its pre-2024 trend (or rents fall) in the two years after the changes take effect; false if rent growth continues at or above that trend.
reasoning: The tax changes took effect 1 April 2024 (interest deductibility) and 1 July 2024 (brightline cut to two years), so the criterion's two-year window is complete and its resolve-by date (2026-06-30) has passed. Pre-2024 trend: rents rose 4.5% in the year to the Dec 2023 quarter (MHUD identifies Dec 2023 as the peak of rental inflation); the long-run average is ~4.2%/yr. Post-change: the Stats NZ CPI 'actual rentals for housing' index rose just 0.5% in the year to the June 2026 quarter — the smallest annual increase since the Dec 2001 quarter. On the new-tenancy/bond measure the criterion also names, MHUD's index (Stats NZ's separate rental price index is paused) had nationwide new-tenancy rents 0.1% BELOW July 2024 levels in July 2025, Wellington down 6%; the national median new-tenancy rent was flat (0.0%) over the most recent 12 months; realestate.co.nz had the national average at $631/wk in April 2026, down 1.4% y/y and about $30 below the May 2024 high of $660. That is rent growth materially below the pre-2024 trend, with outright falls in several regions — the criterion's 'true' condition on both named sources. Caveat, since the criterion is an outcome test and does not isolate causation: market commentary attributes the slowdown mainly to net migration collapsing (net gain 10,681 in the year to Nov 2025, 63% below 2024 and 92% below 2023), elevated rental listings, and would-be sale properties returning to the rental pool — not to the tax changes. The predicted direction happened; the mechanism is not established by this evidence.

statement: This funding will ensure that our current levels of services are maintained and ensures that they can meet the increasing levels of demand.
criterion: Coastguard NZ and Surf Life Saving NZ annual reports for the years to 2028; true if neither organisation reduces patrol hours, station coverage or rescue capability over the funding period and both report meeting demand, false if either cuts services or publicly reports being unable to meet demand on this funding.
reasoning: The criterion requires Coastguard NZ and Surf Life Saving NZ annual reports 'for the years to 2028', and the Budget 2024 package ($63.6m over four years — $19m Coastguard, $44m SLSNZ) runs to 2027/28. Only reports through the financial year ended 30 June 2025 are published (Coastguard 2025 Performance Report; SLSNZ 2025 Annual Report, 17 Nov 2025), so most of the funding period is unreported and the resolve-by date of 2028-06-30 is nearly two years away. I checked for disconfirming evidence and found none: neither organisation has publicly reported cutting patrol hours, station coverage or rescue capability, or being unable to meet demand on this funding. SLSNZ publicly welcomed the boost and received a further $23.1m frontline-services package in Oct 2024 (swift-water training, regional managers, 16 IRBs, satellite comms); Coastguard added 26 new vessels this summer under a $9.8m Lotto grant and reports record activity. Two standing pressures worth noting but not sufficient to falsify: Coastguard still raises roughly 60% of its >$30m annual cost from the public, and Whanganui District Council declined most local surf lifesaving grant requests with patrol hours possibly reduced there — a local-funding issue distinct from the Crown package.

statement: These actions are significant for my home region of Hawke’s Bay, which is a huge export region, and will play a big part in helping us double the value of our exports in the next ten years.
criterion: Stats NZ total goods and services export value for the year to mid-2034 compared with the year to mid-2024; true if at least double in nominal terms, false if less.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Stats NZ export value for the year to mid-2034 versus mid-2024; that date is eight years away, so the prediction cannot be settled. Interim state only (not a verdict): total exports were $80.7b in the year to December 2025, and commentary notes average annual growth of about 2% against the 5-6% needed to double by 2034 — behind pace, but the window is open.

statement: Tax relief will be funded from within a new operating allowance for Budget 2024, and we won’t be borrowing extra for tax relief and will not be adding to inflationary pressures.
criterion: Budget 2024 documents (30 May 2024) plus the subsequent Treasury and Reserve Bank assessments. True if the tax package was funded within the announced operating allowance with no additional borrowing attributed to it and the RBNZ's following Monetary Policy Statements did not identify it as adding to inflationary pressure; false if borrowing was increased to fund it or official assessments attributed added inflationary pressure to the package.
reasoning: The inflation limb of the criterion is satisfied: the package was designed to be fiscally neutral (as the IMF's 2024 Article IV advised), Treasury said the tax changes did not move headline fiscal indicators because of offsetting measures, and the RBNZ's August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement judged that changes to tax and transfer policies were 'likely to be broadly offsetting for inflationary pressure' — no subsequent MPS attributed added inflationary pressure to the package. The funding limb holds only under the government's own accounting. The package cost about $3.7b a year against a $3.2b operating allowance, and was in practice covered mainly by $3.8b of savings and $2.1b of new revenue rather than sitting inside the allowance. At the same Budget, New Zealand Debt Management lifted the bond programme by $12.0b over the forecast period, with accumulated residual cash deficits $18.3b higher than at the Half Year Update. Treasury attributed that to the weaker OBEGAL/revenue outlook rather than to the tax package, so the criterion's 'false if borrowing was increased to fund it' does not trigger; but opposition MPs and commentators (e.g. Bernard Hickey) noted the extra borrowing was close to the size of the tax package and called the distinction semantic. Substance holds; 'funded from within a new operating allowance' with no extra borrowing is true only on the offsetting-measures reading.

statement: Most New Zealanders are expecting $250 a fortnight in tax cuts, so I guess, in eight sleeps, New Zealanders will know whether or not the National Government is going to deliver on that election promise of up to $250 a week—not the few cents that many of them will get while they are paying more for rents, while they are paying more for insurance, while they are paying more for so many other things.
criterion: The tax package published in Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) and Treasury/IRD distributional tables; true if the great majority of households receive substantially less than the headline $250 per fortnight, false if the advertised amount is delivered broadly across households.
reasoning: Budget 2024 (30 May 2024) delivered far less than the $250 a fortnight headline to the great majority of households, which is exactly what the criterion tests. Average-income households received about $102 a fortnight from the bracket changes; the average household overall was about $60 a fortnight and the average household with children about $78. Worked examples: a minimum-wage earner about $12.50 a week, a single adult on $55,000 about $25.50 a week, a superannuitant couple $4.50-$13 a week. Only around 3,000 families qualified for the full $250 from the income tax changes, and about 12,000 once the FamilyBoost childcare rebate was included, out of roughly 1.9 million households. The one overstatement is rhetorical: 'a few cents' understates the $12-$100 a fortnight most people actually got, but the criterion asks whether the great majority received substantially less than $250 a fortnight, and they did.

statement: More people are losing their jobs and will under the economic track that this Government has decided to pursue.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey and filled-jobs series: true if the unemployment rate rises and filled jobs fall over the twelve months following May 2024; false if unemployment falls or is flat and employment grows.
reasoning: Criterion: unemployment rises AND filled jobs fall in the twelve months after May 2024. Stats NZ HLFS: seasonally adjusted unemployment was 4.6% in the June 2024 quarter (up from 4.4% in March 2024) and 5.2% in the June 2025 quarter; the employment rate fell from 68.3% (June 2024) to 66.8% (June 2025). Stats NZ employment indicators (filled jobs): 2.34 million actual filled jobs in June 2025, down 27,850 (1.2%) on June 2024, with falls for both men (-1.7%) and women (-0.9%). Disconfirming check: no series over this window shows employment growing or unemployment flat/falling — the rise continued past the window (5.6% eleven-year high reported later). Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied.

statement: So, for all of the hot air that we hear in here, for all of the rhetoric that we hear from the Government—that they care about people, that they care about the planet—there’s the evidence that bears out completely the contrary of that—that their decisions will increase inequality, they will increase house prices, and they will increase homelessness.
criterion: REINZ/CoreLogic house price indices and Stats NZ severe housing deprivation / MSD emergency and transitional housing data to mid-2026: true if house prices and measured homelessness both rise over the period; false if house prices are flat or falling and homelessness measures do not rise.
reasoning: Criterion requires BOTH house prices and measured homelessness to rise to mid-2026. Homelessness rose: HUD's homelessness insights work put the unsheltered rate at 10.1 per 10,000 (up from 7.8 in 2018, ~5,000 people); Auckland unsheltered clients went 653 (Jan 2025) to 809 (May 2025) and Auckland homelessness more than doubled Sept 2024 to Sept 2025; Christchurch +73%; of 21 agencies surveyed by the National Homelessness Data Project, 14 reported increases and none reported a reduction. (Emergency-housing grant volumes fell, but that reflects the tightened gateway — 32% of applications declined in March 2025 vs 4% in March 2024 — not less homelessness.) House prices did not rise: the REINZ national House Price Index was +0.1% in the year to May 2025, -0.6% in the year to May 2026 and -0.4% in the year to July 2026, i.e. roughly flat in nominal terms and lower in real terms than May 2024; the national median was $775,000 in May 2026 and $760,000 in July 2026, and Cotality/CoreLogic had national values 17.7% below the January 2022 peak in July 2026 (~30% in real terms). Half the criterion holds, half fails.

statement: I predict that, in 2026, Labour will still be blaming things on COVID!
criterion: Public statements by Labour MPs during calendar year 2026 (Hansard, press releases, media interviews); true if Labour MPs are documented attributing current economic or public-service problems to the COVID-19 pandemic, false if no such attribution can be found.
reasoning: Criterion: documented 2026 statements by Labour MPs attributing current economic or public-service problems to COVID-19. Found, within calendar 2026 and before the 31 Dec deadline. Releasing Labour's fiscal strategy on 22-23 August 2026, finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds explained today's debt levels by the pandemic: 'We had to put the umbrella up when we were faced with a 1-in-100-year pandemic. That's why debt levels can change because of extra conditions that the government has no control over,' and said she did not apologise for Labour's Covid-era spending; independent commentary on the same announcement described her as having 'reached for Covid' when asked why debt targets move. Chris Hipkins, 9 September 2026 (Reuters): 'COVID had been all-consuming. We were too slow to revert back to non-COVID-related good governing,' explaining Labour's slowness on cost-of-living. Disconfirming check: Labour's dominant 2026 frame blames the current government, not the pandemic, and in July 2025 Labour publicly mocked Seymour for claiming NZ was still digesting a Covid 'hangover' — so the jibe is not a fair description of Labour's main message. But the criterion asks only whether such attribution is documented, and it is. Caveat on sourcing: RNZ blocks direct fetching, so the Edmonds quote is taken from the search index of the RNZ article and corroborated by a separate 23 Aug 2026 commentary piece.

statement: The projections are out: we’ll see another 26,000 people on the dole.
criterion: MSD benefit statistics for Jobseeker Support recipients: true if the number of recipients rises by approximately 26,000 (within a few thousand) from the May 2024 level over the projection period; false if the increase is materially smaller or numbers fall.
reasoning: MSD quarterly Benefit Fact Sheets put Jobseeker Support at ~189,300 in March 2024 and 196,434 at June 2024, so the May 2024 baseline is roughly 193,000-194,000. By June 2025 — the resolve date — the count was 216,009, an increase of about 22,000, and it had only reached 218,481 (~+25,000) by June 2026. The direction and rough scale of Webb's claim held (benefit numbers rose sharply, well past the BEFU 2024 forecast peak of ~202,000 in Jan 2025), but the rise from the May 2024 level was around 22,000 within the criterion's window rather than the stated 26,000, i.e. materially overstated by ~15%. Checked for disconfirming evidence: numbers did not fall at any point and the increase is not smaller than a 'few thousand' shortfall, so 'wrong' does not fit either.

statement: This reading today is another important step in the settlement process, before the third reading, which will result in the full and final settlement of the historic Treaty of Waitangi claims for Whakatōhea.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading and received royal assent as a settlement Act, false if it lapsed, was defeated, or was not enacted.
reasoning: The Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill passed its third reading in late May 2024 and was enacted as the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Act 2024 (2024 No 15), receiving royal assent in early June 2024 (the Act's first consolidated version is dated 4 June 2024, the day after assent). The settlement is the full and final settlement of Whakatōhea's historical Treaty of Waitangi claims — ~$100m financial, cultural and commercial redress, 33 cultural sites, and 5,000 ha of marine space for aquaculture. Nothing indicates the bill lapsed, was defeated, or was amended out of being a settlement Act.

statement: We have interest payments that will be up at around $10 billion per annum.
criterion: Treasury's Financial Statements of the Government / Budget Economic and Fiscal Update core Crown finance costs; true if annual finance costs reach approximately $10 billion (within about 10%) in a fiscal year up to 2026/27, false if they remain materially below that.
reasoning: Treasury data show core Crown finance costs of $8.862b in the year ended June 2025 (interest on financial liabilities $8,291m plus $571m unwind of provisions), about $9.5b budgeted for 2025/26 — Nicola Willis described the burden at Budget 2026 as '$9 billion in interest each year' — and $10.2b forecast for 2026/27 in the Budget 2026 / BEFU 2026 expense breakdown. The criterion allows any fiscal year up to 2026/27 within about 10% of $10b: 2025/26 at ~$9.5b already sits inside that band and 2026/27 is forecast at $10.2b. Caveat: 2026/27 ends 30 June 2027, so its actual is not yet published; the verdict rests on a completed year plus Treasury's own forecast, and disconfirming evidence (costs falling materially below ~$9b) was looked for and not found.

statement: I predict that in 20 years, 30 years, Māori wards will be normal. They will be universally adopted and people will wonder what the argument was all about.
criterion: DIA / Local Government NZ records of territorial and regional authorities with Māori wards or constituencies in 2044; true if the large majority of councils have them and no party is campaigning to abolish them, false if a substantial share of councils have none or abolition remains an active political contest.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against DIA/LGNZ records of councils with Māori wards in 2044; that date is 18 years away, so the prediction cannot be settled. Context only: the 2025 polls show abolition was still an active political contest in 2025, with 24 of 42 councils polling to remove their ward, which bears on the trajectory but says nothing about 2044.

statement: Very, very few of them will survive a referendum.
criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held with the 2025 local body elections; true if a large majority of the councils polling voted to disestablish their Māori ward, false if most wards were retained.
reasoning: 42 councils (37 territorial, 5 regional) held Māori ward polls with the 2025 local elections. Final results: 24 voted to disestablish, 18 voted to retain — 43% of the wards polled survived, including Wellington, Hamilton, Horizons Regional (35,547–35,424) and Ruapehu (2,098–1,982) on specials. Nationally more voters chose keep than remove (542,134 to 467,923). The criterion's 'correct' branch needs a large majority of polling councils to disestablish (57% is not that) and its 'wrong' branch needs most wards retained (not met either). Foster got the direction right — a majority of councils did scrap — but 'very, very few' materially overstates it when nearly half survived and the national popular vote favoured retention.

statement: And like him—though I don’t agree with Labour’s tax policy at the election; he’s already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he’s going to flip-flop on GST too.
criterion: Labour Party tax policy announcements after 28 May 2024; true if Labour publicly abandons or reverses its GST-off-fresh-produce policy before the next general election, false if it carries that policy into the 2026 campaign unchanged.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether Labour abandoned its GST-off-fresh-produce policy before the next general election, or carried it into the 2026 campaign unchanged. Labour's own published 2026 platform lists 20 policies and contains no GST exemption for fresh or frozen fruit and vegetables; its only GST policy is lifting the small-business registration threshold from $60,000 to $80,000 from 1 July 2028. Labour's 2026 cost-of-living and grocery offering is supermarket wholesale/retail separation plus a price-gouging ban, with no GST measure, and Hipkins has publicly said the capital gains tax is Labour's only tax policy. Disconfirming check: I searched labour.org.nz and 2026 election coverage for any surviving fresh-produce GST commitment and found none. Caveat: I found no single dated statement repudiating the policy — the abandonment is evidenced by omission from the platform plus the 'only tax' framing — and polling day is 7 November 2026, so a late revival is not formally excluded.

statement: I am very confident that once the dust settles around this settlement, there’ll be the inevitable smoothing-out processes, you will seize the opportunity and work and build on the collaborative nature of the mahi that has been carried out over the last three to five years and create New Zealand’s largest and most profitable and most desirable new platform of marine, blue ocean growth, otherwise known as mātaitai, ngā kūtai, ngā kuku, ngā porohe—koia tēnā te kupu i ‘hakatupungia ai mātou mō te kūtai i a mātou i te nohinohi i roto i ō mātou kāinga me ō mātou kuikuia.
criterion: Aquaculture NZ / MPI industry production and revenue data plus Whakatōhea Mussels (Ōpōtiki) reported output; true if the Whakatōhea/Ōpōtiki offshore marine farm is by then the largest NZ marine aquaculture operation by area or volume and reporting profitable operation, false if it is neither the largest nor profitable.
reasoning: Criterion resolves by 2031-12-31; today is 2026-09-26, so the prediction is not yet settleable. Interim state for context only: the Ōpōtiki offshore farm (~3,800 ha, 8.5 km offshore) is among NZ's largest marine aquaculture operations, but Whakatōhea Mussels (Ōpōtiki) Ltd is not profitable — FY2025 loss of $17.4m on $15.1m revenue (FY2024: $12.1m loss on $7.6m), accumulated losses over $48m since 2017, a June 2025 BNZ covenant breach, a Bay of Plenty Regional Council prosecution over wastewater discharge, and an ongoing $15m private raise after the Crown stepped back. The 'most profitable' limb is currently unmet, but the criterion's own horizon has five years to run, so no verdict is available.

statement: The ongoing taking of land, denying of resources, denying of customary entitlement, denying of the mana motuhake and the tino rangatiratanga is, rightly, to some extent, acknowledged and laid out in this very bill, in this deed of settlement, in the bill that will pass its third reading tonight.
criterion: Hansard and the Parliament bills record for 28 May 2024. True if the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill passed its third reading that sitting evening; false if the third reading was not completed that night or the bill was defeated.
reasoning: The criterion asks only whether the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Bill passed its third reading on the evening of 28 May 2024. It did. Te Ao Māori News, published 28 May 2024, reports that the third and final reading was completed that evening (the Assistant Speaker's interruption of Te Kāhautu Maxwell occurred after the reading concluded, during the closing waiata). Treaty Negotiations Minister Paul Goldsmith's release announcing the bill's passage is dated 28 May 2024, and the bill became the Whakatōhea Claims Settlement Act 2024 (No 15). Checked for the disconfirming possibility that the reading was adjourned or interrupted mid-debate: the protocol dispute post-dated passage and did not affect it.

statement: By 2034, the next 10 years, it expects to be employing in the order of 320 people, be operating out of the new harbour entrance, have many more vessels in the ocean, and will fair be pumping along.
criterion: Whakatōhea Mussels Ōpōtiki / Te Tāwharau o Te Whakatōhea annual reporting and Ōpōtiki District employment data as at 2034; true if reported headcount is around 320 and operations are based at the new harbour entrance, false if headcount is materially below that or operations have not moved to the new harbour entrance.
reasoning: Criterion resolves by 2034-12-31; today is 2026-09-26. Interim state for context only: the harbour-entrance component is already satisfied — the two breakwaters opened September 2024, the $115.3m Ōpōtiki harbour development is in its post-construction dredging/optimisation phase, and specialist mussel vessels (Northern Quest, Kukutai, Pakihi Kura) now operate from the new entrance. Headcount is the open variable: reporting puts the processing facility at roughly 190–230 staff and the wider local aquaculture sector at 300+, against the 320-at-the-company figure for 2034. Eight years remain, so the prediction cannot be graded.

statement: I see that on Thursday, Te Pāti Māori is running their protests, and good on them, I say.
criterion: News reporting and Te Pāti Māori communications for Thursday 30 May 2024; true if Te Pāti Māori-organised protest action took place that day, false if no such action occurred or it was held on a materially different date.
reasoning: Jackson spoke on Tuesday 28 May 2024, so "Thursday" is 30 May 2024 — Budget Day. Te Ao Māori News (26 May 2024) reported Te Pāti Māori resharing a Toitū Te Tiriti call for a second national activation on Thursday 30 May, timed to the Budget. The action went ahead on that exact date: 1News reported on 30 May that rallies, hīkoi and rolling car blockades ran at 29 locations nationwide, with a hīkoi reaching Parliament grounds at midday and a crowd stretching from Parliament to the railway station; police reported no arrests. RNZ and the NZ Herald covered the same day's events, and RNZ separately reported the government's pre-event 'scare tactics' row, confirming the protest was Te Pāti Māori-aligned and organised rather than spontaneous. Disconfirming check: I looked for evidence the action was cancelled, postponed or moved to another date and found none — coverage is dated 30 May and describes the event as having occurred. Criterion satisfied: Te Pāti Māori-organised protest action took place on Thursday 30 May 2024.

statement: No, no chance of that, Mr Bennett. The electorate for which Mr Bennett used to be the representative will discover that many of the projects and many of the benefits of the fast-track bill apply to the great electorate of New Plymouth, as will other electorates around the House.
criterion: The schedule of listed projects in the Fast-track Approvals Act as enacted, plus subsequent referred-project decisions: true if multiple listed or referred projects sit within the New Plymouth electorate, false if none or only an isolated one does.
reasoning: I went to the source the criterion names: the schedule of projects included in Schedule 2 of the Fast-track Approvals Bill/Act (Beehive project list, October 2024). It has a Taranaki Region block of exactly four projects out of 149 nationally: Maia Properties – Mangorei Road Development (119 allotments on Mangorei Road, Merrilands, New Plymouth); Stratford Park; the Taranaki VTM Project (Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining); and the Huirangi Solar Farm (Harmony Energy NZ #8). Checking each against New Plymouth electorate boundaries (Parliament's electorate profile and the Greens' electorate map: the seat runs Ōpunake to Waitara and takes in New Plymouth, Bell Block, Ōakura, Inglewood and Waitara communities): Mangorei Road is in New Plymouth city, and Huirangi is in the New Plymouth District's Inglewood community — both inside the electorate. Stratford is in Taranaki–King Country. Taranaki VTM is offshore in the South Taranaki Bight, not within the electorate (its panel declined it and TTR withdrew in Feb 2026). Disconfirming check: I also looked for later referred projects in New Plymouth and found none reported; Govett Quilliam's fast-track commentary states Taranaki secured 'just four out of 149 spots'. So the criterion's stated bar is met — two listed projects, not none and not an isolated one — but Bishop said 'many of the projects', and two of 149 is a material overstatement of that.

statement: It’s been a very disruptive sort of debate, but, finally, we’ve got to this point, and we will actually get this through and into law.
criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bill record for the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill: true if the third reading passed and the bill received Royal assent; false if it was defeated, discharged or lapsed.
reasoning: Judged against the bill the criterion names. The New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill completed its parliamentary stages — second reading 11 April 2024, committee of the whole House 7 May 2024, third reading 9 May 2024 (Parliament's Hansard records for each stage) — and became the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Act 2024, No 16, receiving Royal assent on 4 June 2024 (legislation.govt.nz; Wikipedia's list of acts of the 54th Parliament; Russell McVeagh's June 2024 Watching Brief lists it under 'Acts assented'). Disconfirming check: I looked for any record of the bill being defeated, discharged or lapsed and found none — it is on the statute book. Caveat worth flagging rather than acting on: the third reading was 9 May 2024, nineteen days before Foster's 28 May quote, so the criterion has most likely attached the wrong bill to this speech — on 28 May 2024 the House was taking the third readings of the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill and the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill (the latter interrupted with eleven speeches remaining and resumed in July). That does not change the verdict under the criterion as written, since the named bill did pass and did become law.

statement: But I also do want to take the opportunity to thank him for the support that he’s indicated will be forthcoming from Labour in relation to the bill overall on the basis that certain amendments are made.
criterion: The division/vote record for the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill's remaining stages in 2024; true if Labour voted in favour of the bill once the Government amendments were made, false if Labour voted against or opposed at third reading.
reasoning: The bill passed its third reading on 28 May 2024 and was enacted as the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Act 2024. The Government amendments Penk referenced were made in committee and appear in the enacted Act (warrant-application requirements; members of a mass arrival group cannot be held in a prison or police station before a warrant of commitment). Labour voted in favour at the second reading after select committee: Ayes 102 (National 49; New Zealand Labour 34; ACT 11; NZ First 8), Noes 21 (Green Party 15; Te Pati Maori 6), and reporting on the passed bill records only the Greens and Te Pati Maori as opposing. Caveat: parliament.nz Hansard pages are JS-rendered/bot-blocked, so the third-reading division text itself could not be retrieved directly; no source indicates Labour switched to opposing between 7 and 28 May.

statement: This funding will help Gumboot Friday give more than 15,000 young New Zealanders access to free mental health counselling services each year.
criterion: Ministry of Health / I Am Hope contract reporting on the Gumboot Friday funding: true if annual reported numbers of young people accessing free counselling under the contract exceed 15,000; false if materially fewer.
reasoning: Contract reporting shows the first twelve months of Government funding delivered more than 30,000 free counselling sessions to more than 10,000 young New Zealanders - materially fewer than the 15,000 per year claimed (about a third short). The 2025/26 contract year target was then raised to 40,000 sessions reaching 'as many as 15,000' young people, i.e. 15,000 as a ceiling rather than a level already exceeded. Cumulative figures at 7 November 2025 were 40,700 sessions and 14,350 young people since funding began, and June 2026 was the best month of that year at 2,322 young people / 3,776 sessions. So the funded service is real and substantial, but no reported contract year exceeded 15,000 young people; the figure only clears 15,000 on a cumulative multi-year reading the speaker did not signal.

statement: One such investment is in the beating heart of South Dunedin, which is the Hillside railway workshops, which will open again very shortly. This project has received $20 million from the PGF and will provide heavy manufacturing and service capacity for KiwiRail.
criterion: KiwiRail / Government announcements and media reporting on the opening of the Hillside workshops; true if the facility formally opened within roughly a year of 23 May 2024, false if the opening had not occurred by then.
reasoning: The rebuilt Hillside Workshops were officially opened on 16 May 2025 by Rail Minister Winston Peters and Regional Development Minister Shane Jones - within roughly a year of 23 May 2024, as the criterion requires (about 11 months and 3 weeks). Wagon assembly had already started on site in March 2024, with 401 wagons assembled by end of April 2025. The PGF contribution is reported as almost $20m (with $85m from Budget 2021 and $23m from the rolling-stock programme on top), consistent with the $20 million figure quoted. The only stretch is 'very shortly', which turned out to be close to twelve months.

statement: We’ve heard some contributions tonight where members have highlighted that they’ve thought that it’s unlikely to happen, and, yes, it is unlikely.
criterion: Immigration New Zealand / Government records of maritime mass arrivals; true if no mass arrival group (as defined in the bill) reaches New Zealand by the resolve-by date, false if one or more do.
reasoning: The criterion resolves by 2029-05-28, nearly three years away. The Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Act 2024 passed on 2 May 2024 (defining 'mass arrival group'), and the Government's own material notes New Zealand has not experienced a mass arrival event; no reporting of one since. But absence so far does not settle a prediction whose window runs to 2029, so this is not_yet_due rather than correct.

statement: I shared that our strategy will actually double the mineral exports value and, with the right direction and settings, jobs will grow regional resilience and we’ll no longer rely on the Congo for our minerals.
criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE mineral export value series; true if the annual value of New Zealand mineral exports in 2035 is at least double the 2023/24 baseline (approximately $1.1 billion), false if it falls short.
reasoning: The prediction resolves against a 2035 mineral export value, nine years out. Context confirms the claim tracks a real government target: the Minerals Strategy and Critical Minerals List, launched by Jones on 23 May 2024 (six days before the quote), targets doubling mineral exports to $3b by 2035, from roughly $1.2b in the year to June 2023 — consistent with the criterion's ~$1.1b baseline. No Stats NZ/MBIE series can settle the 2035 figure yet, and the separate 'no longer rely on the Congo for our minerals' element is likewise a 2035-horizon claim.

statement: Well, we know that they’re going to be hiking up public transport costs, we know that they’re going to be taking away free prescriptions, we know that they’re going to be making cuts to the disability sector, we know that they are going to be halving the value of the school lunches programme—it’s kind of gone from a free and healthy school lunch programme to a slightly less healthy snack programme in schools as a result of the Government’s changes—and, of course, we know that they are going to rob a whole generation of New Zealanders of the dream of homeownership by doing something that none of them said they were going to do before the election, in cutting the first-home buyer grant scheme.
criterion: Budget 2024 documents (Vote Health, Vote Education, Vote Transport, Vote Social Development) and associated Government announcements: true if each of the five measures appears; partially/wholly false to the extent a measure (in particular the halving of the Ka Ora Ka Ako school lunch funding) is not in Budget 2024.
reasoning: Spoken the day before Budget 2024 (30 May). Three of five measures are confirmed: (1) public transport — Community Connect free fares for 5-12s and half-price for 13-24s were defunded and ended 1 May 2024 (a $327m four-year scheme scrapped after one year); (2) free prescriptions — Budget 2024 reinstated the $5 co-payment from 1 July 2024, with exemptions for under-14s, over-65s and Community Services Card holders; (5) First Home Grant — scrapped on 22 May 2024, saving $245m over four years, with $140m redirected to 1,500 social housing places. The criterion singles out the school lunch claim, and that one is materially overstated: Budget 2024 provided $478m and cut roughly $107m a year against Labour's ~$323.4m annual funding — about a third, not a half (the steeper per-lunch cut for years 7-13, from ~$7-8.90 to ~$3, was announced in October 2024, after this quote). The 'snack programme' characterisation is broadly borne out by later reporting and evaluation of the years 7-13 offering. The disability claim is not supported by the Budget documents the criterion names: Budget 2024 added $1.1b over five years on top of the existing $2.2b/yr baseline, with no savings or cuts listed; what the sector called cuts was the separate 18 March 2024 Whaikaha purchasing-rule restriction, which preceded the Budget and was partly walked back. So: substance holds on three items, one is overstated, one does not appear.

statement: I do think it’s important that we get the best return and, like reinsurance councils, I’m sure that these long-term investment funds will not wish to invest in stranded assets and will almost certainly continue their very good returns by not investing in coal or gas or oil.
criterion: NZ Superannuation Fund annual reports FY2025–FY2027: true if the Fund maintains or extends its carbon-exclusion / low-carbon policy (no material new coal, oil or gas producer holdings) and reports returns at or above its reference portfolio; false if it materially increases fossil-fuel producer holdings or underperforms the reference portfolio over that period.
reasoning: The criterion runs over NZ Super Fund annual reports FY2025-FY2027; the FY2027 report will not be published until about September 2027, so the window is not closed. Interim evidence is mixed and cuts against the prediction: on 29 April 2026 the Fund dropped its exclusion of companies with incidental or very low fossil-fuel-reserve exposure and reinvested in Genesis Energy (coal/gas generator, Kupe gas stake); and for the year to 30 June 2026 it returned 14.17% against a Reference Portfolio 14.27%, a value add of -0.10%. Against that, the Fund retains 2030 targets of -75% emissions intensity and -80% reserve emissions and was 64.3%/99.4% ahead of benchmark at 30 June 2025, and it outperformed by 1.84% p.a. over 5 years. Neither the exclusion relaxation nor a single year of -0.10% is decisive over the FY2025-FY2027 window as written.

statement: It is a pleasure for once to speak to a bill that is going to have unanimous agreement, if not unanimous comprehension, in this House.
criterion: The Hansard vote record for the third reading of the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill: true if it passed with all parties in favour, false if any party voted against or abstained in opposition.
reasoning: The NZ Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill was a Labour-initiated bill (Grant Robertson) carried through by National (Nicola Willis); it was reported back from the Finance and Expenditure Committee unchanged with unanimous select-committee support, the Green Party spoke in favour at the third reading, and the third-reading debate (begun 9 May, concluded 28 May 2024) ended with the motion agreed to and the bill read a third time with no party vote called - i.e. passed on the voices, no party recording opposition. Royal assent 4 June 2024. Searching specifically for opposition (any party voting against or abstaining, including ACT, NZ First and Te Pati Maori) turned up nothing. Limitation: parliament.nz is behind bot protection and web.archive.org is unreachable from this environment, so the division line itself could not be read verbatim; the verdict rests on the Hansard third-reading page's reported outcome plus converging secondary sources.

statement: We’ve already heard tonight that the fund sits at over $70 billion and is projected to reach $110 billion by the end of the decade.
criterion: NZ Super Fund annual report for the year ending 30 June 2030; true if total fund assets are at or above $110 billion, false if below.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on the NZ Super Fund annual report for the year ending 30 June 2030, four years away. Trajectory to date is consistent with the projection: the Fund stood at $86.6b at 31 March 2026 and $94.4b at 30 June 2026, up $9.3b (9.7%) on the year after a 14.17% return. Reaching $110b by 30 June 2030 requires roughly 4% p.a. growth from there, well below the Fund's long-run 10.26% p.a. since inception, but the date has not passed and no verdict can be given.

statement: The $250 a fortnight that they’ve promised to families—will they get it? Probably not, because $2.9 billion in tax breaks for landlords is a higher priority for them.
criterion: Budget 2024 personal income tax package as published by Treasury/IRD: false if an average family's fortnightly gain is about $250 or more; true if the typical/average family gain is materially below $250.
reasoning: Criterion's "true" branch met decisively. Budget 2024 as published: households with children gained an average of $78/fortnight and working-age New Zealanders $32/fortnight, against a promised headline of up to $250. The $250 was only reachable by stacking the maximum FamilyBoost ($150) on top of up to $102 of tax relief; reporting put the number of households receiving the full amount at ~12,000 or fewer (one estimate under 3,000), and Willis publicly conceded the promise was always "up to $250" with no commitment on how many would get it. The typical family gain is therefore materially below $250. Disconfirming check: the only reading where a family gets ~$250 requires young children in paid ECE plus a specific income band, i.e. the reading the criterion's "false" branch (average family at or above $250) excludes. The criterion does not test his second clause about $2.9b in landlord tax breaks, so that is not weighed here.

statement: We have seen the cuts to the organisation and those that provide the services to them, but we are going to see tomorrow the cuts to the services and the contracts that are provided to them and those services in the community.
criterion: Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki documents and subsequent provider contract decisions; true if community service contracts/funding for children's services are reduced or discontinued, false if provider funding is maintained or increased.
reasoning: Both halves of the criterion confirm the prediction. Budget 2024 Vote Oranga Tamariki booked $120m of "Contracting Service Costs" savings over four years plus a $49.2m back-office reduction, with a $46.6m decrease in 2024/25 attributed to Budget 2024 savings and reprioritisation. The subsequent provider contract decisions delivered precisely the community-level cuts she forecast: 337 services run by 190 providers discontinued, contracted provider spend falling from $577m across 554 providers to a minimum of $438m across 480 providers (-$139m), Family Start losing $14m and 107 FTE, and a counselling service defunded; an inquiry into the provider cuts was launched in October 2024. Disconfirming check: Budget 2024 did add money in places (High Needs Children Services, $69m for serious youth offending) and officials asserted "no reduction in frontline services" — but the criterion asks whether community service contracts/funding were reduced or discontinued, and the contract register shows they were, at scale.

statement: Guess who’s getting rid of that in this upcoming Budget!
criterion: Budget 2024 documents and Government housing announcements; true if the First Home Grant scheme is discontinued in or alongside Budget 2024, false if it is retained.
reasoning: The First Home Grant was discontinued, not retained. Housing Minister Chris Bishop announced its end on 22 May 2024 as a pre-Budget announcement; Kainga Ora stopped accepting new applications that day (existing applications and six-month pre-approvals honoured). The closure booked $245m of savings over the 2024-2028 forecast period, and Budget 2024 redirected $140m of it to 1,500 new social housing places delivered by Community Housing Providers. That is "discontinued in or alongside Budget 2024" as the criterion specifies. Disconfirming check: no reinstatement or replacement grant followed — the scheme remains closed. Caveat on the prediction's difficulty rather than its accuracy: the announcement came a week before the 29 May remark, so he was describing a decision already public rather than forecasting an unknown.

statement: On Saturday, 8 June, I’ll be in Auckland supporting tens of thousands of New Zealanders, many of whom weren’t able to speak in the select committee process.
criterion: Contemporary media and police/organiser crowd estimates for the March for Nature in Auckland on 8 June 2024; true if reported attendance at the Auckland event is 20,000 or more, false if reported attendance is materially below that.
reasoning: The March for Nature took place in Auckland on Saturday 8 June 2024 as predicted. Reported attendance meets the criterion's 20,000 threshold: organisers (Greenpeace, Forest & Bird) said 'over 20,000'; NZ Herald headlined '20,000 estimated' and Te Ao Maori News reported 'One speaker at the March for Nature protest in Auckland estimated their number at 20,000'; RNZ reported 'thousands' filling Queen Street from Aotea Square to the waterfront. Disconfirming check: I looked for a lower independent figure. The only police estimate I found (~6,000 at Te Komititanga Square) belongs to a different March for Nature — the September 2026 protest against the Conservation Amendment Bill — and does not apply. No contemporary source put the 8 June 2024 turnout materially below 20,000. Caveat: all figures for this event trace to organisers or a speaker; no independent police count was published, so the criterion is met on organiser/media estimates rather than an official count.

statement: So, again, I congratulate this House in anticipation of this bill going through today and also the committees that considered it, because I think, once again, this shows that this is a class of offending that we all understand the need to put in place all the protections we can so that those who will predate our children, those who will, basically, rob them of their adulthoods—which, essentially, sex offending does—we can deal with them appropriately.
criterion: The Hansard record and division/voice-vote result for the third reading of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed third reading on 29 May 2024, false if it was defeated, adjourned or not concluded that day.
reasoning: The Hansard Final Daily for Wednesday 29 May 2024 (Fifty-fourth Parliament, for inclusion in Volume 776) lists the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill — Third Reading at page 3657, and the debate closes at page 3674 with 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' It was not defeated, adjourned or left unconcluded: the House then suspended for the dinner break. WhereTheyStand records the third reading as 29 May 2024 and royal assent on 4 June 2024 (Act 2024 No 18), which independently confirms the bill completed its passage that day.

statement: So that’s why it is very important for us to continue to support this bill, and we believe that it will be received very well and we commend it to the House.
criterion: The Hansard third reading record and division (if any) for the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) (Overseas Travel Reporting) Amendment Bill; true if it passed third reading without a party voting against, false if any party opposed it or the bill did not pass.
reasoning: The bill passed its third reading on 29 May 2024 and no party voted against it. The Hansard record (Final Daily, 29 May 2024, p. 3674) shows the motion was agreed to on the voices — 'Motion agreed to. Bill read a third time.' — with no division called. The debate itself establishes unanimity: Grant McCallum (National) said 'it's just great to see that the Greens have reconsidered their position and have rejoined and made it unanimous', and Helen White (Labour) thanked 'the Greens for coming around on this bill and supporting it'. Speakers from National, Labour and NZ First all commended it to the House. Disconfirming check: I looked for any party vote or recorded opposition at the third reading and found none — no division appears in the Hansard for this item, and the bill received royal assent on 4 June 2024.

statement: When interest rates fall, the economy will start recovering, which means higher incomes and more jobs.
criterion: Stats NZ GDP, HLFS employment and average weekly earnings in the 12 months after the RBNZ's first OCR cut: true if GDP returns to sustained quarterly growth and both employment and real incomes rise over that period; false if GDP contracts and employment falls or unemployment rises over the same window.
reasoning: RBNZ's first OCR cut was 14 Aug 2024 (5.50% -> 5.25%), so the criterion's 12-month window is Aug 2024 - Aug 2025. GDP did not return to sustained quarterly growth: -1.1% (Sep 2024 qtr), +0.7% (Dec 2024), +0.9% (Mar 2025), -0.9% (Jun 2025); Stats NZ noted GDP had fallen in 3 of the last 5 quarters. Employment fell over the window (HLFS employed 2,909,000 in Jun 2024 qtr -> 2,882,000 in Jun 2025 qtr) and unemployment rose from 4.6%/4.7% to 5.2%, a post-2020 high, with 16,000 more unemployed year on year. The criterion's false condition (GDP contracts AND employment falls or unemployment rises) is squarely met. The one element that held is real incomes: QES average weekly earnings rose 4.1% to $1,679 against 2.7% annual CPI, so real earnings for those in work rose. But that alone does not satisfy the conjunctive 'true' test, and the explicit false test is satisfied.

statement: I would also say to the young lady that we have taken learnings from what has happened in the past and we have put processes in place to make sure that those horrendous acts that have happened in the past will not continue.
criterion: Findings of the Independent Children's Monitor, the Chief Ombudsman, Oranga Tamariki reviews or coronial/court proceedings concerning the military-style academy pilot; true if no substantiated mistreatment, unlawful detention or abuse of participants is found, false if any such finding is made.
reasoning: Judged strictly against the criterion, which asks whether any substantiated finding of mistreatment, unlawful detention or abuse of MSA participants was made. I found none. The MSA pilot ran Jul 2024 - Jul 2025 at Te Au rere a te Tonga and was scrutinised by three Oranga Tamariki-commissioned evaluations (Malatest residential, community-stage, and the final evaluation released Nov 2025), an Office of the Chief Social Worker practice opinion into the tangi absconding incident, an Ombudsman-prompted information release, and Mana Mokopuna OPCAT monitoring of the host residence. The final evaluation reports no incidents of harm among the rangatahi during the residential phase. The adverse findings that do exist are about programme quality and outcomes, not mistreatment: rushed implementation, insufficient staff ratios, inadequate te ao Maori / te reo content, weak post-residential support, and 7 of 10 participants reoffending. I specifically checked for disconfirming evidence: the leaked Chhour advice warning of 'increasing the potential risk of abuse in custody' is a prospective risk warning, not a finding; the Children's Commissioner's September 2026 statement is explicitly prospective ('will closely monitor'); the RNZ use-of-force investigation concerns Te Puna Wai o Tuhinapo, a different facility, not the MSA. Two open caveats that could change this: one participant died in a three-vehicle road crash in Dec 2024 during the community phase and that review sits with the Coroner without a published finding, and the second MSA programme (started 9 Mar 2026) has not yet been evaluated. Note also that the criterion is narrower than Chhour's actual claim, which was about abuse in state care generally on the day the Royal Commission reported.

statement: The challenging economic situation that we have inherited means that job seeker numbers were always due to increase and to peak at the start of 2025.
criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit statistics for Jobseeker Support recipients: true if the recipient count peaks in roughly Q1 2025 and then declines; false if numbers continue rising materially through 2025 or peak substantially later.
reasoning: MSD Jobseeker Support recipient counts do not peak in Q1 2025 and then decline. The series runs 213,321 (end Dec 2024), 209,838 (end Mar 2025), 217,818 (Sep 2025 quarter), 223,512 (Dec 2025 quarter - the highest in five years), then a fall of 8,289 (-3.7%) to about 215,200 in the Mar 2026 quarter, and back up to 218,481 by the Jun 2026 quarter. So numbers rose materially through 2025 and peaked in the December 2025 quarter, roughly a year later than Upston predicted, and remain well above the Q1 2025 level. Both of the criterion's false conditions are met. Checking the other direction: the government's own framing points to flow measures (86,544 benefit-to-work exits in the year to Jun 2026, up 5,772), but the criterion is about the recipient stock, which did not peak when claimed. The December 2025 HYEFU forecast also had the working-age benefit total still climbing to a peak around January 2026.

statement: If someone wants to bring a bill along that line—and I’m expecting to see Dr Webb’s name on one of those bills in the ballot, very shortly—that would be where they would go through all those potential fish-hooks that could be ironed out.
criterion: The Clerk's published list of members' bills in the ballot; true if a bill in Duncan Webb's name dealing with brewery or beer cellar-door tastings is lodged in the ballot by the resolve-by date, false if no such bill appears.
reasoning: No member's bill in Duncan Webb's name dealing with brewery or beer cellar-door tastings was lodged in the ballot by 2025-12-31. Webb's member's bills on record are Fair Trading (Oppressive Contracts) 2018, Girl Guides Association Incorporation 2021, Companies (Directors Duties) 2021, and a bill to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act lodged 25 November 2025 — none about alcohol. The brewery/distillery cellar-door issue Webb raised during the winery bill was instead taken up by the Government in the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Improving Alcohol Regulation) Amendment Bill, introduced in March 2026 (wrong sponsor, and after the resolve-by date). Webb did lodge Amendment Papers on beer tasting sizes during the 29 May 2024 committee stage, but that is not a ballot bill. Caveat: the Clerk's live proposed-members'-bills page is a JS app that would not render for fetching, so absence rests on Webb's bill record, searches of parliament/bills domains, and the government bill superseding the issue.

statement: I’d like to extend, first of all, my congratulations to Melissa Lee, assuming that this will go through.
criterion: Parliamentary records for the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed the reading being debated on 2024-05-29 and continued its passage, false if it was voted down at that reading.
reasoning: The debate on 29 May 2024 was the second reading of the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill (Hansard HansDeb_20240529_20240529_40) — Melissa Lee's ballot bill, carried by Dan Bidois after she became a minister. The second reading concluded and passed 112–11 on 31 July 2024 (ACT alone opposed, matching White's remark in the same window about the House not being unanimous), the committee stage was 21 August 2024, and the third reading passed 111–11 on 11 September 2024. It is now the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Act 2024 No 35, in force 16 March 2026. The reading being debated passed and the bill continued its passage, as the criterion requires.

statement: Well, the market’s expectation and the Reserve Bank’s expectation is that inflation will fall within the 1 to 3 percent target range this calendar year.
criterion: Stats NZ annual CPI prints for quarters within calendar 2024: true if at least one annual CPI reading published for a 2024 quarter falls between 1.0% and 3.0%; false if every 2024 quarterly annual print remains above 3.0%.
reasoning: Stats NZ published annual CPI of 2.2% for the September 2024 quarter (released 17 October 2024) and 2.2% again for the December 2024 quarter — both inside the 1–3% target band and both readings for quarters within calendar 2024, satisfying the criterion. The June 2024 annual print was still 3.3%, so the fall into the band occurred during the calendar year Willis named, exactly as the market and RBNZ expectation she reported had it.

statement: Emissions budget 1 has been delivered, emissions budget 2 is being delivered, emissions budget 3 will be delivered, but we have time for that to happen, and the draft for a plan is out there.
criterion: Climate Change Commission / Ministry for the Environment final accounting of net emissions for the third emissions budget period (2031–2035) against the legislated budget; true if net emissions are within budget, false if they exceed it.
reasoning: The criterion requires a final Climate Change Commission / MfE accounting of net emissions for the third emissions budget period (2031-2035). As of September 2026 that period has not started, no final accounting exists, and the third emissions reduction plan (the plan that delivers EB3) is not due until 2030 and has not been released. Disconfirming check: the Commission's 2026 monitoring report finds current policies leave a gap of roughly nine million tonnes against EB3 and warns the budget becomes infeasible without action in the next one to two years - so the trend runs against Luxon - but a projection is not the final accounting the criterion names, and the resolve-by date is 2037-06-30.

statement: We are committed to a programme of work, and we will achieve Smokefree Aotearoa 2025—highly likely that will be achieved this year.
criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the 2024/25 year; true if the adult daily smoking rate is below the Smokefree 2025 threshold of 5 percent, false if it remains at or above 5 percent.
reasoning: The criterion names the New Zealand Health Survey 2024/25 daily smoking prevalence against the Smokefree 2025 threshold of 5 percent. The published 2024/25 NZHS result is 6.8 percent of adults smoking daily (about 294,000 people), above the 5 percent threshold - so false on the criterion as written. The margin is not marginal and the trend is flat, not falling: prevalence sat between 6.8 and 6.9 percent for three consecutive years (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25), the first such plateau since the survey began. Costello's claim was also stronger than the criterion - she said achievement was highly likely 'this year' (2024) - and it fails on that reading too. Disconfirming check: no population-group cut of the data comes in under 5 percent on the goal's own terms; Maori are at 15.0 percent and Pacific peoples at 10.3 percent, and the goal is defined as under 5 percent for all population groups. Analysts conclude directly that the goal will not be achieved.

statement: When we see that coming down, that will give the Reserve Bank the reason to drop the official cash rate.
criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement / OCR review decisions after 23 July 2024; true if the OCR was reduced at any review within the resolve-by window, false if it was held or raised throughout.
reasoning: The criterion is true if the OCR was reduced at any RBNZ review after 23 July 2024 and before 31 December 2024. The RBNZ cut the OCR from 5.50 to 5.25 percent on 14 August 2024, three weeks after the statement, then to 4.75 percent on 9 October and 4.25 percent on 27 November - three cuts inside the window. Disconfirming check: there was no hold-or-raise outcome in that window, and the mechanism Bayly named holds too - the RBNZ cited easing consumer price inflation as its reason, which is the 'when we see that coming down' link he predicted. The August cut came earlier than market consensus expected, so if anything the prediction was conservative.

statement: Today is 23 July, and in eight days’ time, most New Zealanders will see that they will have more money in their wallets because of the prudent financial management of this Government.
criterion: IRD/Treasury implementation records for the Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold changes; true if the changes took effect on 31 July 2024 and the majority of income earners received higher take-home pay from that date, false if the date slipped or if most earners saw no increase.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether the Budget 2024 personal income tax threshold changes took effect on 31 July 2024 and whether the majority of income earners got higher take-home pay from that date. Both hold. The Taxation (Budget Measures) threshold changes commenced 31 July 2024 — exactly the 'eight days' time' Parmar named (the date had already been shifted from 1 July to 31 July before the speech, to give payroll software vendors time, and it did not slip again). The three lowest thresholds rose ($14,000→$15,600, $48,000→$53,500, $70,000→$78,100), the IETC upper limit went from $48,000 to $70,000, and the in-work tax credit rose $50/fortnight. Everyone earning over $14,000 received a cut; the Government's figure was ~3.5 million New Zealanders (83% of individuals, 94% of households) out of roughly 3.9 million income earners, so 'most' is met. Two minor qualifications that do not change the verdict: the 2024-25 year used composite rates/thresholds because the change landed mid-year, so some people squared up at year end, and employees saw the change in their first pay period on or after 31 July rather than literally on the day. The attribution to 'prudent financial management' is rhetoric the criterion does not cover.

statement: We will be looking into the primary production side of it as well—rural lending—and it will be something that will tie in nicely with the final draft of the Commerce Commission’s market study which will be released soon.
criterion: Commerce Commission publications: true if the final report of the personal banking services market study is published within roughly six months of 23 July 2024; false if publication slips beyond that.
reasoning: The criterion asked only whether the Commerce Commission's final report on the personal banking services market study was published within roughly six months of 23 July 2024. It was published on 20 August 2024 — 28 days later — so 'released soon' is comfortably satisfied. The Commission's own study page and the final report PDF (dated 20 August 2024, amended 27 August 2024) both confirm the date, as does contemporaneous reporting that trailed the 20 August release. I checked for any later or superseding final report and found none; the August 2024 document is the final report. Note for context, not for the verdict: the rural/primary-production lending work Smith refers to was the separate Finance and Expenditure Committee banking inquiry, not part of the ComCom personal banking study, whose scope was personal banking services only. The criterion as written is about the ComCom publication date, so that is what I judged.

statement: The Budget Economic and Fiscal Update shows unemployment is increasing. Poverty will increase. Child poverty will increase.
criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics releases for the years ended June 2025 and June 2026; true if the material hardship rate or a primary child poverty measure rises outside sampling error relative to the year ended June 2024, false if the measures are flat or fall.
reasoning: The criterion points at Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics for the years ended June 2025 and June 2026, true only if a primary measure rises outside sampling error against the year ended June 2024, false if the measures are flat or fall. Only one of those two releases exists. The year ended June 2025 release (published 26 February 2026) is headlined by Stats NZ itself as 'No annual change in child poverty rates': material hardship 14.3% (~169,300 children) against 13.4–13.5% a year earlier, a change Stats NZ reports as not statistically significant; BHC50 12.6% (~148,700) against 12.7% (~149,200); AHC50-fixed 17.8% (~210,600) against 18.2%. So of the three primary measures, one drifted up within sampling error and two drifted down — flat, by the criterion's test. I looked specifically for the disconfirming case and it is real but does not meet the criterion: material hardship IS significantly up against 2022 (10.6%) and sits well above the 9.0% statutory target, and sub-groups are far worse (about one in four disabled children and tamariki Māori, nearly a third of Pacific children). That is a longer baseline than the criterion names. The outstanding caveat: the year ended June 2026 release is not due until early 2027, so the second leg of the criterion cannot be checked yet and could still flip this. On the one published leg, the prediction has not come true. Separately, the non-predictive first clause of the quote — that BEFU showed unemployment increasing — was borne out, but the criterion does not test it.

statement: Irresponsible fiscal management by a National coalition Government, to ensure that child poverty will go up, unemployment will go up.
criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship and after-housing-costs measures) and the HLFS unemployment rate; true if both series are higher in the years following Budget 2024 than at the time of the statement, false if either fails to rise.
reasoning: Both series named in the criterion are higher than at the time of the statement. Unemployment (HLFS, seasonally adjusted) was 4.6% in the June 2024 quarter (4.4% in March 2024, the latest print available on 23 July 2024) and is 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter, the most recent release. Child poverty: the latest published data when he spoke was the year ended June 2023 (material hardship 12.5%, AHC50 fixed-line 17.5%); the post-Budget-2024 releases show material hardship 13.5% (YE June 2024) then 14.3% (YE June 2025, ~169,300 children) — a 10-year high and a statistically significant rise on 2022 — and AHC50 fixed-line 18.2% (2024) then 17.8% (2025). Disconfirming evidence checked and noted: Stats NZ reports no statistically significant annual movement in any child-poverty measure for YE June 2025, AHC50 fell back from its 2024 peak, and BHC50 was essentially flat (12.7% -> 12.6%); the YE June 2026 child-poverty release does not appear until Feb 2027, outside the resolve-by date. Neither qualification makes either series fail to rise relative to the statement-time baseline, which is the test the criterion sets. The criterion does not ask about causation, so the attribution to 'irresponsible fiscal management' was not assessed.

statement: I would not be surprised if this ends up being a one-term Government.
criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election and subsequent government formation; true if the National-led coalition parties do not form the government after that election, false if they return to government.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the official result of the next general election and the government formed after it. The 2026 New Zealand general election is scheduled for Saturday 7 November 2026, with advance voting from 26 October and official results declared 27 November 2026. As of today (26 September 2026) the election has not been held and the National-ACT-NZ First coalition remains in office under PM Christopher Luxon, so the evidence the criterion names does not yet exist. The resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has not passed; this should be re-checked after the official declaration in late November 2026.

statement: This was the signing of a licence—the signing of a licence that proves that this will only ever be a one-term—thankfully—coalition Government.
criterion: The official Electoral Commission result of the next general election and the government formed after it: true if the National–ACT–NZ First coalition parties do not together form the government; false if they are returned to office.
reasoning: Same evidence base as the other one-term-government prediction: the criterion requires the Electoral Commission result of the next general election and the government formed after it. That election is set for 7 November 2026 with official results declared 27 November 2026; as of 26 September 2026 it has not been held and the National-ACT-NZ First coalition is still the government. No result exists to judge against, and the resolve-by date (2026-12-31) has not passed. Pre-election polling is not the evidence the criterion names and was not substituted for it.

statement: Good news too, because in a few days’ time, they are going to find out that the average household in New Zealand and in Tauranga is $102 a fortnight better off—how good?
criterion: Treasury/IRD Budget 2024 tax package distributional analysis of the tax changes effective 31 July 2024: true if the average household gain is approximately $102 per fortnight; false if the average household gain is materially below that (for example if $102 applies only to households with children on average incomes).
reasoning: The tax changes did take effect 31 July 2024 as predicted, and $102/fortnight is the government's own published figure — but as a ceiling for one household type, not the average household. The Budget 2024 release states the package 'gives average income households UP TO $102 a fortnight' (an illustrative ~$125,000 two-average-earner household), while the actual averages in the same release are materially lower: households with children $78/fortnight ($2,028/yr) and working-age New Zealanders $32/fortnight ($832/yr). A single person on $75,000 got ~$36.50; a superannuitant ~$9. The criterion's test — average household gain approximately $102 — therefore fails, since the mean gain is well below $102. Direction correct, magnitude overstated by dropping 'up to' and applying a subgroup ceiling to 'the average household'. No Treasury/IRD distributional analysis supports a ~$102 mean.

statement: It is an expensive experiment, and that money could be better spent in providers that I visited during the recess like Kirikiriroa Family Services Trust or Ko Wai Au in Te Awamutu, who said that they could do better work with our rangatahi and get better outcomes than a boot camp experiment that this Government is hell-bent on starting on Monday.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki / Ministerial announcements and news reporting on the military-style academy pilot start date; true if the pilot commenced on or about 29 July 2024, false if it began later or was deferred.
reasoning: 23 July 2024 was a Tuesday, so 'starting on Monday' means 29 July 2024. The Military Style Academy pilot commenced exactly then: ten young people (boys aged 15-18) began on 29 July 2024 at Te Au rere a te Tonga youth justice residence in Palmerston North, with a three-month residential phase followed by nine months in the community. Oranga Tamariki's own page records the 12-month pilot as running 'from July 2024 through to July 2025', and it concluded in August 2025 with 8 participants completing. There was no deferral or later start, so the criterion ('commenced on or about 29 July 2024') is met. The comparative claim that named providers would get better outcomes is not what the criterion tests.

statement: So when you set up a gang unit and it’s meant to be operating by 1 July and it’s not, and it’s only got five staff in it—not even necessarily police officers—that’s because the 500 promised to New Zealanders will not be delivered in two years. There is no way that that is going to happen.
criterion: NZ Police constabulary strength reporting against the coalition's commitment to 500 additional officers by late November 2025; true (prediction correct) if fewer than 500 additional officers were on the front line by that deadline, false if the 500 target was met on time.
reasoning: The National-NZ First coalition commitment was to lift constabulary strength from the 10,211 sworn officers at swearing-in (27 November 2023) to 10,711 within two years, i.e. by 27 November 2025. That deadline was officially missed: as at 17 November 2025 police had 10,449 constables (about 238 of the 500 additional, roughly 262 short) with 313 recruits still in training. The target had already been pushed publicly from November 2025 to June 2026, then August, then September 2026, and a Treasury report to the Finance Minister put September 2026 as the likely date requiring 'significant catch up'. Earlier in 2025 only 361 extra officers had been added since November 2023, and numbers fell at points during the period. Fewer than 500 additional officers by the late-November 2025 deadline is exactly the criterion's 'prediction correct' condition. Her side-reasoning about the five-staff gang unit is not tested by the criterion.

statement: Imagine if we were to create a Māori bank today while the Māori economy sits at $70 billion and is projected to reach $100 billion in the next five years.
criterion: A published Māori economy valuation (e.g. BERL/Reserve Bank Te Ōhanga Māori series) dated on or before mid-2029; true if the Māori asset base is assessed at $100 billion or more, false if below.
reasoning: The criterion asks for a published Māori economy valuation dated on or before mid-2029 assessing the asset base at $100b or more. Te Ōhanga Māori 2023 (BERL for MBIE and Te Puni Kōkiri, released March 2025) puts the Māori asset base at $126 billion at 2023 — $66b Māori businesses/employers, $41b trusts and collectives, $19b self-employed — up from $69b in 2018, the same series the speaker's ~$70b figure came from. The $100b mark was therefore not just met within five years but already exceeded by the time of the statement's own measurement year; commentary noted it outstripped the earlier '$100 billion by 2030' projection. The only caveat is that the speaker's stated baseline ($70b) was the 2018 vintage, so the growth had largely already happened rather than being still to come.

statement: This funding will mean at least 15,000 young people across New Zealand will have access to free mental health counselling services every year.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health contract reporting on the Gumboot Friday (I Am Hope) contract: true if reported numbers of young people accessing funded counselling reach 15,000 or more in a contract year, false if annual reported reach falls materially short of 15,000.
reasoning: Two Gumboot Friday contract years have now been reported and neither reached 15,000 young people. Year one (2024/25): 10,192 children and young people, 30,842 sessions (Ministry of Health year-one proactive release; the Minister's own release rounded it to 'more than 10,000'). Year two (2025/26, 1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026): 12,242 rangatahi and 37,630 sessions, against a raised contract target of 15,000 people / 40,000 sessions. Year one was 32% short and year two — the better year — 18% short, so the 'at least 15,000 every year' floor failed in both. Looked for disconfirming evidence: monthly reach was still climbing (June 2026 was the busiest month of 2026 at 2,322 rangatahi, 3,776 sessions) and counsellor numbers grew from ~550 to 900+, so the programme is scaling and may hit 15,000 in a later year — but the prediction as stated has not held in any completed contract year.

statement: And, of course, with the Defence Capability Plan shortly due to come out as well, we’ll have a road map that enables the future spending to be done in a coherent fashion that enables the Government’s outcomes to be met in relation to foreign relations and of course, but more particularly, national security.
criterion: Publication record of the New Zealand Defence Capability Plan by the Ministry of Defence/Minister of Defence; true if released within roughly six months of 23 July 2024 (i.e. by 31 January 2025), false if release slips materially beyond that or does not occur.
reasoning: The Defence Capability Plan was published — the Ministry of Defence released the 2025 Defence Capability Plan on 7 April 2025, launched by PM Christopher Luxon and Defence Minister Judith Collins, and it is exactly the multi-year capability road map for coherent future spending that Penk described. But the criterion set 'shortly' at roughly six months, i.e. by 31 January 2025, and the release came 8.5 months after the 23 July 2024 statement — about two months past that window. Substance correct, timing overstated, so partly_correct rather than correct.

statement: Well, I know what Chris Hipkins is getting for Christmas: he’s getting that dodo ticket because after they vote against this Budget—after they vote against tax cuts for working New Zealanders—his leadership will be dead as a dodo, as will the Labour Party.
criterion: Whether Chris Hipkins ceases to be leader of the Labour Party following the Budget 2024 votes; true if he is replaced as Labour leader (party leadership records/news reporting) before the resolve-by date, false if he remains leader.
reasoning: Hipkins has been Labour leader continuously since 22 January 2023; the caucus reconfirmed him in November 2024 and he was still leader and fronting media as "Labour leader" on 25 September 2026, leading the party into the 7 November 2026 election. So the Budget-2024 mechanism Meager named ('after they vote against this Budget... his leadership will be dead as a dodo') did not occur over 26 months. However, the criterion as written runs to 2026-12-31 and that window is still open — the general election falls inside it and a post-election leadership change remains possible — so the claim is not yet settled under its own criterion. Worth flagging for the criterion's author: a resignation after losing in November would satisfy the criterion's letter but would not vindicate the prediction as made.

statement: In this Budget, we haven’t just set out a framework that forecasts lower inflation—3.3 percent, by the latest number; lower than it was forecast to be, on track to allow Mr Orr to do his magic with those interest rates.
criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee decisions: true if the Official Cash Rate is reduced at least once within twelve months of this statement, false if the OCR is held or raised throughout that period.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee reduced the OCR at least once within twelve months of 2024-07-23.
