It did, three weeks later: on 14 August 2024 the MPC cut the OCR by 25bp from 5.50% to 5.25% — the first cut since March 2020, and against economist expectations of a hold. Further cuts followed through 2025 (the OCR was 3.5% by April 2025), so the 'held or raised throughout' disconfirming condition clearly does not hold. The wider rhetorical framing (that the Budget caused it) is not what the criterion tests.

statement: I guarantee, in the future, they will look back on this moment, because inevitably it will pass because they have the numbers, and when they’re old, they’ll look back on their career, and none of them will highlight this as a highlight in their career.
criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill: true if the bill passed on Government party votes; false if it was defeated, withdrawn or lapsed.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on Government party votes. It passed its third reading on 30 July 2024 by 68 votes to 55, with the coalition parties (National, ACT, New Zealand First) in favour and Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed; the Act was enacted. It was not defeated, withdrawn or lapsed. Note the criterion tests only the bill's passage ('inevitably it will pass because they have the numbers'), not the quote's other limb about how MPs will regard it late in their careers, which is unfalsifiable.

statement: Rents will continue to go up, house prices will go up, house builds will go down, and if they don’t believe me, look at the stats, because it’s already happening.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index, REINZ House Price Index, and Stats NZ building consents for new dwellings, measured over the 12 months from July 2024; true if rents and house prices are higher and new dwelling consents lower at the end of that period, false if any of the three moves the other way.
reasoning: All three indicators named in the criterion moved in the predicted direction over the 12 months from July 2024, so nothing moved the other way: Stats NZ CPI rents +3.2% in the year to the June 2025 quarter; REINZ House Price Index July 2025 +0.1% year-on-year nationally (Auckland -0.1%, outside Auckland +0.2%); new dwellings consented in the year ended July 2025 33,879, down 0.1% on the year ended July 2024. A strict directional reading of the criterion therefore yields 'correct'. It is partly_correct rather than correct because the substance is materially overstated: two of the three moves are 0.1% — statistically indistinguishable from flat, and a fall of about 34 dwellings in the consents case — and the rent rise McAnulty said was 'already happening' turned out to be the smallest annual increase in four years, i.e. decelerating, not accelerating. House prices were flat nominally and down in real terms. The direction held; the deteriorating trajectory he was asserting did not.

statement: Interest rates are forecast to come down, and that is a result of the work that this Government is doing to get on top of spending and get on top of inflation.
criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions and RBNZ published mortgage/retail interest rate series in the 12 months following the statement: true if the OCR and average new-lending mortgage rates are lower on 23 July 2025 than on 23 July 2024; false if they are level or higher.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. OCR: 5.50% on 23 July 2024 (the peak set in May 2023 and held through the 24 July 2024 MPS; the first cut was 14 August 2024, to 5.25%), versus 3.25% on 23 July 2025 (lowered to 3.25% at the May 2025 MPS, held at the 9 July 2025 Monetary Policy Review after six consecutive cuts). Retail mortgage rates: the average one-year fixed rate fell from roughly 7.2-7.5% in mid-2024 to about 4.97% by July 2025, per RBNZ B21/B30 series and market reporting. So both the OCR and average new-lending mortgage rates were materially lower on 23 July 2025 than a year earlier. Note that the criterion tests only the direction of rates, not the causal attribution in the second half of her sentence; RBNZ's own stated reasoning for easing was declining core inflation and spare productive capacity rather than fiscal consolidation, but that attribution was not what was written down to be checked.

statement: A retired couple on superannuation will get an extra $9 a fortnight, rising up to around $26 a fortnight by 2026.
criterion: NZ Superannuation payment rates published by MSD for the April 2026 adjustment compared with the counterfactual rates absent the 2024 threshold changes, plus Treasury's published projections; true if the additional after-tax amount for a qualifying couple is around $26 a fortnight, false if materially below or above.
reasoning: Both figures she quoted are the Budget 2024 numbers and the mechanism behind them delivered. Immediate leg: the 31 July 2024 threshold changes were passed through to net super rates, worth about $4.50 a week ($9 a fortnight) to a couple on NZ Super with no other income; the tax saving on roughly $20.9k of super income per person is about $112/yr, i.e. ~$8.6 a fortnight for the couple. Flow-through leg: NZ Super's couple rate is set at 66% of the net average ordinary-time wage, so the threshold package (maximum individual saving $1,043/yr) raises the floor by 0.66 x $1,043 = $688/yr = $26.5 a fortnight combined - exactly the '$680 a year or $26 a fortnight' the Herald reported and Willis's stated justification for giving superannuitants less direct relief. The floor actually bound: the April 2025 adjustment was about 3% 'because of the relationship to the net average wage level' (couple rate $828.34 each, from $803.72), and MSD confirmed the 1 April 2026 rates ($854.08 each, $1,708.16 combined per fortnight) keep NZ Super aligned with the 66% couple floor. Reconstructing the counterfactual from those published rates gives a gap of $26.4-$26.5 a fortnight at both April 2025 and April 2026 - 'around $26', neither materially below nor above. Caveat on method: MSD does not publish a counterfactual rate, so this leg is resolved by arithmetic from the published rates plus the statutory 66% rule rather than by a single published figure; and the $26 is a nominal cumulative gain, not a real-terms one. Note also that the April 2026 per-person increase of $25.74 is the ordinary annual adjustment and coincidentally similar to $26 - it is not the tax-cut effect, which is the $26 on the couple's combined rate.

statement: We’re going to force you to go to a referendum; a referendum that we know will be much harder to succeed in than the local bodies would otherwise want.
criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held with the 2025 local body elections; true if a majority of the councils polled voted to disestablish their Māori ward, false if most polls returned a vote to retain.
reasoning: Māori ward polls were held with the 2025 local elections across 42 councils (37 territorial, 5 regional). Official/collated results: 24 councils voted to disestablish their Māori ward, 18 voted to retain. The criterion as written — majority of councils polled voting to disestablish — is met. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the nationwide popular vote went the other way (542,134 keep / 50.25% vs 467,923 remove / 43.37%, ~74,000 more votes to retain), and large urban councils (Wellington, Hamilton, Porirua, Hutt, Palmerston North, Nelson) voted keep. That cuts against a broader reading of Webb's claim but not against the council-count test the criterion specifies.

statement: Even our colleagues across the aisle support it, and I’d just like to acknowledge previous commerce and consumer affairs Ministers who have worked on this bill.
criterion: The division records for the Customer and Product Data Bill's first and subsequent readings; true if Labour voted in favour at each reading, false if Labour voted against at any reading.
reasoning: The Customer and Product Data Bill passed its first reading on 24 July 2024 with 'unanimous cross-party support', and its second reading (House accepted the bill as amended 6 March 2025) also with unanimous cross-party support — so Labour voted in favour at both. Committee stage and third reading followed 25–26 March 2025, with Royal assent on 29 March 2025 (Customer and Product Data Act 2025). Labour's select-committee minority view supported the bill's intent while arguing it fell short in places — a supportive, not opposing, position. Caveat on evidence: I could not retrieve the third-reading division record itself (hansard.parliament.nz and parliament.nz both blocked automated fetching, returning 404 / bot-protection pages), so the third reading is inferred rather than directly verified; no source found reports any party voting against at any stage. The criterion's failure condition (Labour voting against at any reading) is not met by any evidence located.

statement: Whether through regulatory changes such as the proposals in these bills or through the tremendous efforts across the whole of Government in 2024, this Government will see results achieved for New Zealand and we will get business confidence restored again in New Zealand.
criterion: ANZ Business Outlook net business confidence series: true if the headline net confidence reading is positive and at or above its long-run average for a sustained period (three consecutive months) at any point before the resolve-by date; false if it remains negative or below the long-run average throughout.
reasoning: ANZ Business Outlook headline net business confidence was positive and far above its long-run average for a sustained run well before 31 December 2025. From the 19 December 2025 ANZBO report: December net 73.6 ('highest level in 30 years'), November 67.1, with October ~58 and September ~50 — at least four consecutive months strongly positive. Earlier 2025 months were also positive (e.g. April ~49, May ~36.6, the year's low). The long-run average of the series is about +3.9 (1970–2026, Trading Economics), so readings of 50–74 are well above it. Looked for the disconfirming case — a year spent negative or below average — and the series never went negative in 2025. Note the criterion tests the indicator only, not whether government policy caused the move.

statement: As we look towards the future and what that means, I’m excited that Te Ohu Kai Moana is going to go around again and engage with iwi on a roadshow, starting in August.
criterion: Te Ohu Kaimoana's own website/news and hui notices: true if iwi roadshow/engagement hui were held commencing in August 2024, false if no such hui series ran or it began materially later.
reasoning: Te Ohu Kaimoana did run an iwi roadshow — its first since 2021 — but it began on 8 October 2024 (Te Tai Tokerau), continuing 5, 6, 19 and 20 November. TOKM's own notice announcing the dates is dated 1 October 2024 and states the schedule 'differ[s] to those circulated on Thursday 19 September', so even the superseded schedule was September-based, not August. Searches of TOKM's August 2024 activity found only a 21 August meeting with the Minister of Conservation and an extension of the four-year audit feedback deadline — no iwi hui series. The criterion explicitly makes a materially later start false, and a ~2-month slip from 'starting in August' to 8 October is material.

statement: Wing 376 will graduate next week on 1 August and a further wing will graduate every five weeks from then on.
criterion: NZ Police graduation records and media releases; true if Wing 376 graduated on 1 August 2024 and successive wings graduated at roughly five-week intervals through the following year, false if the graduation slipped or the cadence was not maintained.
reasoning: Wing 376 graduated on 1 August 2024 at Te Rauparaha Arena, Porirua (58 officers, Associate Minister Nicole McKee attending), exactly as stated. Successive wings then graduated at five-week intervals: 377 on 5 Sep, 378 on 10 Oct, 379 on 14 Nov, 380 on 19 Dec 2024, 381 on 6 Feb 2025, 382 on 13 Mar, 383 on 17 Apr, 384 on 22 May, then further wings on 26 Jun, 31 Jul and 4 Sep 2025. Every gap is five weeks except the Christmas/New Year break (19 Dec to 6 Feb, ~7 weeks). No graduation slipped and the cadence was maintained within the criterion's 'roughly five-week intervals' through the following year, with that single seasonal exception.

statement: We expect interest rates to come down when we get it back in the band.
criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions after the first quarter in which annual CPI inflation prints within 1–3%; true if the OCR is reduced from 5.5% within roughly a year of that return to band, false if the OCR is held or raised over that period.
reasoning: Annual CPI first printed inside the RBNZ's 1-3% band in the September 2024 quarter (2.2%, Stats NZ, released October 2024). The OCR came off 5.5% to 5.25% on 14 August 2024 as inflation converged on the band, was cut to 4.75% on 9 October 2024, and then successively to 4.25% (Nov 2024), 3.75% (Feb 2025), 3.5% (Apr), 3.25% (May) and 3.0% (Aug 2025) - 250bp of easing, far inside the criterion's 'roughly a year' of the return to band. I checked for the disconfirming case (OCR held or raised over that period) and found no hold or hike in that window. The only nuance is that the first cut slightly preceded rather than followed the in-band print, which makes the prediction earlier-fulfilled, not less fulfilled.

statement: I’m sure it’s so well done that we will just pass it all the way through, and I’m looking forward to that process.
criterion: The parliamentary record for the Customer and Product Data Bill: true if the bill is reported back and passes its third reading into law; false if it is defeated, withdrawn, or still not passed by the end of the parliamentary term.
reasoning: The Customer and Product Data Bill was reported back by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on 23 December 2024, passed its second reading on 18 February 2025, and received Royal assent on 29 March 2025 as the Customer and Product Data Act 2025 — i.e. reported back and passed into law well within the parliamentary term, which is what the criterion requires. The one qualification is that it did not pass unchanged: the committee recommended substantive amendments (deleting 'derived data', removing policy/infringement requirements, adding a good-faith liability defence), so the flourish about it being 'so well done that we will just pass it all the way through' is looser than the record. The criterion as written asks only whether it was reported back and enacted, and it was.

statement: I will be on that select committee and I’ll be zealously guarding the needs of the ordinary New Zealanders when we look at the detail, because we, sure as eggs, will have people lobby us on that committee to try and water it down, to try and say it’s too hard.
criterion: Published submissions to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee on the Customer and Product Data Bill: true if bank, telco or electricity industry submitters sought narrowed scope, delayed commencement or reduced obligations citing implementation difficulty or cost; false if no such submissions were made.
reasoning: The committee received and considered submissions from 40 groups and individuals. The New Zealand Banking Association's select committee submission (5 September 2024) sought exactly the kind of narrowing the criterion describes: exclusion of derived data from the definition of customer data, a staged/phased commencement with extended transition periods, narrower designation criteria and transitional exemptions for legacy systems — justified by the time and cost of reconfiguring core banking systems, API/security complexity and compliance expenditure, particularly for smaller banks. The committee's report then recommended deleting all reference to 'derived data', deleting the customer-data/product-data policy requirements and the related infringement offence expressly to reduce compliance costs, and adding a good-faith defence for data holders; the eventual banking designation was itself staged (majors from 1 December 2025, Kiwibank later). Disconfirming check: fintech, consumer and Law Society submitters pushed in the opposite direction (broader scope, stronger protections), but the criterion asks only whether bank/telco/electricity submitters sought narrowed scope, delayed commencement or reduced obligations on cost/difficulty grounds — they did. Caveat: the NZBA PDF was read via an automated summariser, so the exact wording of its asks is paraphrase; the substance is corroborated by the committee's own recommendations.

statement: We are at the third stage, so this will become law if it goes through today, which I suspect it may very well do, from what I’m hearing from various parts of the House.
criterion: The Hansard third-reading record for the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed its third reading on 23 July 2024, false if the reading was not completed that day or the bill was defeated.
reasoning: The substance held — the bill passed its third reading unanimously (12 speeches from NZ First, Labour, Te Pāti Māori, Green, ACT and National, all supportive) and received Royal assent on 26 July 2024 as the Māori Fisheries Amendment Act 2024. But the date did not. Parliament's own daily progress for Tuesday 23 July 2024 records that the House agreed to extend the sitting from 9.00 am to 1.00 pm on Wednesday 24 July 2024 for business including 'the interrupted debate on the third reading of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill' — so the third reading was explicitly interrupted on 23 July and not completed that day. Te Ohu Kaimoana's contemporaneous newsletter states Parliament concluded the third reading on Wednesday 24 July 2024, and the Hansard item is filed as HansDeb_20240723_20240724_20 (sitting day 23 July, calendar date 24 July). The criterion says false if the reading was not completed that day; since the outcome he predicted did occur but one sitting later, this is materially overstated rather than simply wrong.

statement: This investment is expected to increase regional GDP by around 7 percent once the track is fully operational again.
criterion: Infometrics/Stats NZ regional (Thames-Coromandel district) GDP series for the years after the track reopens; true if regional GDP rises by roughly 7 percent attributable to the reopening, false if growth is materially lower or no such uplift is identifiable.
reasoning: The track in question (Mautohe Cathedral Cove, the subject of Potaka's July 2024 announcements about track reinstatement and regional economic benefit) reopened on 1 December 2024, closed again after an extreme rain event in January 2026, and reopened on 31 January 2026 under a rainfall trigger-closure plan — so 'fully operational again' is recent and intermittent. The criterion calls for the Infometrics/Stats NZ Thames-Coromandel district GDP series for the years AFTER reopening; the only district GDP reporting I could retrieve is Infometrics' year-to-March-2024 estimate (zero growth), which predates the reopening, and Infometrics' district GDP pages are behind a paywall/JS so no post-reopening annual series is publicly readable yet. Resolve-by is 2027-06-30, still nine months out. Noted for the eventual resolution, not used to grade now: the only public economic figure attached to the reopening is DOC/Potaka's ~$12m/year of visitor spending into the region, which is an order of magnitude short of 7% of a district economy, so the claim looks unlikely to be borne out — but absence of the named series is not evidence of falsity.

statement: We have to recognise the economic conditions we are in today, and the forecasts show, unfortunately, those numbers are due to get worse before they get better.
criterion: MSD quarterly benefit statistics from July 2024 onward: true if the jobseeker support recipient count peaks and then shows a sustained decline by mid-2026; false if the count is still rising, or higher than its 2024 level, at that point.
reasoning: MSD's Benefit Fact Sheets give the series the criterion names. Jobseeker Support recipients: 196,434 at end-June 2024; 216,009 at end-June 2025; 218,481 at end-June 2026 (up 2,472 or 1.1% on June 2025). At the criterion's mid-2026 checkpoint the count is both still rising year-on-year and ~22,000 above its 2024 level — the two conditions the criterion states make it false. Checking for the opposite: the quarterly peak was 223,512 in the December 2025 quarter, so the count has eased ~5,000 off that peak, and June quarters are seasonally higher; but a June-on-June increase is not the 'sustained decline by mid-2026' the criterion required, and main benefit numbers overall also rose to 413,691 in June 2026. So the first half of Upston's prediction ('get worse') held while the second half ('before they get better') did not arrive inside the window the criterion set.

statement: Aucklanders will continue to reject the Labour Party.
criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the next general election: true if Labour's Auckland party vote share is at or below its 2023 Auckland share and it wins fewer Auckland general electorates than National; false if Labour's Auckland party vote share rises materially and it wins a majority of Auckland general electorates.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Electoral Commission official results for the next general election. The Prime Minister announced that election for Saturday 7 November 2026, with advance voting opening 26 October 2026 and enrolment closing 25 October. Today is 26 September 2026, so no votes have been cast and there are no Auckland party-vote shares or electorate results to compare with Labour's 2023 Auckland performance. Resolve-by 2026-12-31 leaves room for the official count (usually declared within about three weeks of election day).

statement: But they knew, as Mr McAnulty said, that if they went to referendum—because of demography both of their constituencies and of the people who get out and vote—that it would essentially be a veto on Māori wards.
criterion: Official results of the binding Māori ward polls held at the 2025 local elections; true if a clear majority of the councils polled voted to remove their Māori ward or constituency, false if most polls returned a vote to retain.
reasoning: The criterion's true-branch is met: of the 42 councils that held binding polls at the 2025 local elections, 24 (57%) voted to remove their Maori ward or constituency and 18 voted to retain — a majority to remove, not 'most polls returned a vote to retain'. Webb's mechanism (a whole-of-electorate vote acting as a veto) did cost more than half the wards, effective 2028 and 2031. Checked for the opposite: nationwide the popular vote went the other way, 542,134 keep (50.25%) to 467,923 remove (43.37%) on 73.4% turnout, a ~74,000-vote keep margin; six of seven city councils retained while only nine of 29 district councils did, and four removals were decided by fewer than 750 votes. So 'essentially a veto' is stronger than the result — the veto was rural and partial, not universal — but the pre-registered test is passed.

statement: He said that, actually, if we go out for referendum it will be the death star for Māori wards.
criterion: Results of the binding Māori ward polls held alongside the October 2025 local body elections: true if a majority of the councils polling voted to disestablish their Māori ward or constituency, false if most voted to retain them.
reasoning: Criterion as written asks whether a majority of the councils polling voted to disestablish. Final results (including special votes): 24 of 42 councils voted to remove, 18 to retain; with Kaipara and Upper Hutt, which abolished without a poll, 26 of 44 councils lose the seats for the 2028 and 2031 elections. Disconfirming evidence checked and found: the nationwide vote favoured keeping by about 74,000 (542,134 to 467,923), city councils retained almost uniformly (Napier the only exception), and Ruapehu and Horizons flipped to 'keep' on specials by 116 and 123 votes. 'Death star' therefore overstates the scale — 18 wards survived and more voters voted keep than remove — but on the council-count test the prediction holds.

statement: Because, again, as we’ve heard in this House, if we allow the entire community to vote on Māori wards, then we will get voted down.
criterion: Official results of the 2025 binding polls on Māori wards across the councils required to hold them: true if the majority of those polls returned a vote to remove the ward, false if the majority voted to retain.
reasoning: The pre-written test — did the majority of the 2025 binding polls return a vote to remove the ward — resolves yes: 24 of 42 councils voted to remove, 18 to retain, binding for 2028 and 2031. I specifically looked for the opposite result and it exists in aggregate but not at council level: across all polls combined, more people voted to keep (542,134, 50.25%) than to remove (467,923, 43.37%), so 'the entire community' as a national electorate did not vote Maori wards down; the removals came from district councils (20 of 29 voted to remove) while six of seven city councils retained theirs. On the criterion's own unit of account — polls won and lost — the prediction is right.

statement: Another highlight was sharing with my neighbours in Takanini and beyond the excellent news that Mill Road is on the list of seven roads of national significance, and work will begin in three years.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project pages and construction-start announcements for Mill Road: true if construction is recorded as starting on or before mid-2027, false if the start date has slipped beyond that or the project has been deferred/cancelled.
reasoning: Mill Road was indeed one of the seven first-phase RoNS in the July 2024 announcement, but the predicted construction start (~mid-2027) has failed the criterion's explicit falsifier. NZTA's own mid-2026 construction target passed with Stage 1 still in pre-implementation (design/consenting; only an ROI out for the first technical-works package). In July 2026 the Government's phased RoNS pipeline put Mill Road Stage 1 on the slow track: Phase 2 'preparing for construction, and route protection by the end of 2027', then 'implementation ready' with 'progression subject to funding availability' and no construction funding date given. NZ Herald (15 Aug 2026) reports the project 'now on ice' with Stage 1 costs up to $1.75-2.05b, while property acquisition continues (68 of 73 land blocks in Crown control, $131m spent). Route protection running to end-2027 plus unallocated construction funding rules out a start by mid-2027.

statement: The school is going to cater for 600 children from years 1 to 6, and the intended building will be complete by 2026. Construction will begin later this year.
criterion: Ministry of Education school property announcements and the school's opening record: true if the new primary school at 121 Murphys Road, Flat Bush is completed during or before 2026, false if completion slips into 2027 or later.
reasoning: The new primary school at 121 Murphys Road, Flat Bush — Te Kura Rau Iti (formerly Flat Bush Southwest Primary School) — was completed and opened in Term 1 2026, with its first day on 9 February 2026 following a blessing ceremony. Its own website carries newsletters from February through September 2026, confirming it is operating. It has 30 classrooms with an initial capacity of 600 pupils, serving new entrants to year 6, under foundation principal Libby Slaughter. The criterion (completed during or before 2026) is met. Two immaterial imprecisions in the quote: the school serves new entrants to year 6 rather than 'years 1 to 6', and it opened with roughly 100 students against the 600 capacity — neither bears on the criterion.

statement: We welcome the apology that will be offered by the Prime Minister on behalf of the State.
criterion: Hansard and official records of a formal Crown apology delivered in the House by the Prime Minister to survivors of abuse in care; true if such an apology is delivered, false if none is given by the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon delivered a formal apology on behalf of the Crown to survivors of abuse in state and faith-based care in the House of Representatives at 11.30am on 12 November 2024, followed by a statement from the Leader of the Opposition; it was screened on Parliament TV and to survivor events in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and 12 November is now a National Remembrance Day. Official records (Beehive speech text, Ministry of Justice, abuseinquiryresponse.govt.nz, Crown Law) and independent reporting (CNN, ABC, Al Jazeera) all confirm delivery. Checked the disconfirming case — a cancelled, downgraded, or out-of-House apology — and found none; criticism in the record concerns the adequacy of redress, not whether the apology was given.

statement: It is forecast that job seeker numbers will continue to increase until January 2025.
criterion: MSD monthly/quarterly benefit statistics for jobseeker support; true if the caseload peaks around January 2025 and declines thereafter, false if numbers continue rising materially beyond that date.
reasoning: The criterion required the jobseeker caseload to peak around January 2025 and decline thereafter. It did not. The forecast Upston was quoting (PREFU, July 2024) put the peak at ~214,000 in January 2025. MSD's actual quarterly data: 213,321 at December 2024, 209,838 at March 2025 (normal seasonal dip), 216,009 at June 2025, and 223,512 at December 2025 — described by MSD as the highest in five years. At June 2026 it was still 218,481, ~2,500 above June 2025. MSD itself pushed the forecast peak out a full year, to ~221,900 in January 2026, at HYEFU 2025. Numbers therefore continued rising materially beyond January 2025 — about 10,000 above the forecast peak a year later — which is the criterion's explicit false condition. The direction of travel up to January 2025 was right; the turning point was not.

statement: In time, the consumer data framework will likely be extended to other industries such as the telecommunications and insurance sectors.
criterion: Regulations made under the Customer and Product Data Act designating sectors; true if telecommunications or insurance is designated by the resolve-by date, false if only banking (and/or electricity) remains designated.
reasoning: Resolve-by is 2028-06-30, nearly two years away. Status as at September 2026: banking is the only sector designated under the Customer and Product Data Act 2025, with banking standards in force from 1 December 2025. Electricity retail is the second sector in the pipeline — MBIE consulted in 2024 and again in Sept/Oct 2025 on draft designation proposals, with Cabinet decisions expected mid-2026 and the regime starting roughly a year later. Telecommunications and insurance are repeatedly named as candidate future sectors in MBIE material and law-firm commentary, but no designation regulations exist for either. So the criterion's false condition (only banking and/or electricity designated) is what currently holds, but the window has not closed; the claim was hedged with 'in time' and no date, and the criterion's deadline has not passed.

statement: It will ensure that there are fewer Māori wards in the future than there are now.
criterion: Count of New Zealand local authorities with Māori wards or Māori constituencies in the term following the 2028 local elections, compared with the number in place at July 2024 (approximately 45), per Local Government Commission / Department of Internal Affairs records; true if the number is lower, false if it is the same or higher.
reasoning: The event that decides the criterion has already occurred. Under the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Maori Wards and Maori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024 — the bill Webb was speaking against — the 42 councils (37 territorial, 5 regional) that had established Maori wards or constituencies since 2020 without a poll had to hold a binding referendum at the October 2025 local elections. Final results: 24 voted to remove, 18 voted to keep. The results are binding and take effect from the 2028 local elections, for two electoral terms; the wards elected in 2025 serve out that term. Against a July 2024 baseline of about 45 councils with current or proposed Maori wards, the 2028-2031 term is set to have roughly 21 (the 18 that voted keep, plus the few long-standing wards not required to poll). So the number will be lower, which is the criterion's true condition. Caveat on the residual: the 2028 count itself cannot be read from Local Government Commission / DIA records until October 2028, and the only path to a different outcome is Parliament legislating before then — Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori all backed the pro-ward side, and the 2026 general election falls in the interval, but I found no specific Labour 2026 policy commitment to reinstate the wards or repeal the poll requirement.

statement: Because what will inevitably happen as a result of this bill is there will be referenda.
criterion: Local authority election records for the 2025 local elections: true if one or more binding polls on Māori wards were held under the Act, false if no such poll occurred.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether one or more binding polls on Māori wards were held under the Act at the 2025 local elections. They were: binding polls ran in 42 councils (37 territorial authorities and 5 regional councils) alongside the October 2025 local elections, with results declared mid-October 2025. Checking for the disconfirming case — that the Act's poll requirement was repealed, deferred or otherwise never triggered before October 2025 — finds no such thing; the polls went ahead as legislated.

statement: And I guess we have to be realistic on this side of the Chamber; when this passes into law, it’s going to mean the end for many, many council Māori wards and constituencies.
criterion: Results of the binding Māori ward polls held under this Act at the 2025 local elections (and any pre-poll council resolutions to disestablish): true if a large majority of the affected councils' Māori wards were voted out or removed; false if most councils retained their Māori wards.
reasoning: Of the 42 councils polled, 24 voted to remove their Māori wards and 18 voted to keep them; adding the two councils that disestablished by resolution in 2024 (Kaipara District and Upper Hutt City) gives 26 removals against 18 retentions, with Tauranga still undecided at the time of the final-results report. Removals take effect for the 2028 and 2031 elections. So many wards did end, and Bennett's direction was right — but the criterion's bar was a 'large majority' of affected councils, and ~59% is a slim majority, while its falsifying condition ('most councils retained') is also not met. Disconfirming evidence is substantial: nationally the aggregate vote favoured retention, 50.25% keep versus 43.37% remove (about 75,000 more keep votes), and several large councils including Greater Wellington Regional (84,067 to 52,203) and Hamilton retained their wards. The substance holds but the sweep is materially overstated.

statement: Local Water Done Well for Auckland will substantially reduce Aucklanders’ future water bills from the previous projections of a 25.8 percent increase in water rates down to 7.2 percent.
criterion: Watercare / Auckland Council adopted water price schedule for the 2024-25 year; true if the adopted increase is about 7.2%, false if the actual increase is materially higher.
reasoning: The criterion named the adopted Watercare / Auckland Council price schedule for 2024-25. Watercare's own pricing notice confirms water and wastewater prices increased by 7.2% on 1 July 2024 (about $8.08 more per month for a household with average use), matching Brown's figure. The 25.8% baseline he cited is also documented as the increase proposed in the draft Long-term Plan for 1 July 2024, avoided under the Local Water Done Well model; Auckland Council adopted the LTP on that basis on 27 June 2024. Looking for the disconfirming case — an adopted increase materially above 7.2%, or a mid-year revision upward — turns up nothing: 7.2% is the figure in the operator's own schedule and in contemporaneous reporting. Note the criterion covers only the single 2024-25 year, so this verdict says nothing about the multi-year 'substantially reduce future water bills' framing.

statement: You will not be finding relationships anywhere else, from a PPP perspective.
criterion: Public records of Crown or local-government public-private partnership / major infrastructure agreements entered into with iwi or iwi investment entities between this statement and the end of the parliamentary term; true if no such agreements are concluded, false if iwi enter PPP or comparable infrastructure investment arrangements with the Government.
reasoning: Iwi and iwi investment entities did enter PPP and comparable infrastructure arrangements with the Crown and local government during the term. Te Aka Haumi LP, an iwi-only sidecar to the Zealandia PPP infrastructure fund (raise of ~NZ$500m across Zealandia Fund I and Te Aka Haumi announced 27 August 2026, iwi minimum $2m), holds equity in Crown PPP concession companies: 40% of Wellington Gateway (Transmission Gully, NZTA) and 23.4% of NX2 (Puhoi-Warkworth), with the Auckland South Corrections Facility carved out of the iwi vehicle. The Western Bay of Plenty Regional Deal (May 2026) was signed by central government, councils and iwi, hapu and Maori land trusts, covering public infrastructure, social procurement, housing/papakainga and land leasing. Tupu Tonu (Ngapuhi Investment Fund) took a 7% stake in Marsden Maritime Holdings/Northport in a 2025 consortium with Northland Regional Council (43%) and Port of Tauranga (50%). Senior representatives of iwi investment companies also attended the March 2025 Infrastructure Investment Summit, where ministers made iwi infrastructure partnership a headline theme. Caveat: the quote is terse and could instead be read as saying the Crown will find no substitute for its relationship with iwi; I judged it against the criterion as written, which asks whether iwi entered PPP or comparable arrangements. I could not recover the Hansard context for 24 July 2024 to settle the reading.

statement: Oranga Tamariki continues to work in partnership with providers, communities, Māori, iwi, hapū, and whānau, and nothing about the repeal of section 7AA will affect the support services and the programmes Oranga Tamariki provides for Māori or the partnerships it has and will continue to develop.
criterion: Oranga Tamariki annual reports and Independent Children's Monitor reporting for 2025 and 2026 on strategic partnerships under section 7AA and on Māori service provision; true if partnership arrangements and Māori service funding continue at comparable levels after the repeal takes effect, false if partnerships lapse or Māori-focused services/programmes are reduced following the repeal.
reasoning: The partnership half of the claim held; the services half did not, on the criterion's temporal test. Partnerships: the select committee amended the bill to retain the chief executive's duty to develop strategic partnerships with iwi and Maori organisations, now carried in a new section 7; the Act received royal assent 7 April 2025. Oranga Tamariki still lists nine strategic partnerships (Ngai Tahu, Ngapuhi, Waikato-Tainui, Ngati Kahungunu, Tuhoe, Eastern Bay of Plenty Iwi Provider Alliance, Ngati Toa Rangatira & Te Ati Awa, Te Kahu Oranga Whanau, Maori Women's Welfare League), and the Independent Children's Monitor's 2024/25 Maori outcomes report (released June 2026) treats them as ongoing and worth continued investment. I found no evidence a partnership lapsed. Services: Oranga Tamariki discontinued funding to 190 providers and reduced funding to a further 142, scrapped 337 service contracts and recovered about $22m; provider contracting fell from $577m across 554 providers in FY2024 to a minimum $438m initiated for FY2025, with marae-based and iwi providers among those affected, and Budget 2026 left Maori and iwi provider investment static or lower. So Maori-focused services and programmes were reduced over the period the repeal took effect. What keeps this short of wrong: those cuts were commissioning and budget decisions running in parallel with the repeal rather than consequences of it, so the literal 'nothing about the repeal' clause is defensible; what keeps it short of correct is that the assurance as heard - that Maori services and programmes would be unaffected - did not hold.

statement: According to the after housing cost measure, which is most closely connected to material hardship, Budget 2024 is forecast to see 17,000 fewer children in poverty.
criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics, AHC 50% of median measure, for the years following Budget 2024; true if the number of children below the AHC line falls by about 17,000 relative to the pre-Budget baseline, false if it falls materially less or rises.
reasoning: On the AHC50 fixed-line measure the criterion names, the number of children below the line has not fallen. Stats NZ / CPAG: 2023/24 was 17.7% (208,000 children); 2024/25 (released 26 February 2026) was 17.8% (210,600 children) - a rise of roughly 2,600, not statistically significant, but no fall, let alone one of about 17,000. 2024/25 is the first full year in which Budget 2024's tax cuts, FamilyBoost and the in-work tax credit increase were all in effect. Material hardship, the measure Upston explicitly tied the AHC line to, moved the other way and significantly: from 13.4% (157,048 children) in 2023/24 to 14.3% (about 169,300) in 2024/25, a statistically significant increase on 2022, with severe material hardship at 6.0%. Stats NZ recorded no statistically significant movement in any measure for the year ended June 2025. One genuine qualification: the Treasury modelling Upston was quoting ran to 2026/27, and statistics for that year will not publish until February 2028, so the forecast's terminal year is unmeasured. But the criterion's resolve-by date has passed and its test - falls materially less or rises - is met on the data now available.

statement: So now we have the opportunity for those mayors and councillors to go out to the public and get a mandate to support what has been so effective for them, and I’m sure many will get across the line and retain their Māori wards.
criterion: Official results of the Māori ward polls held alongside the 2025 local body elections (Local Government NZ / council declarations); true if a substantial share — say a majority — of the councils polling vote to retain their Māori ward, false if the large majority vote to abolish.
reasoning: Of the 42 councils that held binding Māori ward polls with the 2025 local elections, 18 voted to retain and 24 to remove (and nationally the 'keep' vote led, 542,134 / 50.25% vs 467,923 / 43.37%, turnout 73.4%; margins on the 'remove' side were often tiny — Ōtorohanga by 141 votes, Whanganui ~600, Waikato ~900). So 'many will get across the line and retain their Māori wards' did happen — 18 councils did — but the criterion's bar was a substantial share/majority of polling councils retaining, which was not met; equally it was not the 'large majority voting to abolish' that would make the prediction false. Checked the opposite direction too: no source shows a majority of councils retaining, and no source shows a lopsided abolition.

statement: To those councils that installed Māori wards without referendum, they will now have their decision tested at the 2025 local government elections.
criterion: Local government election results for October 2025; true if the affected councils held binding Māori ward polls alongside those elections, false if the poll requirement was repealed, deferred, or not in fact held.
reasoning: The poll requirement was neither repealed nor deferred. Under the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024 (enacted 30 July 2024), councils that had established Māori wards without a poll had to decide by 6 September 2024 whether to hold a binding poll at the 2025 local elections or reverse the decision. Polls ran 9 September to 11 October 2025 at 42 councils (37 territorial, 5 regional) alongside the local elections, and the results are binding for the terms beginning October 2028 (binding for the 2028 and 2031 elections). Partial caveat, not enough to downgrade: two affected councils (Kaipara DC, Upper Hutt CC) took the disestablish/rescind option in 2024 rather than putting it to voters, and Tauranga CC's position was unresolved after the election.

statement: Here’s one more message to our whānau out there—and Andy Foster, thank you for your statistics, and if this Government carries on the way it’s going, every Māori’s going to be forced to get on the Māori roll so we might have to make room for more Māori seats in this House; how exciting is that, how exciting if that was to happen under this Government.
criterion: Electoral Commission Māori electoral option / Māori roll enrolment statistics and the Representation Commission's determination of Māori electorates for the next general election: true if a substantial net shift onto the Māori roll occurs under this Government and the number of Māori electorates rises above seven, false if the number of Māori electorates remains at seven.
reasoning: The criterion is conjunctive and explicitly false if the number of Māori electorates stays at seven. Stats NZ's calculation and the Representation Commission's final determination for the 7 November 2026 general election give 64 general electorates (down from 65) and seven Māori electorates — unchanged — calculated from the 2023 Census and Māori enrolment data as at 1 April 2024. The roll half of the claim did move in her direction: the Māori roll is at a historic high, with about 49,224 more enrolled Māori voters than on the general roll, and 37,919 of 60,736 first-time Māori-descent enrolees (62.4%) between 1 April 2023 and 3 August 2026 chose the Māori roll. That shift was not large enough (and came too late relative to the 1 April 2024 snapshot) to add a seat, so the prediction's substance — more Māori seats in the House — did not eventuate. Settled, not not_yet_due: the electorate count for the next general election is final.

statement: Councils cannot do it by themselves, and they cannot afford to do it even if they are under a CCO, because they won’t be able to get the required level of balance sheet separation.
criterion: LGFA lending policy and credit-rating treatment of water services organisations established under the Local Government (Water Services) legislation, plus Audit NZ/council accounting treatment; true if such organisations are generally not granted debt treatment separate from their shareholding councils, false if they obtain separate ratings/LGFA borrowing outside council debt-to-revenue limits.
reasoning: Split outcome against the criterion, which named both LGFA treatment and rating-agency treatment. LGFA DID grant water CCOs debt treatment separate from their shareholding councils: bespoke covenants tested at the water CCO rather than consolidated into the parent's, and leverage supported to 500% of operating revenue against ~285% for councils — i.e. borrowing outside council debt-to-revenue limits, the criterion's explicit 'false' trigger. The framework is operational: Waikato Waters was the first water CCO onto the LGFA programme, Selwyn Water acceded 8 April 2026, and up to 18 water organisations are expected by 1 July 2027. Watercare went further, separating financially from Auckland Council on 1 July 2025 with its own standalone Moody's rating (Aa3) and a $3.4b bank debt raise. But McAnulty's narrower point survives: external agencies do not accept the separation. S&P includes CCO debt in a council's tax-supported debt where council support is likely, was unconvinced CCOs create enough balance sheet separation, and said moving assets off balance sheet 'may ease the optics, but not the underlying credit risk'; S&P/Fitch consolidate water debt where a council owns >50%. The LGFA structure itself depends on parent-council guarantees and security over water charges, which is why the agencies consolidate. So the borrowing headroom he said was unobtainable was delivered, while the credit-rating separation he warned about was not.

statement: Budget documents, including the Budget at a Glance document, clearly show that the $3.7 billion per annum of tax relief is fully funded from savings and revenue initiatives, so the Government is not borrowing to fund tax relief and it won’t add to inflation.
criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statements and Treasury economic updates through 2025 assessing the fiscal impulse of Budget 2024, together with Stats NZ CPI; true if official assessments find fiscal policy did not add to inflation pressure and annual CPI continued to fall back into the 1–3% band over 2025, false if RBNZ/Treasury attribute added inflation pressure to the Budget 2024 tax package.
reasoning: The criterion's first limb is met, the second is not. No official assessment attributes added inflation pressure to the Budget 2024 tax package: Treasury's BEFU 2024 states the decisions taken through Budget 2024 'will on balance reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure' — tax changes boost aggregate demand but are more than offset by lower spending and lower allowances — and the fiscal impulse is contractionary on average over the forecast period. RBNZ's August 2024 MPS treated the Budget as roughly neutral for monetary policy (contractionary spending against expansionary tax cuts, broadly offsetting), and annual CPI did fall into the 1-3% band in the September 2024 quarter (2.2%). But CPI did not continue falling over 2025: it rose every quarter — 2.5% (Mar), 2.7% (Jun), 3.0% (Sep), 3.1% (Dec 2025, above the band) and 3.1% again in March 2026. RBNZ attributes that to food, household energy and government-set prices such as council rates and rego fees, not to the tax package. Two further caveats on the claim as spoken: Treasury's own BEFU notes that because deficits were larger than at the Half Year Update, fiscal policy 'has been and will continue to make a greater contribution to inflation pressures than previously assessed'; and the 'not borrowing' framing sits against ~$12b more borrowing over four years and a deficit widening to $13.4b. The mechanism he predicted held; the framing is materially overstated.

statement: Sadly, I suspect today is going to be another one of those days.
criterion: Hansard third-reading division record for the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Constituencies) Amendment Bill: true if the bill was read a third time and passed on 30 July 2024, false if it did not pass that day.
reasoning: Judged against the criterion as written (did the bill pass its third reading that day), the record confirms it. The Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Maori Wards and Maori Constituencies) Amendment Bill was read a third time on 30 July 2024, passing 68-55 (National, ACT, NZ First for; Labour, Greens, Te Pati Maori against) — the same margin as its first and second readings — and received royal assent the same day. The Beehive release 'Maori wards Bill passes third reading' confirms the third reading was held on Tuesday 30 July. The quote itself is a vague expression of expectation rather than a testable forecast, so the verdict rests entirely on the pre-registered criterion.

statement: It will stop the violence and prevent the antisocial behaviour of gangs becoming normalised in New Zealand.
criterion: NZ Police recorded violent offence and gang-related offending statistics for the 12 months after the Act's commencement on 21 November 2024, compared with the preceding 12 months; true if gang-related violent offending falls substantially, false if it is flat or rises.
reasoning: Serious violent crime did fall over the period: the NZCVS recorded 147,000 victims of serious violent crime in the 12 months to August 2025, 38,000 fewer than when the coalition took office — but that is a victimisation survey over a two-year span, not the NZ Police recorded gang-related offending series the criterion specifies. The gang-specific half of the criterion is not satisfied: no published police series shows gang-related violent offending falling substantially in the 12 months after 21 November 2024, the government's own one-year release cites only overall NZCVS totals plus enforcement counts (856 insignia charges, 182 patches, 178 firearms, 188 convictions), and the National Gang List reached a record 10,242 in early November 2025, up more than 700 over the year. CNN's one-year field reporting found the local mayor and the Mongrel Mob chapter captain both saying the ban made no real difference to crime, and the Ministry of Justice CEO attributed an increase in drug possession charges partly to the patch ban. The second limb of Goldsmith's claim fares better — patches have largely disappeared from public and police report high compliance, so public normalisation of gang display did reduce. 'Stop the violence' is materially overstated and the gang-specific test is unmet, but the direction of overall violent crime went his way.

statement: There are parts of New Zealand where there are insufficient police and insufficient resources to be able to enforce this law, so it might work in urban areas, but it definitely won’t work in parts of rural New Zealand.
criterion: Police enforcement data and reporting on gang insignia offences and dispersal notices after the Act's commencement; true if rural districts record negligible enforcement alongside substantive urban enforcement, or police/Police Association publicly report inability to enforce in rural areas; false if enforcement activity occurs across rural districts at broadly comparable rates.
reasoning: The predicted urban-works / rural-fails split is the reverse of what enforcement data shows. The districts with the most gang insignia seizures and charges were Bay of Plenty, Wellington and Eastern, and Newsroom's analysis of the ministerial data found those charged were concentrated in regional areas with high gang membership, particularly Bay of Plenty and the East Coast — provincial and rural districts, not the main urban centres. Enforcement operations ran in small rural towns including Opotiki, Kawerau, Whakatane and Hastings. The only evidence in her favour is the first week, when Northland and Southern districts laid zero charges; Northland police attributed that to gang compliance ('signs of good decision making from gangs on the new rules') rather than inability to enforce, and pre-commencement Northern Advocate reporting of rural officers' fears predates the Act. Dispersal notices were indeed barely used — the first nationally was issued in Torbay, Auckland in March 2025, and none had been issued as at February 2025 — but that is a nationwide non-use of one tool, not the rural-specific enforcement failure she predicted. Her resolve-by date of 2026-11-30 has not passed, but roughly 22 months of enforcement reporting is sufficient to settle the criterion as written.

statement: These tools—the non-consorting orders, the dispersal notices, and adding being a gang member to the aggravating factors within sentencing—will disproportionately impact Māori, as we have seen in other jurisdictions around the world where indigenous people bear the brunt of tools like this.
criterion: NZ Police / Ministry of Justice data on the ethnicity of people issued dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, or sentenced with gang membership as an aggravating factor after the Act commenced; true if the Māori share materially exceeds the Māori share of the general population, false if it is at or below population share.
reasoning: Data released by Police Minister Mark Mitchell in answer to a written parliamentary question, reported by Newsroom, shows that of 222 people charged under the new gang laws between 21 November 2024 and 18 February 2025, 184 (83%) were Maori, 22 Pasifika, 13 European and 3 unknown. Maori are about 17.8% of the general population, so the Maori share of those charged exceeds population share by roughly 4.7 times — comfortably 'materially exceeds' under the criterion. Two caveats on the criterion as written: it named dispersal notices, non-consorting orders and the sentencing aggravating factor specifically, and the first two were essentially unused in the period (no dispersal notices or non-consorting charges as at February 2025; the first dispersal notice came in March 2025), so the available ethnicity evidence comes from gang insignia and associated charges rather than those three instruments. Second, the disconfirming check: measured against the gang population rather than the general population the disproportion is much smaller (77% of the National Gang List identified as Maori in 2022 police data), so this partly reflects who is in gangs rather than differential enforcement. But the criterion specifies the general-population comparison, and on that test the claim holds. Broader justice-system figures point the same way (Maori are 37% of people proceeded against by police and 45% of those convicted).

statement: And it’s a senior Government Minister, who will shortly be deputy Prime Minister, who’s doing it; it’s utterly unacceptable.
criterion: The official record of ministerial appointments (DPMC / Governor-General's warrant list): true if David Seymour is sworn in as Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand; false if the handover does not occur and someone else holds the office through the parliamentary term.
reasoning: The criterion named the official appointment record. The Governor-General's own site records that Dame Cindy Kiro signed David Seymour's warrant as Deputy Prime Minister on 31 May 2025 at Government House, Auckland, succeeding Winston Peters under the coalition's mid-term rotation of the office. The handover occurred and no one else held the office for the remainder of the term, so the false branch of the criterion does not apply. Checked for the disconfirming case (rotation cancelled, Peters retaining the role) and found no such evidence. The only imprecision is 'shortly' — the handover came 10 months after the statement — which the criterion does not test.

statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets.
criterion: New Zealand's Greenhouse Gas Inventory and the Climate Change Commission's final accounting against emissions budget 1 (2022–2025) and budget 2 (2026–2030); true if net emissions fall within both budgets, false if either is exceeded.
reasoning: The criterion requires final accounting against BOTH emissions budget 1 (2022-2025) and budget 2 (2026-2030). Budget 2's period runs to 2030, so it cannot be settled. For budget 1, the Climate Change Commission states explicitly in its 2026 emissions reduction monitoring report that it will provide a full assessment using final emissions data only in its end-of-budget report in 2027; the Greenhouse Gas Inventory data for 2025 is not yet final. Interim evidence is mixed rather than decisive: the 2026 report projects budget 1 (290 MtCO2e) likely to be met with a 7.7 MtCO2e buffer, while noting the budget became easier than intended because of GHG Inventory methodology improvements and higher-than-projected forest planting; budget 2 is described as facing significant and increasing risk, with 12.4 MtCO2e of planned reductions at risk and only a projected 3.6 MtCO2e margin, and it is now too late to plant additional forest to close a shortfall. The item's own resolve-by date is 2032-12-31.

statement: Getting rid of the Auckland regional fuel tax, restoring interest deductibility so we can see our rents go down and more housing supply, getting things built in this country—all about delivery.
criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (flow and/or stock measures) and consent/dwelling completion data; true if national rents decline in nominal terms over the two years following the statement, false if rents continue to rise.
reasoning: The criterion turns on whether national rents declined in nominal terms over the two years after 2024-07-31, on Stats NZ's flow and/or stock measures, plus consent/completion data. The two measures diverge. Stock rents (all tenancies, the CPI 'actual rentals for housing' series) rose 3.2% in the year to June 2025 and a further 0.5% to June 2026 — about +3.7% cumulative, so no decline for sitting tenants. Flow rents (new tenancies) did register a genuine nominal fall mid-window: Stats NZ flow rents were 0.1% below year-earlier levels in July 2025 and 0.4% down y/y for three months to September 2025, and the average advertised rent eased from $638/week in 2024 to $627 in 2025, the first annual fall since 2015. But flow rents turned back up, +1.0% y/y by June 2026, with average asking rent $637 in August 2026 versus $628 a year earlier — roughly flat over the full two years rather than declining. Deliberately checked the disconfirming side (whether any national measure shows a sustained two-year fall) and found only regional declines (West Coast -6.5%, Gisborne -5.2%, Southland -4.8%) against a flat-to-up national aggregate. The other limbs of the statement did land: the Auckland regional fuel tax ended 30 June 2024, full interest deductibility was restored from April 2025, and supply rose — 40,581 new dwellings consented in the year to June 2026, up 19%, the first year above 40,000 since 2023. So the prediction is right that rent inflation stopped (slowest stock-rent rise in 25 years) and right on supply, but the specific claim that rents would go down holds only on the new-tenancy measure and only temporarily.

statement: What this means, if this bill passes successfully today, is that these important changes will allow cellar doors to be able to start using the flexibility straight away, just in time for the summer season.
criterion: The commencement provisions and Royal assent date of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Act: true if the amendments were in force before 1 December 2024; false if commencement was deferred past that point.
reasoning: The Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Winery Cellar Door Tasting) Amendment Act 2024 (No 29) received Royal assent on 1 August 2024 and commences on the day after Royal assent, so it was in force from 2 August 2024 — well before the criterion's 1 December 2024 cut-off, and ahead of the summer season. ODT reported on 2 August 2024 that cellar doors 'can now charge for tasting'. No deferred commencement or Order in Council was required; I checked for one and the Act's commencement clause is assent+1 day.

statement: I think the fears of these speakeasys popping up around the place are misplaced.
criterion: Media reporting, District Licensing Committee / Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority decisions, and any amending legislation in the three years after enactment: true if no documented instances of non-winery businesses using the cellar-door tasting provision to operate as de facto bars; false if such cases are documented or the provision is tightened in response to that behaviour.
reasoning: The criterion's observation window is three years from enactment, i.e. to 31 July 2027, which has not passed (today 2026-09-26). Interim evidence points toward the prediction holding: I found no media report, District Licensing Committee or ARLA decision documenting a non-winery using the cellar-door tasting provision to operate as a de facto bar, and the criterion's other falsifying condition — the provision being tightened in response — is contradicted by the subsequent Sale and Supply of Alcohol (Improving Alcohol Regulation) Amendment Bill (2026), which widens the provision to breweries and distilleries via a new 'producer tasting room' category. Ministry of Justice material on that reform records no misuse problem. Absence of reported cases two years in is not yet a full three-year clearance, so the criterion is not settled.

statement: But, as I said in my second reading speech on this bill, that’s fast-approaching to be a $3 billion industry and is growing.
criterion: New Zealand Winegrowers annual reports on wine export/industry value; true if the reported value reaches or exceeds $3 billion by the resolve-by date, false if it remains below $3 billion or declines.
reasoning: The criterion's resolve-by date is 31 December 2027, which has not passed. The named source (New Zealand Winegrowers annual reports) shows export value essentially flat rather than approaching $3b: $2.10b in the FY2025 report (down slightly, US sales off 4% to $762m) and $2.108b in the FY2026 report (volume up to 306.2m litres, value broadly flat; vintage 2026 harvest down ~15%). Reaching $3b by the resolve date would require roughly +40% in about 18 months against three flat years, so present evidence points toward 'wrong', but the window is still open and I am not settling it early.

statement: He hīkoi nui kei te haere. He whawhai nui kei te haere.
criterion: News and police/organiser crowd reporting on national Māori protest marches in the period following the statement; true if a large-scale national hīkoi on Treaty/Māori rights takes place, false if no significant national march eventuates.
reasoning: The Hīkoi mō te Tiriti took place 10–19 November 2024, travelling ~1,060 km from Te Rerenga Wairua to Wellington in opposition to the Treaty Principles Bill. Police estimated ~42,000 people at Parliament on 19 November (an initial 35,000 revised upward during the day); estimates ranged from 22,000 (Peters) to 100,000 (Waititi/Waatea). Media described it as the largest protest Wellington has seen and possibly the largest in NZ history (Spinoff, BBC). The criterion — a large-scale national hīkoi on Treaty/Māori rights in the period after the statement — is met unambiguously, well inside the 2025-12-31 resolve-by date. Checked for the disconfirming case (no significant national march eventuating); nothing supports it. Note the criterion tests only the hīkoi half of the quote, not 'he whawhai nui kei te haere'.

statement: This crowd have upped it to 3.1 percent. It’s probably going to be worse.
criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025 (and Budget 2025 forecasts); true if the OBEGAL deficit exceeds 3.1% of GDP, false if it comes in at or below 3.1%.
reasoning: The referent of '3.1 percent' checks out: Budget 2024 (BEFU, May 2024) forecast a 2024/25 OBEGAL deficit of $13,372m, ≈3.1% of forecast GDP (~$427b). The audited Financial Statements of the Government for the year ended 30 June 2025 report an actual OBEGAL deficit of $13,973m (Fiscal Indicator Analysis — Reconciliation between the Operating Balance, OBEGAL and OBEGALx, p.159). Nominal GDP implied by Table 1 (total expenses $183,502m = 42.1% of GDP; net core Crown debt $182,171m = 41.8%) is ~$435.9b, so the OBEGAL deficit was ~3.2% of GDP — above 3.1%, and $0.6b worse than the Budget 2024 forecast. Under the criterion as written ('true if the OBEGAL deficit exceeds 3.1% of GDP') this resolves correct, but the margin is only 0.1pp. Disconfirming evidence checked: on OBEGALx — the measure the Government adopted as its headline in the Budget Policy Statement 2025 — the deficit was $9.3b, or 2.1% of GDP, well below 3.1%, and it came in $0.9b better than the Budget 2025 forecast. The criterion names OBEGAL, so the verdict follows OBEGAL.

statement: We hope that now, once this passes, shortly, after a few more filibustering speeches, this will pass, finally, and the board members will be able to get on and implement their deed in the way in which they wanted to.
criterion: Hansard and the NZ Parliament bill record for the McLean Institute (Trust Variation) Bill: true if the third reading is agreed and the bill passes on 31 July 2024 (or receives Royal assent shortly after); false if the third reading is not completed that day or the bill is defeated.
reasoning: NZ Parliament's Hansard record contains 'McLean Institute (Trust Variation) Bill — Third Reading' dated 31 July 2024 (HansDeb_20240731), the same sitting day as the statement. The bill passed and became the McLean Institute (Trust Variation) Act 2024 (Private Act No 1), which received Royal assent on 1 August 2024 — the day after — and came into force the day after assent. Both limbs of the criterion (third reading agreed that day; Royal assent shortly after) are satisfied, well within the 2024-09-30 resolve-by date. Checked for the disconfirming case (third reading adjourned/interrupted or the bill defeated); the assent date one day later rules it out.
